requirements.heading: `.IMG` widget images - format (decoded)
requirements.text: Note the widget sets extend to a 1280×1024 tier (`*1024*.IMG`), matching the fifth [MicroANSI resolution record](3.3-microansi-fonts.md#resolution-directory-60-byte-records).

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: Four proportional bitmap fonts for RIPterm's own dialog/menu text, one per video resolution (the 1024×768 file doubles for 1280×1024 - there is no fifth file). These are **not** MicroANSI containers and not the wire-selectable fonts; RIPTERM.DOC's font-directory rule names the extension family ("All font files end in a .CHR, .FNT, or .FF1 file extension", §2.1.4).

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: | File           | Size (bytes) | Internal name (Pascal string)          |

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: | `1024X768.FNT` | 5,573        | `SYS 24 9x13` (same name, larger data) |

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: Decoded header region (all four files):

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text:
```text
0x00  u16   0x1122                  ; magic
0x02  u8    nameLen                 ; Pascal-style length prefix (9, 10, 11, 11)
0x03  char[nameLen] name           ; "sys08 8x8", "SYS16 8x13", "SYS 24 9x13"
…     byte[…]                      ; fixed-size name/style buffer, padded with
                                    ; uninitialized memory (leaked "…ormal" fragments
                                    ; of the string "Normal" appear in 0640X350.FNT)
0x32  char[10] "METAFONTP\0"        ; container tag
0x3C  u32   fileSize                ; equals the file's own byte length in all four
                                    ; files (0x0C8B, 0x0E8B, 0x1045, 0x15C5)
```

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: Beyond the header the structure is **only partially decoded** and is documented here as observed: at ~0x52 a field group reading `20 FF 08 00 08 00 …` is consistent with firstChar = 0x20, lastChar = 0xFF and an 8×8 cell for `sys08` _(interpretation unverified)_; from 0x11C runs an ascending u16 table of 45 entries with a constant stride of 8 (0x240, 0x248, 0x250, … 0x3A0), consistent with per-glyph data offsets for an 8-byte 8×8 glyph; and the file tail contains what appear to be per-character width bytes for the proportional metrics. The internal pointer tables contain values that overlap the table region itself, so the exact base of the glyph-data pointers has not been established; a full decode needs the loader code in `RIPTERM.EXE` disassembled. Implementers do not need this format - it renders no host-visible content - but any future decode should live on this page.

requirements.heading: Per-resolution system `.FNT` fonts (partially decoded)
requirements.text: Evidence that these are the UI fonts: the 2.0 `RIPTERM.EXE` embeds all four filenames (strings `0640X350.FNT` … `1024X768.FNT`) and the internal names match the "sys…" naming; the files are absent from the wire-selectable font systems (BGI `.CHR` by number, FastFont by style name, MicroANSI by text mode).

requirements.heading: Connection Directory Model (delta)
requirements.text: The storage model - a per-host [connection directory](../../glossary.md#client-storage) checked first, the shared [default icon directory](../../glossary.md#client-storage) as fallback, [file override](../../glossary.md#client-storage) semantics, auto-creation, case-insensitive lookup - is established for 1.54 in the [v1.54 connection directory model](../../1.54/techspecs/4.0-connection-directory-model.md) and does **not** change in 2.x. What changes is the **scope of what flows through it**: 2.x adds JPEG images, WAV audio, and host-deliverable `.RIP` scenes to the icon family, and adds a block-transfer mode whose extension table routes each received file automatically. Quotations below are from the RIPterm 2.30 manual (`~/src/rip-tools/artifacts/ripterm-2.30/extracted/RIPTERM.DOC`), the definitive 2.30 client documentation.

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: There was never a separate audio (or image, or scene) directory: the default directory - `ICONS\` historically - houses the entire host-deliverable media family. RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.4 ("Move Files To Their Correct Directories") tabulates it:

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: > There are other categories of files that must also be in the ICONS sub-directory for RIPterm to be able to use them:

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: | File Category            | File Extension       |

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: | RIPscrip v1.x Icon Files | `.ICN` `.MSK` `.HOT` |

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: | RIPscrip v2.x Icon Files | `.BMP` `.BMM` `.BMH` |

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: | Image Files              | `.JPG`               |

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: | Sound Files              | `.WAV`               |

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: | RIPscrip Files           | `.RIP`               |

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: The same section's startup-housekeeping dialog groups them identically ("Icon Files (BMP, ICN, etc.) - Sound Files (WAV) - Image Files (JPG) - RIPscrip Files (RIP) … These files need to be moved into the ICONS directory"), and confirms the per-connection side applies to the whole family:

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: > NOTE: A host system can have its own ICONS directory containing any of the file type listed as valid for an ICONS directory. See Section 5.2 - The Dialing Directory for details on how to set this up.

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: **Fonts are the explicit exception** - they are global client resources, never per-connection:

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: > All font files must be in the FONTS directory. RIPterm does NOT scan the host system directories for font files, and ask to move them. _(RIPTERM.DOC §2.1.4)_

requirements.heading: One directory family for all host media
requirements.text: So a 2.x implementation applies the v1.54 lookup order (connection directory first, then default) to `.BMP`/`.BMM`/`.BMH`, legacy `.ICN`/`.MSK`/`.HOT`, `.JPG`, `.WAV`, and `.RIP` - and resolves fonts (`.CHR`, `.FF1`/`.RFF`, terminal fonts) only from the global font store. The shipped distribution itself models the layout: the 2.30 `ICONS\` directory carries 164 icons (142 `.BMP` + 22 `.BMH`), 7 JPEGs, and 36 RIP scripts side by side - 207 files in all ([asset inventory](../../2.0/assets/icons/README.md)), with `.WAV` listed as valid but none shipped ([audio](3.4-audio.md)).

requirements.heading: The per-connection directory catches the whole family
requirements.text: The dialing-directory entry's "System Dir" field (the RIPterm 2.30 name for the connection directory - the 1.54 manual's DIR field) is documented with the widened scope. RIPTERM.DOC §5.2.1, "System Dir":

requirements.heading: The per-connection directory catches the whole family
requirements.text: > Each entry in the directory can have a sub-directory associated with it. This directory is used when RIPscrip graphics are being viewed on the host. Any icon, RIPscrip, sound, or image files that are sent by the host are automatically placed in the System Dir. This in effect, helps keep your icons separated from each other.

requirements.heading: The per-connection directory catches the whole family
requirements.text: The lookup order and override rule restate the 1.54 model verbatim in behavior:

requirements.heading: The per-connection directory catches the whole family
requirements.text: > If the System Dir field is not blank, RIPterm checks in that directory FIRST for any necessary files. If the files are not found in that sub-directory, RIPterm will check the ICONS\ sub-directory afterward to see if it is there. This facilitates the concept of "file override".

requirements.heading: The per-connection directory catches the whole family
requirements.text: Auto-creation likewise: "You do not need to create the sub-directory yourself. RIPterm will create it for you automatically."

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: New in 2.x, [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) (`!|9<ESC>`, level 9) auto-initiates a file transfer whose `<file_type>` parameter tells the client what it is receiving - a `.RIP` sequence to play, generic files to store, icons, images to display - and, for the batch DYNAMIC modes, hands routing to a **per-extension table**: `RIP`, `BMP`, `BMH`, `BMM`, `JPG` (and `GIF`, v2.A4) are each placed "in proper directory", with ACTIVE DYNAMIC mode additionally playing/displaying `.RIP` and `.JPG` on arrival. The catch-all is explicit:

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: > If you receive file(s) with extensions other than the ones listed above, then no processing will be done on the files other than placing them in the appropriate Host Directory. _(spec v2.A0, [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode))_

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: "Proper directory" resolves through the model above - the connection directory when one is set, else the default - and **not** through the user's ordinary download directory. The manual closes the loop (§5.2.1 NOTE):

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: > Any files received in this mode are automatically placed in the proper System Dir. If no System Dir is defined, then the ICONS\ sub-directory is used as the destination sub-directory. The Download Directory as set in the File Transfer Settings dialog box is not used in this situation as the destination directory.

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: Two implementation footnotes: `.WAV` is absent from the DYNAMIC extension tables (audio arrives via the generic file type and still lands in the media directory per §2.1.4), and the `GIF` rows are speculative spec surface - no shipped 2.x-generation client decodes GIF (see [JPEG images](3.1-jpeg-images.md)). The same delivery path serves [RIP_FILE_QUERY](../ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) update checks and the v2.A4 RIP_FILE_DELETE cleanup of "unneeded JPEG or WAVE files".

requirements.heading: Manual Connect - a connection directory for unlisted hosts
requirements.text: The RIPterm 2.30 client extends the model to hosts that have no dialing-directory entry: the Manual Connect dialog (RIPTERM.DOC §3.3, "Manual Connect Alt-M") prompts for a phone number **and a System Directory** - i.e. an ad-hoc connection directory for the session:

requirements.heading: Manual Connect - a connection directory for unlisted hosts
requirements.text: > You are prompted you to enter the Phone Number to dial, and the name of the System Directory to use for icons and any other files the host needs while you're connected (if any).

requirements.heading: Manual Connect - a connection directory for unlisted hosts
requirements.text: > For the icon directory, enter the name of the directory that contains the icons this system may need, or a directory that you use for temporary files. If you never call this system again, you won't want to keep its icons hanging around on your hard disk taking up space.

requirements.heading: Manual Connect - a connection directory for unlisted hosts
requirements.text: The manual is emphatic that bypassing both mechanisms breaks the model - "if you dial a host by typ[ing] modem commands directly … the correct directory may not be used since RIPterm has no way of knowing which Dialing Directory entry you are calling … You can use the Manual Connect option to dial a host and set the correct System Dir" (§5.2.1). For a modern implementation the takeaway is that **every session has a connection-directory binding** - persistent for known hosts, ad-hoc (and user-discardable, per the temporary-directory advice) for unlisted ones - never an unscoped shared write.

requirements.heading: Implementer summary
requirements.text:
- Resolution order, override semantics, auto-creation, and case-insensitivity: identical to [v1.54](../../1.54/techspecs/4.0-connection-directory-model.md).
- Apply them to the full 2.x media family - icons (both generations), `.JPG`, `.WAV`, `.RIP` - in **one** per-connection namespace plus **one** shared default; do not invent per-type directories.
- Fonts resolve globally only; host-delivered font files are not part of the model.
- Block-mode/UU-encoded deliveries route by extension into that namespace, bypassing any user download directory; unknown extensions are stored, not processed.
- Sessions to unlisted hosts still get a connection directory (the Manual Connect prompt is the historical UI for it); a temporary, discardable directory is an explicitly sanctioned choice.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip 2.00 - Technical Specifications
requirements.text: Original byte-level documentation of the binary file formats and implementation details of the RIPscrip 2.x product family - RIPterm Professional 2.0 through the final **RIPterm 2.30** release, which is treated throughout as the definitive reference. These are original techspecs, not spec conversions: every reverse-engineered claim cites the ALPHA 4 specification section, a recovered document, or an artifact path with observed bytes, and details that could not be verified are marked as such. Note that none of the open-source RIP reference implementations (SyncTERM `ripper.c`, icy_tools, RIPtermJS, PabloDraw) parses the 2.x binary containers documented here - they implement the 1.54 wire language - so these pages are currently the only implementer documentation for these formats.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip 2.00 - Technical Specifications
requirements.text: Chapter numbers align with the [v1.54 techspecs](../../1.54/techspecs/README.md); per the earliest-version rule (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../../CONTRIBUTING.md#technical-specifications-techspecs)) these pages are **deltas** - formats already documented for 1.54 are referenced, not repeated, and the [3.0 techspecs](../../3.0/techspecs/README.md) in turn document only their deltas against these pages. Language semantics live in the companion [language reference](../ripscrip/README.md); shared terminology is defined in the [glossary](../../glossary.md).

requirements.heading: Contents
requirements.text:
- **1. Parsing & wire protocol**
  - **[1.0 2.x Stream Conventions (delta from 1.54)](1.0-stream-conventions-delta.md)** - the SOH-prefixed `\x01|*` reset opener, prologue/epilogue conventions of the shipped 2.x script corpus, line-length and continuation realities, multi-level command parsing notes
- **2. Rendering semantics**

  - **[2.1 Fill Defects in the Shipping Implementation](2.1-fill-defects.md)** - three defects in TeleGrafix's own fill code: pie and chord fills leaking through boundary gaps, the patterned flood brush that was never applied, and the 1.5x seed-stack drop. What to implement instead, and what it means for content targeting era clients
- **3. File formats**
  - **[3.0 Icons (.BMP / .BMM / .BMH)](3.0-icon-formats.md)** - the BMP-family delta from 1.54 icons: full-BMP reality vs the spec's bare DIB, writer conventions, hot and mask roles

  - **[3.5 UI Resources (.FNT / .IMG)](3.5-ui-resources.md)** - the client's per-resolution system fonts and planar widget images (host-invisible; preserved formats)
- **4. Storage & asset delivery** _(delta from v1.54)_

requirements.heading: 1.0 Introduction
requirements.text: [Contents](README.md) · [Next: 1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy ▶](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md)

requirements.heading: 1.0 Introduction
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 1.0 Introduction
requirements.text: The RIPscrip 3.x generation - the completed, shipping form of the 2.0 redesign: its inherited design goals, the 3.0 identity evidence, the revision history and its differences from 1.54 and from the last published specification draft, the state of modern implementations, and the evidence model this reference rests on.

requirements.heading: What RIPscrip 3.x Is
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP; 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: What RIPscrip 3.x Is
requirements.text: RIPscrip ("Remote Imaging Protocol script") is TeleGrafix Communications' text-based graphical scripting language for online services. It encodes vector graphics, bitmapped images, mouse-driven user interfaces, fonts, audio, and terminal text into a stream of 7-bit printable ASCII that can be transmitted over any connection capable of carrying text, and intermixed freely with ordinary TTY and ANSI/VT-102 output. The language is object-oriented rather than raster-oriented: a scene is a sequence of compact drawing commands, not a bitmap.

requirements.heading: What RIPscrip 3.x Is
requirements.text: RIPscrip 3.x is the third generation of the language - the completed form of the 2.0 design that TeleGrafix circulated as the ALPHA specification drafts of 1993-1994, shipped in RIPterm 2.0 and RIPtel 3.1, and described publicly in the December 1996 [RIPscrip 3.0 Technical White Paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt). It adds to the 1.54 baseline: [drawing ports](../../glossary.md) and offscreen bitmaps, [world coordinates](../../glossary.md) and resolution independence, 256-color and direct-RGB color, data tables with protection, a save/restore backup system, outline fonts, JPEG images, WAV audio, a flowed-text column system, and a greatly expanded text-variable/host-command language.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: The founding rationale of the language, in TeleGrafix's own words from the 2.00 specification, applies unchanged to 3.x. As system operators of many bulletin board systems, they had wished for some form of Graphical User Interface for their boards, found every existing solution inadequate in one way or another - incomplete, difficult to implement, too complex, or lacking in graphics development tools - and so decided to write their own graphical script language.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: RIPscrip is a text based script language for displaying online graphics. The script language conforms to 7-bit ASCII, avoiding the use of Extended ASCII characters. This allows transmission over X.25 networks and other carriers that do not support full 8-bit binary transfers easily. RIPscrip allows RIPscrip graphical statements to be mixed with printable ASCII text and [de facto standard] ANSI/VT-100 directives. RIPscrip can dynamically determine what is graphics and what is text and display them appropriately in separate windows (a graphics window and a [text window](../../glossary.md)). And if you must have your own proprietary commands, RIPscrip has room for that too.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: The language's efficiency stems from its compactness and developmental planning. It is entirely Object Oriented instead of Raster Oriented for efficient transmission of data and powerful editing capabilities. Earlier graphical script languages (Avatar and Skypix among others) used special command characters; traditional script languages use English words ("BOX 0,0 100,50") - incredibly bulky when pictures are comprised of hundreds or thousands of individual graphical operations. The main strategy was therefore to make the language as efficient as possible without going completely binary, allowing immediate installation onto any ASCII text-based host system. The unreadability of the language was justified by the limited bandwidth of the era's modems - the language must be compact.

requirements.heading: Design Goals Inherited from the Original Language
requirements.text: The RIPscrip language is made publicly available and is freely licensed by TeleGrafix Communications, Inc. - the language can be used in the creation of other products, but it is not public domain; TeleGrafix maintains the copyright. RIPscrip, RIPaint, RIPdraw, and RIPterm are trademarks of TeleGrafix Communications, Inc., and products that use RIPscrip were required to state so with the trademark statement. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Evidence Basis for This Edition
requirements.text: Unlike the [1.54](../../1.54/ripscrip/README.md) and [2.0](../../2.0/ripscrip/README.md) references, this edition is **not** a conversion of an official document. TeleGrafix's own product list advertised a "RIPscrip 3.0 protocol specification," and the white paper promises a "RIPscrip 3.0 Language Reference," but no such document has ever been located. This edition therefore reconstructs the 3.x language from five converging sources:

requirements.heading: Evidence Basis for This Edition
requirements.text:
1. **The RIPscrip 2.00 ALPHA 4 specification** (December 1994) - the last published TeleGrafix language reference, and the documented baseline that 3.x completes. Where 3.x evidence shows a behavior unchanged from 2.00a4, this edition adapts the [2.0 reference's](../../2.0/ripscrip/README.md) text.
2. **The RIPscrip 3.0 Technical White Paper** (December 1996) - architecture and feature prose, [preserved in full](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt) as the verbatim source document.
3. **RIPSCRIP.HLP recovered strings** - the complete error-message and command-name string table of the RIPSCRIP.DLL 3.0.7 parser, extracted from the RIPtel 3.1 install. It fixes the 3.0 command inventory (~90 `RIP_*` names) and many hard limits. See the [help extraction report](../../3.0/research/riptel-help-extraction.md).
4. **The 116-script RIPtel demo corpus** - TeleGrafix's own demo scenes (22,921 parsed commands, self-documented with 305 prose comments), the primary source for on-the-wire opcodes and syntax. See the [script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md).
5. **SyncTERM's implementation** - `ripper.c` in the Synchronet source tree, the only open-source implementation that answers the version query as RIP 3.0. Cited by line number throughout.

requirements.heading: Evidence Basis for This Edition
requirements.text: Every section in this edition carries an _Evidence:_ line naming which of these sources supports it (`2.00a4`, `WP`, `HLP`, `corpus`, `SyncTERM`); editorial inferences are marked _(hypothesis)_. The full legend is in the [Contents](README.md). Material inherited from the published 2.x specification additionally keeps the spec's own revision markers - `_Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._` lines and `_(v2.A3)_` margin notes - exactly as the 2.0 reference preserves them, so a reader can always tell which ALPHA draft introduced a given behavior.

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:7619)._

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text: "RIPscrip 3.0" is a renaming, not a redesign. The evidence from RIPtel 3.1 (October 1997) is unambiguous:

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text:
- RIPtel 3.1 ships **driver version 3.0.7** of RIPSCRIP.DLL, per its readme.
- The engine's internal file headers self-identify as **"RIPterm v2.0"** - the resource file, the MicroANSI font file, and the help resources all carry `RIPterm v2.0` signatures.
- The RIPTEL.HLP FAQ gives the auto-detect reply as **`RIPSCRIP03000`** (see [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md) for the handshake; SyncTERM answers with the 14-byte `RIPSCRIP030001`).

requirements.heading: The 3.0 Identity
requirements.text: In other words, RIPscrip 3.0 **is** the completed RIPscrip 2.x engine: the 2.00 ALPHA feature set, finished, debugged, and shipped under a new major version number. This is why the 2.00a4 specification remains the structural backbone of this edition.

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP; HLP._

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | Revision | Date | Notes |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 1.54 | 1993 | Last published 1.x specification; the universal interoperability baseline. See the [v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/README.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 2.00 A0-A4 | 1993-Dec 1994 | The five ALPHA drafts of the 2.0 specification, introducing ports, tables, world coordinates, UltraNums, and the rest of the modern architecture. Per-revision change logs are preserved in the [2.0 Introduction](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 2.0 / 2.1 / 2.2 | 1995-1997 | The undocumented "RIPscrip-2" product era: the engine as shipped in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (Jan 1995), 2.20.00 (Nov 19, 1995), 2.20.01 (Nov 28, 1995), and 2.30 (Oct 27, 1997), with **no specification published after ALPHA 4** (no product labeled "2.1" has surfaced). The shipping engine moved past the draft from day one - RIPterm Pro 2.0 already used the 26-character RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE argument block (SHADOW.RIP) rather than ALPHA 4's 13-character form, and v2.20.01 added the icon-transparency flag (`<flags2>` bit 128) to RIP_BUTTON_STYLE, absent from the ALPHA 4 table. Features often credited to "3.x" were already shipping in the January 1995 2.0 release - background **.WAV audio playback** (specified since ALPHA 3; HMI sound drivers), JPEG image display, SVGA/256-color modes, BMP icons, and Atech `.FF1` outline fonts (see the [RIPterm 2.30 font assets](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md)). See [4.5 Audio Files](4.5-audio-files.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 3.0 | 1995-1996 | The 2.x design finalized and renamed. Publicly described by the Dec 1996 white paper; no language reference published. |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 3.0.7 | Oct 1997 | Driver shipped with RIPtel 3.1 "Visual Telnet" - the concrete engine this edition documents. |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: One notable change between the 2.00a4 draft and the shipping 3.0: **GIF support was dropped.** The 2.A4 draft added GIF alongside JPEG for compressed images, but the white paper explains it had to be removed "due to outrageous licensing conditions for the compression algorithm LZW," leaving JPEG as the sole compressed image format (with PNG named as the intended successor). See [the white paper on image formats](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt).

requirements.heading: The 2.0 ALPHA Drafts and the Shipping Engine
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The 2.0 ALPHA Drafts and the Shipping Engine
requirements.text: The 2.00 ALPHA 4 draft ("RIPscrip Graphics Protocol Language, Technical Reference" - Version 2.00, Revision ALPHA 4, December 13th 1994) is the last published specification of any kind, and its ALPHA lineage matters for reading this reference: the drafts were an ongoing culmination revised as A0 through A4, each sub-revision flagged in the document's margin (`_(v2.A3)_`-style markers, preserved throughout this reference on inherited material). The A0 draft defined the resolution-independent coordinate system, 24-bit color encoding, the 36-slot text-window/viewport/style tables, and base-math variation; A1 added the header command, save/restore protection, extended fonts, and UU-encoded data blocks; A2 added command grouping and borderless fills; A3 added drawing ports, WAV audio, and file deletion; A4 reworked text variables, data tables, and the extended text window. The complete per-revision change logs - creator-relevant history for understanding why commands look the way they do - are carried in full in the [2.0 Introduction](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md). The shipping 2.30-generation clients already diverged from the draft in documented places (auto-sense reply, the Base Math opcode, the extended-font layout - see the [2.0 reference's spec-status note](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md)); the 3.0 engine this edition documents inherits those shipping resolutions, not the draft positions.

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; HLP; WP._

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text: Relative to the last published specification draft, the shipping 3.0 engine differs as listed below. Note that these differences accumulated **across the 2.0-2.2 product releases as well as the 3.0 renaming** - with no specifications published after ALPHA 4, the exact release where each feature landed is mostly unrecorded; where evidence exists (e.g. WAV audio and the reworked extended-font-style block shipping in RIPterm Pro 2.0), the relevant section says so.

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text:
- **Adds new drawing primitives** never documented in any spec: skewed ovals (`&`, `-`, `]`, `[`, `+`), the filled oval chord (`_`), markers (`;`), poly-polygons with even-odd fill (`<`), and bounded text (`"`). All are named or demonstrated in TeleGrafix's own NEWCMDS.RIP and companion demos - see [the script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md) and the [2.2 Curves](2.2-curves.md) and [2.3 Shapes & Fills](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md) pages.
- **Resolves the 2.00a4 opcode collision**: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH is level-0 `J` on the wire, leaving `b` to RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW. See [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md).
- **Adds the flowed-text column system** - `1e` column regions, linked multi-column layouts, overflow paging, and RIP_SelectArticle - the "powerful column system" advertised for newspaper-style presentation. See [3.1 Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md).
- **Adds a conditional/macro layer**: `<<IF …>> <<ELSE>> <<ENDIF>>` inline conditionals, `<<NAME>>` macro expansion, the `$&VAR$` dereference form, and `ID=n:` mouse-field identities. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md).
- **Adds web integration**: `$GOTOURL(var)$` launches a URL held in a text variable - 1997-era web/BBS convergence.
- **Formalizes scene header segments** - a per-scene header mechanism carrying data-table flags and entries, coordinate size, direct-RGB bit count, general flags, and a revision code. See [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#scene-header-segments).

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: Everything the 2.00 ALPHAs introduced applies: ports, tables, backup areas, world coordinates, 256/direct-RGB color, base-math variation, and the expanded command levels - the fundamentals chapters of this edition cover each. For interoperating with 1.54-era content, 3.x provides the **`$COMPAT$`** text variable, which sets the environment to RIPscrip 1.54 settings - the classic 640×350 EGA coordinate space and defaults. TeleGrafix's own demo scenes issue `$COMPAT$` before playing 1.54-style artwork (21 uses in the corpus), making it the standard bridge between the two coordinate worlds. The driver also retains 1.54 `.ICN` icon handling, converting old icons to BMP on the fly ("Can't convert RIP 1.54 Icon %s to 2.0 BMP format!").

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: Two backward-compatibility subtleties inherited from the 2.0 redesign are worth restating for authors converting 1.54 material: XOR (and the other raster write modes) now apply to **all** primitives including curves and filled areas, where 1.54 limited XOR to simple line primitives _(v2.A1)_; and the resolution-independent fill model means filled rectangles inset one pixel from their right and bottom coordinate lines, which can open one-pixel gaps in 1.54 artwork replayed under a non-1.54 environment - see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#the-mathematics-of-graphics-and-coordinates) for the full rules _(v2.A1)_. Filled objects' borders, always drawn in 1.54, can be turned off from 2.0 onward (they default on for compatibility) _(v2.A3)_. _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Implementation Status
requirements.text: The practical takeaway: **1.54 is the interoperable floor**, SyncTERM is the only living implementation of anything beyond it, and the original RIPSCRIP.DLL 3.0.7 driver (via RIPtel under emulation) remains the reference behavior for the full language. See [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ansi-sequences-auto-sensing) for version identification details.

requirements.heading: 1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy
requirements.text: The wire-level form of a RIPscrip 3.x command - the `!|` line prefix, the `|` delimiter, the ten [command levels](../../glossary.md), escaping and line continuation - plus the [auto-sense](../../glossary.md) handshake and its 3.x-era `RIPSCRIP03000…` replies, the scene header segments the 3.0 driver formalizes, and the protocol commands that open and close a scene.

requirements.heading: 1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy
requirements.text: _The 3.x syntax is the 2.0 syntax verbatim - the inherited rules below are the published 2.00a4 language definition - overlaid here with the byte-exact behavior of the shipping 3.0.7 driver (observed through the RIPtel corpus) and SyncTERM's 3.0 parser._

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18516-18608)._

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: RIPscrip is organized into 10 levels of graphical commands (low Level-0 to high Level-9). Level-0 commands are the building blocks of RIPscrip. The basic graphics primitives of the system are all Level-0, including the commands Line, Rectangle, Circle, Color, Font, etc. Each level of RIPscrip gets progressively higher-level in concept. For example, Level-1 commands use Mouse Regions, Icons, and Formatted Text Regions.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: The basic syntax rules are as follows:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 1. A RIPscrip command line starts at the beginning of a line of text. A RIPscrip command line moved to the middle of a line of text is treated as literal text. This prevents people inserting mischievous things in teleconference messages, or similar pranks. The only exceptions to this rule is stated below under item 6, "continuation of long lines", and item 12 "alternate RIPscrip starting sequences".

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 2. A RIPscrip command line begins with an exclamation mark `!` (ASCII code 33 decimal).

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 3. Every RIPscrip command is preceded by the universal RIPscrip delimiter, vertical-bar `|` (ASCII code 124 decimal).

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 4. Individual RIPscrip commands may be combined on the same line providing they are separated by the vertical bar delimiter. There are some exceptions to this ([RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode), and a few others). See individual command descriptions for exceptions. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 5. RIPscrip commands or command lines may be split across multiple lines with a backslash `\` (ASCII code 92 decimal) just before each split. This helps RIPscrip commands conform to right margins and escape word wrapping.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: An example:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 6. RIPscrip must allow for normal text to be intermixed with RIPscrip commands. If unrecognized text appears after a RIPscrip command, on the same line, the text is ignored (the command is not ignored). A line that does not begin with `!|` is considered raw text and is routed to the TTY text window (see "8" below).

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 7. RIPscrip makes provisions for multiple Graphical Windows and multiple Text Windows. A Graphical Window is where all RIPscrip graphics appear. A Text Window is where raw text appears. Raw Text includes ANSI color and cursor movement codes (a subset of VT-100 terminal emulation), and possibly other terminal emulations like VT-100, VT-102, VT-220, etc.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 8. The vertical bar (`|`) of a RIPscrip command can be followed by a level number. If the 1st character after (`|`) is a numeric digit (1-9), then that's the RIPscrip Command Level. If the very 1st character is NOT a digit 1-9, then it is the command type character and the command is a Level-0 command. If the 1st character is a digit 1-9, and the second character is also a digit, then that defines a sub-level of a RIPscrip level. For example:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
         !|L     RIPscrip Level-0 Command "L"
        !|1L     RIPscrip Level-1 Command "L"
       !|15L     RIPscrip Level-1, sub-level 5 Command "L"
   ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Each of the above examples are unique commands not to be confused with each other. You may continue the sub-levels up to a maximum level of 9 (e.g., `!|123456789<cmd>`").

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 9. Every RIPscrip command includes a command type character. In Level-0 commands, this character immediately follows the vertical bar. At all other levels, it follows the level digits. The command type character may be any of the following characters:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
   ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
   abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz
   @#$&*()[]{}<>:;'",.?-_=+!
   ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 10. Following the command type character are 0 or more parameters. If the command requires a text-string, it is always the LAST parameter. Numeric parameters DO NOT have any delimiters (commas, dashes, spaces, etc.). A variable width numeric parameter may be used as the last parameter. This allows for maximum efficiency.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: If a RIPscrip command does not have a string parameter, but does have numeric parameters, the last parameter may be shortened to get a bit more efficiency out of it. If the last parameter is more than one digit long and the left-most digits are zeros, they may be omitted. At least one digit must remain though after all of the shortening is done (eg, "0001" can be shortened to "1" but "0000" cannot be shortened to "", it can only be shortened to "0"). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: For example, the [RIP_COLOR](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_color) command, used to set the current drawing color, requires one parameter - a color number. If we were going to set color 1 (usually dark blue), then the command would appear formally as follows: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Under this shortening clause, you could omit the "0" and make the command appear like this: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: This allows you to shave one byte off of the command. If you were trying to set color number zero (normally black), then you could still shorten the parameter, but you still have to leave at least one digit there (0), so the command would appear like this: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: There is an additional optimization that can be used for commands that have no string parameter, and have a reserved parameter as the LAST parameter for that command. In this case, the reserved parameter may be omitted completely, and the value should be assumed to be zero (`0'). Please take note that the previous paragraphs still apply! You can omit the reserved parameter AND shorten the last transmitted parameter so as to squeeze out as many unnecessary characters from the command as possible. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Numbers are normally represented in base-36 (unless altered by a RIPscrip command). This compacts numbers down to roughly 3/5 of their decimal form. This numbering system, technically called "Hexa-Tri-Decimal" or "MegaNums" is unlike Hexadecimal which uses 0-9 and A-F. MegaNums take advantage of the entire alphabet, using characters 0-9 and A-Z. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: See [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md) about Base Math variations. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 11. An exclamation mark (`!`) or vertical bar (`|`) character can appear in a RIPscrip text parameter by preceding it with a backslash (`\`). This is known as "quoting" a special character. A literal backslash is represented with a double-backslash (`\\`). Also, in some situations you need to quote specific characters so that they are not misinterpretted. For example, in a button host string, the characters `[`, `]`, `(`, and `$` are used as special host command characters and will need to be quoted (eg, `\[`, `\]`, `\(` and `\$` respectively). See rule #14 below for more details on quoting these special sequences. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 12. A RIPscrip sequence CAN begin in a column other than column #0, if the exclamation mark prefix is replaced with a Ctrl-A (Start Of Header [SOH] - ASCII character 1) character, or Ctrl-B (STX - ASCII character 2) character. Since 99.9% of all BBS' do not allow users to enter most control characters, users will be unable to begin RIPscrip sequences in the middle of a command line. Only the host should be able to do this. This prevents people from cluttering teleconference, or other areas of a host with spurious RIPscrip sequences.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Let's take an example, where we have a piece of raw text and then a RIPscrip command immediately following the text before the carriage return (in this example `<STX>` stands for the STX character): _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    This is raw text<STX>|c01|@1010hello world
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: In the above example, the text "This is raw text" would be sent to the active text window, then the RIPscrip sequences would be processed - set the color to blue (01), then print the text "hello world" on the screen at (10,10) in meganums or (36,36) in decimal. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 13. If the last couple of bytes on a RIPscrip text line are backslashes, special care must be taken to make sure that they are not interpreted as a line-continuation. If a literal backslash is desired as the last position on the line, it must be specified as a double-backslash (eg, `\\`). If a line-continuation is used then there would have to be three backslashes used on the line as in the following example: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    !|@2233this is a text line with a literal \\\
    used in the message
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: This would text output at (22,33) [meganum] the message: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    this is a text line with a literal \used in the message
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 14. Some character sequences in text parameter strings can be misinterpreted as RIPscrip command sequences (eg, `$`, `<>`, `((`, `))`, `[`, `]`, `[]`, etc). To avoid syntax confusion these sequences can be "escaped" to indicate that they are actually literal sequences, not to be confused with a RIPscrip command sequence identifier. For example, the sequence: _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    $Name$
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: would normally be interpreted as a RIPscrip text variable that requires the user's response. If however, you wanted this sequence to be interpretted as literal text, you should perform the following escape sequences:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
    \$Name\$
    ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: This makes it so a RIPscrip terminal doesn't misinterpret the dollar signs as text variable delimiters.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 15. Extraneous information. If too much data is encountered for a particular RIPscrip command, or too little information is found (aside from a short last parameter) then the command is considered "hopelessly corrupted" and discarded. The RIPscrip parser should synchronize to the next vertical bar delimiter to begin the next command. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Command Syntax - Parser-Exact Behavior
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM; corpus._

requirements.heading: Command Syntax - Parser-Exact Behavior
requirements.text: The rules above are the published language definition. The subsections below overlay the byte-exact behavior of SyncTERM's 3.0 parser (`cb_feed`, ripper.c:18516-18608) and the shipping driver's observed tolerance in the RIPtel corpus - the precision an implementer or a careful author needs.

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 1-2, 12; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18189-18202)._

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: Three bytes can begin a RIP command sequence:

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text:
- **`!`** (exclamation mark, 33) - the standard introducer, valid **only at the beginning of a line**. SyncTERM implements "beginning of line" precisely: the previously emitted byte must be NUL, CR, LF, or VT (ripper.c:18198-18200), _or_ the text cursor must already sit at column 1 - e.g. placed there by an ANSI cursor-position sequence (ripper.c:18201, rationale comment 18180-18188). The mid-line restriction exists so users can't inject RIP sequences into teleconference text.
- **SOH** (Ctrl-A, `0x01`) and **STX** (Ctrl-B, `0x02`) - accepted **anywhere** in the stream (ripper.c:18196-18197). Since BBSes strip control characters from user input, only the host can start a mid-line sequence.

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: An introducer immediately preceded by `\` is escaped into literal text (ripper.c:18194-18195). Every introducer must be followed by **`|`** (vertical bar, 124) to form a command header; if the next byte is anything else, the parser takes the **"un-rip" fallback** (ripper.c:18540-18554): both the bogus introducer and the following byte are re-emitted to the text window and parsing resets - stray `!` characters in ordinary text render normally.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 8; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18275-18281)._

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: After the header `|` (or a chaining `|`), an optional level digit `1`-`9` selects the command level, and an optional second digit `1`-`9` a sublevel. Three consequences the code makes exact:

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text:
- **`0` is never a level digit.** `!|0X` is a _level-0 command whose command character is `0`_ - not "level 0, command X". Level 0 is reached by writing no level digit at all.
- Nesting stops at two digits in SyncTERM's parser (level + sublevel), although the 2.00a4 grammar reserves up to nine level digits (`!|123456789<cmd>`).
- The command character is whatever single byte follows the level digits, and **need not be printable**: ESC (`0x1B`) is a real command character (`!|1<ESC>` RIP_QUERY, `!|9<ESC>` RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE) (ripper.c:18289).

requirements.heading: Parameters
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 9-10._

requirements.heading: Parameters
requirements.text: Zero or more parameters follow the command character, with no delimiters between numeric fields. Numeric parameters are fixed-width [MegaNums or UltraNums](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md) per the current base math. A text parameter, if present, is always last. The last numeric parameter may be shortened by dropping leading zeros (`!|c01` → `!|c1`; at least one digit must remain), and a trailing _reserved_ parameter may be omitted entirely (assumed `0`).

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 4-5, 13; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18556-18607); corpus._

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text:
- **`|` chains commands**: a bare `|` dispatches the buffered command and starts the next on the same line (ripper.c:18583-18602). Some commands ([RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) and a few others) must stand alone.
- **CR dispatches** the pending command and returns the parser to idle (ripper.c:18561-18580) - _unless_ the buffer ends in an **odd** number of backslashes, in which case the final `\` is stripped and the command continues on the next physical line (ripper.c:18563-18576). This is the classic line-continuation rule for keeping long commands inside right margins; a literal backslash at end-of-line must be doubled (`\\`), and continuation after a literal backslash needs three (`\\\`).
- **LF is unconditionally swallowed** mid-command (ripper.c:18557-18559) - which is why the CRLF line endings throughout the RIPtel corpus (the 1.54 spec said bare CR) parse identically.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 11, 14; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18204-18227)._

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: `!` and `|` appear literally in text parameters by quoting with backslash (`\!`, `\|`); a literal backslash is `\\`. SyncTERM's preprocessor (`cb_unescape`) makes `\|` a literal pipe in arguments (held as a placeholder through argument slicing, ripper.c:18291-18298) and collapses `\X` to `X` for any other character; at feed time an odd number of trailing backslashes before a `|` marks that pipe as data, not a command boundary (ripper.c:18583-18596). Host-command and text-variable metacharacters inside text parameters - `$`, `[`, `]`, `(`, `)` - must likewise be quoted (`\$Name\$`) to avoid interpretation.

requirements.heading: Raw Text and Error Handling
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 6, 15; corpus._

requirements.heading: Raw Text and Error Handling
requirements.text: A line that does not begin with an introducer is raw text, routed to the current [text window](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) (or consumed as column content inside a flowed-text region - see [3.1 Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md)). Unrecognized text _after_ a complete command on the same line is ignored - the command still executes. A command with too much or too little data is "hopelessly corrupted" and discarded; the parser resynchronizes at the next `|`.

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: As previously described, RIPscrip is composed of ten different levels of commands. The distribution of commands over different levels is done in a rather organized fashion based on command type. Each level of command in general, is progressively higher level in concept. For example, level 0 commands are the most basic building blocks of RIPscrip (eg, graphical primitives, protocol setup, etc). Level one commands are simple user interface objects. Level 2 commands are higher level still in that they deal with context swapping issues. At the highest level, level-9, we deal with binary transfer modes like file transfer protocols, etc. A more formal definition of the currently used levels are:

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | Level | Description |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 0 | Lowest-level RIPscrip primitives. Simple graphical drawing primitives, low-level RIPscrip protocol mode settings, etc. |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 1 | Simple user interface objects (buttons, mouse fields, clipboard slots, formatted text regions). This level consolidates one or more simple building blocks from level 0 and also introduces more abstract user interface objects (eg, mouse fields). |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 2 | Basic context switching information (switching styles, and other window or context senstive commands. |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 3 | Basic time-related commands (baud rate emulation and delay commands). |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 4 | Open for future development |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 5 | Open for future development |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 6 | Open for future development |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 7 | Open for future development |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 8 | Open for future development |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 9 | Binary related data transfer functions (ie, block protocol modes, UU-Encoding, etc). |

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: Each level/character pair is a unique command: `!|L`, `!|1L`, and `!|15L` are three different commands. The consolidated 3.x inventory across all levels is [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md).

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (RIPTEL.HLP FAQ); SyncTERM (ripper.c:7619, 18437-18470)._

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: RIPscrip predominantly uses non-ANSI command sequences. In a couple of situations though, an ANSI-like sequence is allowed to perform a specific function. There are currently four separate escape sequences defined in the RIPscrip protocol to perform various actions. They are as follows:

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | Sequence | Effect |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[!` | Query RIPscrip version - the terminal replies with its version string (below) |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[0!` | Same as `ESC[!` |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[1!` | Disable all RIPscrip processing (sequences render as raw text) |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[2!` | Enable RIPscrip processing |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: Hosts auto-sense a RIP terminal by sending the query at login and sniffing for the reply; a non-RIP terminal ignores the sequence. The reply format is the literal text `RIPSCRIP` followed by version digits in **`MMmmrr`** form (2-digit major, minor, revision), optionally followed by a 2-character **`pp`** vendor/patch suffix (vendor code + sub-version, per the 1.54 convention - for v1.54, RIPterm with Vendor Code "1" returned `RIPSCRIP015410`). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: Valid Vendor Codes were:

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | CODE | VENDOR                                              |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | 0    | Generic RIPscrip terminal (vendor unknown)          |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | 1    | RIPterm (from TeleGrafix Communications)            |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | 2    | Qmodem Pro (from Mustang Software, Inc)             |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | 3    | deltaComm Development (Telix) _(v2.A1)_             |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | 4    | Qmodem Pro for Windows (Mustang Software) _(v2.A1)_ |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** This method of vendor determination is obsolete in RIPscrip 2.0 and later. You still use this escape sequence to detect RIPscrip capability, but to determine the specific terminal program or manufacturer, use the `$TERMINFO()$` text variable. To determine specific capabilities of the terminal, use the `$IFS()$` text variable (Is Function Supported). To determine the current language that the terminal is running in, use the `$LANGUAGE$` text variable (see [5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md)). _(v2.A1, revised v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The 3.x-Era Replies
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP (RIPTEL.HLP FAQ); SyncTERM (ripper.c:7619, 18437-18470)._

requirements.heading: The 3.x-Era Replies
requirements.text: The 3.x-era replies on record:

requirements.heading: The 3.x-Era Replies
requirements.text:
- **`RIPSCRIP03000`** - the reply RIPtel's own FAQ documents (RIPTEL.HLP: the string appears on the login line when MajorBBS/WorldGroup hosts time out waiting for it; servers allow only ~1-1.5 s). Read as major 03, minor 00, revision 0 - 13 bytes, without the vendor suffix.
- **`RIPSCRIP030001`** - SyncTERM's 14-byte reply (`ripver[]` at ripper.c:7619, sent without CR/LF via `conn_send(…, 14, 1000)` at ripper.c:18447): major 03, minor 00, revision 01. For comparison, its RIPv1 reply is `RIPSCRIP015410` (v1.54, vendor 1, sub-rev 0).

requirements.heading: The 3.x-Era Replies
requirements.text: Host software probing for "any RIP 3.0" should therefore match on the prefix `RIPSCRIP03` rather than a fixed length. The same string is available to host scripts as the **`$RIPVER$`** text variable (RIPTEL.HLP's own example for it is `RIPSCRIP015300`).

requirements.heading: The 3.x-Era Replies
requirements.text: Two behavioral notes from SyncTERM. First, its `ESC[1!` handling is a one-way door - once disabled, its parser never sees the `ESC[2!` that should re-enable it (ripper.c:18453-18459). **This is a SyncTERM bug, not a protocol delineation**: the language defines disable (`ESC[1!`) and enable (`ESC[2!`) as a reversible pair, and a conforming terminal must resume RIPscrip processing when it receives `ESC[2!`. Do not treat SyncTERM's inability to restart RIP processing as license to drop the feature - implementations should keep watching for `ESC[2!` while disabled. Second, the RIP version SyncTERM answers with is per-BBS _configuration_, not negotiated from the wire.

requirements.heading: The 3.x-Era Replies
requirements.text: > **Editor's note - the RIPterm 2.30 product era:** every shipping 2.30-generation RIPterm binary - Professional 2.0, 2.20.01, and 2.30 - carried the same literal auto-sense response string `RIPSCRIP020000`: version 02.00 with the trailing vendor/sub-version digits zeroed. The reported language level never advanced past 2.00.00 through the end of the RIPterm line in October 1997, even as the product versions did; the jump to `RIPSCRIP03000…` arrives with the RIPtel-era 3.0 driver documented here (see [1.0 Introduction](1.0-introduction.md#the-30-identity)).

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text: The 3.0 engine formalizes the 2.A1 [RIP_HEADER](#rip_header) idea into **scene header segments** - a structured header at the start of a scene that declares the environment the scene expects, so the terminal can validate and configure before drawing. RIPSCRIP.HLP's error-string family maps its contents:

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text:
- **Per-table segments** carrying flags and entry numbers for each object class: button style, graphics style, drawing port, text window, color palette, environment, mouse field, **audio**, and graphics screen (see [7.1 Data Tables](7.1-data-tables.md)).
- An **environment segment** carrying the coordinate size ("Invalid coordinate size in environment header segment") and the direct-RGB bit count ("Invalid direct RGB bit count in environment header segment").
- **General header flags** ("Invalid general header flags").
- A **revision code** identifying the RIPscrip revision of the code that follows ("Invalid RIPscrip revision code").

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text: No wire-format example of a header segment has been recovered - the RIPtel demos use the explicit prologue commands instead (below) - so the segment encoding itself remains undocumented _(hypothesis: a parameterized RIP_HEADER-style command, per the 2.A1 design)_.

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text: The 116 TeleGrafix-authored RIPtel demo scripts are the best available picture of real 3.x on the wire:

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text:
- **SOH marks scene start.** 111 of 116 files begin their _first_ command line with SOH + `|`, then use `!|` for every subsequent line - SOH apparently flags start-of-scene to the 3.0 stream parser, while `!|` remains the 1.54-compatible introducer. (Three files invert the pattern, nearly all-SOH.)
- **The standard prologue** opens 90+ files: `J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO` - base math 36, 2-digit coordinates, 8-bit palette color mode, 1280×960 world frame (see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md)).
- **Trailing text after fixed-length arguments is tolerated** and used as inline commentary - the driver stops reading once the fixed fields are consumed: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960`. Chained `!|command|! comment` forms (the `!` comment opcode) are ubiquitous.
- **Typo tolerance is high.** A missing `!` introducer (`|1<ESC>0000$COMPAT$`, CURVES.RIP), separator lines `!|----` that accidentally parse as the `-` opcode with dash arguments (`-` reads as MegaNum 0), and bare `!|` no-op lines all pass through the shipping driver without visible failure. Robust parsers should degrade as gracefully.
- **Line endings are CRLF**, with `\` continuation across physical lines for long vertex lists (POLYPOLY.RIP). See [6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files](6.0-writing-rip-files.md) for authoring conventions.

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (90+ files)._

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: Nearly every TeleGrafix scene opens with the same chained sequence:

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: | Piece | Command | Meaning |

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: | `!\|` | - | line introducer + command delimiter |

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: | `J10` | [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math) | base math ← 36 (`10` base-36 = 36): MegaNums |

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: | `\|n2000` | [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size) | coordinates ← 2-digit fields |

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: | `\|M08` | [RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_set_color_mode) | 8-bit palette color mode |

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: | `\|fZKQO` | [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) | world frame ← 1280×960 (`ZK`=1280, `QO`=960) |

requirements.heading: The standard prologue, decoded
requirements.text: The order matters: the scene pins its numeric conventions _before_ any coordinate-bearing command arrives.

requirements.heading: A real scene opening (DRAGON.RIP)
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (DRAGON.RIP; annotations editorial)._

requirements.heading: A real scene opening (DRAGON.RIP)
requirements.text:
```text
\x01|!                                    SOH scene-start + comment (no text)
!|*                                       RIP_RESET_WINDOWS - clean slate
!|1\x1b0000$-=NO_WIPES=Disabled$          query cmd sets variable NO_WIPES=Disabled
!|1\x1b0000$SBAROFF$                      hide the status bar
!|w0000000000                             RIP_TEXT_WINDOW - zero-size (off)
\x01|1\x1b0000$DTW$                       disable text window
\x01|1\x1b0000$COFF$                      cursor off
\x01|1\x1b0000$RESET(OVERFLOW)$           clear column-overflow state
\x01|n2000                                2-digit coordinates
\x01|M08                                  8-bit palette mode
\x01|W00                                  RIP_WRITE_MODE - COPY
\x01|fZKQO                                world frame 1280x960
\x01|2P10000ZKQO00030000                  RIP_DEFINE_PORT - offscreen port 1, 1280x960
\x01|J10                                  base math 36 (MegaNums)
\x01|1b0000HS0Y000G000000STRIP6.BMP       RIP_LOAD_BITMAP at (0,0), 640x34 region
\x01|c0F                                  draw color 15
\x01|y0000BW0X040000001a1a000000dixon     extended font style - outline font "dixon"
```

requirements.heading: A real scene opening (DRAGON.RIP)
requirements.text: (`\x01` = SOH, `\x1b` = ESC; both are literal single bytes on the wire. Lines end CRLF. Note the mixed introducers - SOH mid-scene is legal - and `$…$` terminal-control variables doing setup work alongside drawing commands.)

requirements.heading: Chaining, escaping, and continuation
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18204-18232, 18563-18576)._

requirements.heading: Chaining, escaping, and continuation
requirements.text:
```text
!|c0F|=00000001|S010F                     three commands, one line: color,
                                          line style, fill style
!|@0A0ASay \| for a pipe                  \| = literal pipe inside a text
                                          parameter (not a delimiter)
!|p04000A000A0M0M2S0M2S000A00\            RIP_FILL_POLYGON with the vertex
0A                                        list continued across lines: odd
                                          trailing backslash before CR
!|! any prose after the bang-pipe-bang    comment command - ignored by the

```

requirements.text: _(Constructed example - not from the corpus; commands and field widths follow the entries in this reference.)_

!|c0F|=00000001|S010F                     white pen, solid 1px line, solid fill
!|K05052S1U                               filled rectangle (5,5)-(100,66)
