requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: _Evidence: editorial; format follows 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: The chapters of this reference detail the reconstructed RIPscrip 3.x command set (the consolidated index is [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md)). Each command has these aspects:

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **SYMBOL** - the symbolic constant that is referenced in RIPscrip documents. This is the universal name for the command. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FUNCTION** - A short description of the command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **LEVEL** - The Command Level. Sub-levels (if any) are represented with decimal points (eg, 1.3.5 for Level-1, Sub-level 3, Sub-Sub-level 5). This is for discussion purposes only. The decimal points are never part of the actual command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **COMMAND** - The character identifying the command

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **ARGUMENTS** - The arguments or parameters for the command. Commands that do not require any parameters after the command type character are shown here as "\<none\>". Each parameter is shown in the order it appears in the command, and is represented by a name. If a parameter is numeric, it is followed by a width specifier indicating how many meganum or ultranum digits the parameter consists of (e.g., ":2" means a 2-digit number, or a value between 0 and 1295 for meganums, or 0 and 4095 for ultranums). If a parameter does not have a width specifier, it is by default a text parameter, and should be the last parameter of the command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If a command is variable length (see [POLYGON](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_polygon)), then it will appear with an ellipe (...), meaning that the command repeats the specific parameters a variable number of times. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If the parameter is a variable-width coordinate that can be set by the [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size), or via the [RIP_HEADER](#rip_header) commands, then the parameter will be followed by a coordinate specifier (e.g., ":XY" means that the parameter is a variable-width coordinate). _(v2.A2, revised v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If the parameter is a color parameter whose format is determined by the [RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_set_color_mode) command, (ie, the parameter switches between "color mapping mode" or "direct RGB encoding" mode), then a color mode specifier will come after the parameter name (e.g., ":CM" indicates this parameter uses the current color mode). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: Some commands do not allow color parameters to switch modes based on RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE. These exceptional commands document these exceptions and the :CM specifier will not be present. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FORMAT** - This represents the format of the command, with the starting `!|`, the level digits, the command type character, and the parameter list, with the parameter names in angle brackets. (These parameters are spaced apart, but these spaces never appear in the physical commands.)

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **EXAMPLE** - An actual example of the RIPscrip command. In this reconstructed edition, examples are drawn from the RIPtel corpus wherever one exists.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **DRAW COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Drawing Color.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **BACK COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses (or affects) the current background pen drawing color. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **LINE STYLE** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Line Style Pattern.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FILL COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Fill Color.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FILL PATRN** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Fill Pattern.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **WRITE MODE** - If YES, then this command will take advantage of the current Write Mode (eg, COPY, or XOR).

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FONT STYLE** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Font Style/size/orientation. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **VIEWPORT** - If YES, then this command adheres to the graphical viewport (draws inside it). Any RIPscrip command that adheres to the graphical viewport will be drawn (when received) only if the viewport is activated. If the viewport is deactivated, then the command is parsed, but completely ignored. _(v1.54, revised v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **USES PORT** - If YES, then this command adheres to, is affected by, or modifies the definition of a [port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **BASE MATH** - Indicates which base math this command responds to. The possible settings are N/A (does not apply), Meganums (uses meganums ONLY), Ultranums (uses Ultranums ONLY), and Current (uses current base math setting as set by either RIP_HEADER or [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math)). _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: In addition - because this is a reconstructed edition - every command entry carries an **_Evidence:_** line naming the sources for that command: `2.00a4`, `HLP` (the RIP_* name in the 3.0.7 inventory), `corpus` (with file names), and/or `SyncTERM` (with ripper.c line cites). Commands attested only by a single source, and argument layouts inferred rather than documented, are flagged in the entry.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (header-segment error strings - see [Scene Header Segments](#scene-header-segments)) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: _Header command for subsequent RIPscrip sequence_

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `h`                        |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `revision:2 flags:4 res:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|h <revision> <flags> <res>` **Example:** `!|h010A0100`

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Port, Base Math (Ultranums only)

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: This command was introduced in RIPscrip 2.0. It is specifically designed with two purposes in mind. First, it is defined to provide a consistent method for determining the revision of RIPscrip that is to follow in subsequent RIPscrip code (up to a [RIP_NO_MORE](#rip_no_more) command). Second, it provides a way of performing many different kinds of reset operations (if any) in one command - much more flexible than the older [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command. This command has the ability to set many states and situations for subsequent RIPscrip code (whether MegaNums are to be used, or UltraNums, what gets reset and what doesn't, etc).

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The `<revision>` code of this command defines the revision of RIPscrip code that is to follow. The valid defined revisions are as follows:

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | Revision | Description           |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 00       | RIPscrip 1.54.00 code |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 01       | RIPscrip 2.00.00 code |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The real heart of this command is the `<flags>` parameter. This field defines all of the attributes of the header command other then the revision field. The possible values which may be combined in this parameter (OR'ed together) are as follows:

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | Value | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 0 | Do nothing |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 1 | Use MegaNums for subsequent RIPscrip code |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 2 * | Use UltraNums for subsequent RIPscrip code |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 4 * | Auto-set world coordinate frame |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 8 | Set world frame to 640x350 (backward compatible mode). NOTE: This flag should be used in revision "00" code. |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 16 | Perform a hard reset - this resets everything. This includes clearing all data backup area, even if entries are protected. The entry is protected, then cleared. |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 32 * | This performs a soft reset. The screen is cleared, all viewports are reset and viewport slot 0 is made full screen, text windows are deleted and text window 0 is made full screen. All resident queries are deleted, graphical style slots are erased as are the button style slots. This is identical in nature to the RIP_RESET_WINDOWS. |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 64 | Clears port data table |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 128 | Clears resident queries only |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 256 | Clears mouse/button definitions only |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 512 | Clears all data save slots and resets stack pointers |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 1024 | Clears all base save areas |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 2048 | Clears and stops any playing sound/music |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 4096 | Clears the screen to background color (usually black) |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 8192 | Resets all viewports of all drawing ports to the full size of their respective ports (no erasing performed). |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 16384 | Clears all text window data table entries and makes entry 0 full screen in default text (no window clearing performed) |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 32768 | Clears all graphical style data table entries |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 65536 | Clears all button style data table entries |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 131072 | Resets all palette data table entries to defaults |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 262144 | All existing viewports are erased. If combined with flag 8192, then this is done first, then flag 8192 is executed. |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 524288 | All existing text windows are erased. If combined with flag 16384, then this is done first, then flag 16384 is executed. |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | 1048576 * | Disables all mouse/keyboard input (discards) until a RIP_NO_MORE command is encountered thus signifying the end of a RIPscrip sequence. This prevents the user from accidentally interrupting the data stream with keyboard activity. The mouse cursor should be changed to something like an hourglass or disabled entirely. If no RIP_NO_MORE is found and no RIPscrip or raw text data is being received, then a RIP_NO_MORE should be assumed after some suitable timeout (up to the developer's discretion). |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: **NOTE:** Items marked with a `*` are recommended defaults.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: As you can see, the `<flags>` parameter allows you to reset only segments of things that you want to reset giving you considerable flexibility in starting off RIPscrip scenes.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: Most of the flag options are fairly self-explanatory. Some mention should be made to several of them. Note that the flags described above are grouped into logically related flag groups. Flags 1 and 2 are mutually exlusive meaning only "1" or "2" may be used, but not both. Choosing either flag 1 or 2 resets coordinate sizes to 2 bytes.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: Flag 4 requires some explanation. Auto-setting the world coordinate frame (WCF) will auto-set the world coordinate frame to a set of high-resolution world coordinates. The exact choices of coordinates chosen depend on whether you specified UltraNums or MegaNums. If you specify flag 4, then you must specify either flag 1 or flag 2 to determine which base math to use. MegaNums set the width of the world coordinate frame to 1280, and the WCF height to 960. This provides for a square world frame pixels. If UltraNums are used, then the width of the world frame is set to 4096 and the height is set to 3072. Again, this provides for square world frame pixels. If you physically need a larger world frame then you either need to alter the base math setting explicitly or alter the X/Y coordinate parameter size (see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md)).

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: Most video displays have a 4:3 width to height pixel ratio. For example, 640x480 is 4:3, 1024x768 is 4:3, etc. Note that 1280x1024 is NOT a 4:3 ratio (the 4:3 ratio for 1280 would be 1280x960.) _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The Hard Reset option (flag 16) will perform a complete reset of the RIPscrip environment. This is equivalent to choosing flags 64 through 131072. In effect, this clears everything including data save slots and the base save areas.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The Soft Reset option (flag 32) will perform a reset that is identical in nature to the RIP_RESET_WINDOWS reset. This is equivalent to choosing flags 1, 8, 64, 128, and 2048 through 131072. This doesn't delete any data save slots or base save areas, doesn't intentionally affect the world frame except that it sets it to 640x350, and chooses MegaNums as the numbers of choice.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: **NOTE:** This command ALWAYS sets the mouse cursor back to the default arrow pointer unless the "disable mouse input" flag is used whereas the mouse will be temporarily changed to an hourglass or disabled entirely until a RIP_NO_MORE. After this, then the pointer will be reset back to an arrow. See [RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_set_mouse_cursor) for details.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: **3.x status:** the 3.0 driver clearly retains and extends this mechanism even though the demo corpus (local scene files) never sends the command itself: RIPSCRIP.HLP's error strings describe the **header segments** listed [above](#scene-header-segments), carrying flags plus entry numbers for the object tables plus environment settings. The demos achieve the same effect piecewise with `!|*` plus the `J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO` prologue. _Evidence: HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus (287 uses in 95 files); SyncTERM (ripper.c:13315)._

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: _End of RIPscrip Scene_

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `#`      |

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | \<none\> |

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** none

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: This command indicates that RIPscrip commands are complete. This allows the terminal program to activate Mouse Regions, or respond to queued up Mouse Clicks without disturbing the natural flow of the script transmission.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: For noise-immunity, the Host should transmit three or more RIP_NO_MORE command consecutively to make sure the message gets to the terminal. The terminal should also time-out if no data is received for a while, and assume RIP_NO_MORE.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: The actual duration of the "time-out" is entirely up to the implementor of their terminal program. A good recommended setting would be at least an entire second or more after the receipt of the last RIPscrip command. Raw ASCII/ANSI text does not contribute to the time-out in any way. Only an actual RIPscrip command could cause the time-out counter to be reset (thus starting the time-out countdown all over again). Timing-out is not a pre-requisite to supporting RIPscrip. It is a highly desirable feature to do this, but it is not required. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: This command also re-activates user input previously disabled with a [RIP_HEADER](#rip_header) command. This is useful to prevent the user from clicking on buttons before the scene is completely drawn. See the RIP_HEADER command for more details on this mode of operation. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: Nearly every RIPtel demo scene ends with one (287 uses in 95 of 116 files). _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A2._

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus (1,683 comment commands across the RIPtel demos, 305 with prose)._

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: _Put in a comment as part of a RIPscrip sequence_

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `!`         |

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `string...` |

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|!This is a comment` **Example:** `!|!Show RIP_SKEWED_OVAL`

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (N/A)

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: A comment may be embedded inside a RIPscrip file. A comment is one line or longer in length. A comment is a special case of a RIPscrip command letter. In this case, it is the command letter "!". If a "!" is encountered right after a "!|", a "SOH |" or an "STX |" sequence, then the remainder of the command line is a comment. Comments may be line-continued with backslashes just like regular RIPscrip commands can. Some examples of comments might be:

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text:
```text
!|!This is a comment

!|c0F|!Set the color to white|c00|!Set the color to black

!|c0F|!this is a very long, continued\
comment line.  Line-continued comments\
adhere to standard RIPscrip line continuation rules
```

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: Note that the second example shows a comment starting after a legitimate RIPscrip command (set color). This is valid.

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: The RIP_COMMENT is treated exactly like any other RIPscrip command for the purposes of parsing RIPscrip commands, EXCEPT that the string is explicitly ignored for [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md). Any use of `|` will be interpreted as the beginning of the next command, and `\` will interpreted as a line continuation. No other characters need be escaped out.

requirements.heading: RIP_COMMENT
requirements.text: In the RIPtel corpus, comments are the single most valuable evidence stream: `!|command|! comment` chains are ubiquitous, and TeleGrafix's authors used comments to name six otherwise-undocumented drawing primitives outright (NEWCMDS.RIP) and to leave positional field-layout cribs above complex commands. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A2._

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 - not in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory, not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: _Start a grouping of RIPscrip commands_

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `(`      |

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | \<none\> |

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** none

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: This command has one special usage, that is to group blocks of commands together into logical groupings. This has no functional use to a terminal program, but to a paint program, it can be used to perform block moves of commands from one area in a scene to another. In order to accomodate this, a standardized method of doing group definitions is being created.

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: To specify a command grouping, specify the commands like this:

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text:
```text
!|(

  ...
  ... RIPscrip commands
  ...

!|)
```

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: When putting RIPscrip data files online on a host, you would typically want to remove groupings for efficiency, although this is not required. A terminal program should just ignore RIP_GROUP_BEGIN and [RIP_GROUP_END](#rip_group_end) commands, at it has no conceivable use for the information at this time.

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: Also note that a group may consist of several groups and commands. In other words, groups may be nested inside of each other for the purpose of bundling them together.

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: **NOTE:** Any currently active group definitions are "closed" when a [RIP_NO_MORE](#rip_no_more) command is encountered in a paint program or some kind of conversion utility that uses groups. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_BEGIN
requirements.text: The 2.00a4 spec's suggestion to strip groupings from files placed online is consistent with their total absence from the shipping demo corpus. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_GROUP_END
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A2._

requirements.heading: 1.2 Math & Coordinates
requirements.text: The numeric foundations of RIPscrip 3.x: the base-36 [MegaNum](../../glossary.md) system carried forward from 1.54, the base-64 [UltraNum](../../glossary.md) system introduced by the 2.0 redesign, the global [Base Math](../../glossary.md) setting that selects between them, and the mathematics of the resolution-independent [world-coordinate](../../glossary.md) model.

requirements.heading: Numerical Parameters - Formats and Base-Math Variations
requirements.text: Throughout the RIPscrip specification, numeric parameters are used extensively to indicate where to draw things, how to draw things and various other pieces of information. For compactness, we do not use numbers that are normal decimal numbers (base-10). By default, RIPscrip uses base-36 numbers (Hexa-Tri-Decimal or more fondly, MegaNums) which use the digits 0-9 followed by A-Z. This was the original numbering system used in the 1.xx specification.

requirements.heading: Numerical Parameters - Formats and Base-Math Variations

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Both systems are plain positional numerals in RIPscrip's own digit alphabets - **not** the RFC 4648 "Base32"/"Base64" encodings, which share nothing with these beyond the number 64.
requirements.reason: Representation terminology or worked-example table header; behavior is covered by the adjacent digit/value requirements.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text:
- **MegaNum digit alphabet (base 36):** `0`-`9` (values 0-9), then `A`-`Z` (values 10-35). Writers emit uppercase by convention.
- **UltraNum digit alphabet (base 64):** `0`-`9` (values 0-9), `A`-`Z` (values 10-35), `a`-`z` (values 36-61), `#` (value 62), `&` (value 63). Case is significant - `A` is 10 but `a` is 36.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Calculating multi-character values:** most-significant digit first, each position worth a power of the base - value = d₀·bⁿ⁻¹ + d₁·bⁿ⁻² + … + dₙ₋₁ (b = 36 or 64). To _decode_: MegaNum `1M` is 1×36 + 22 = 58; MegaNum `HR` is 17×36 + 27 = 639; UltraNum `R9a` is 27×64² + 9×64 + 36 = 111,204. To _encode_ a decimal value, take `value ÷ b^k mod b` for each position, highest power first: decimal 250 as a 2-digit MegaNum is 250 ÷ 36 = 6 remainder 34 → `6Y`; the same 250 as a 2-digit UltraNum is 250 ÷ 64 = 3 remainder 58 → `3w`; decimal 360 (a full circle in degrees) is `A0` in MegaNums.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Fixed widths and zero padding:** a `:2` width specifier means exactly two digits in the current base, zero-padded on the left (decimal 10 is `0A` as a 2-digit MegaNum, `0A` as a 2-digit UltraNum too). Numeric parameters have no delimiters between them - the fixed widths are what let the parser slice them apart, so a missing pad digit shifts every following parameter. `:XY` coordinate parameters are 2 digits by default, adjustable via [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](#rip_set_coordinate_size); `:CM` color parameters follow the current color mode ([2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_set_color_mode)). Per-command field widths are collected in [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md).

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Last-parameter rules:** a variable-width numeric parameter may be used only as the last parameter of a command, and syntax rule 10 allows the last numeric parameter to be shortened by dropping leading zeros (`!|c01` → `!|c1`); a trailing reserved parameter may be omitted entirely ([1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ripscrip-protocol---syntax-and-general-structure)). A text string is likewise always last and never number-encoded.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Base Math switching:** the global setting starts at base 36, is changed with [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](#rip_set_base_math) or the [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) flags, and resets to base 36 on any [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows). Commands documented as exceptions ignore it - direct-RGB color values and drawing-palette RGB parameters are always UltraNums, and RIP_SET_BASE_MATH's own parameter is always a MegaNum.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Parser-side edge cases (early termination behavior, out-of-alphabet bytes, and the like) are implementer material - see the [MegaNum encoding techspec](../../1.54/techspecs/1.1-meganum-encoding.md) and the [2.0 stream conventions delta](../../2.0/techspecs/1.0-stream-conventions-delta.md).

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:9107-9131)._

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text: Which base a command's parameters use is a **global mode**, not a per-command choice: after `!|J10` every base-math-governed field in every subsequent command reads as base-36; after `!|J1S`, base-64. Individual commands differ only in whether they _obey_ the mode - each command entry in this reference carries a base-math line, which is one of:

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text:
- **current setting** - the common case: coordinates, dimensions, radii, vertex counts, and most numeric fields.
- **MegaNums only** - commands that must parse before the mode is knowable or that reset it: [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](#rip_set_base_math) itself (its `10`/`1S` argument is always base-36), and anything that follows a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) (a reset silently returns the mode to base 36 - re-send `J` immediately if the scene needs otherwise).
- **UltraNums only** - direct-RGB color values and drawing-palette RGB parameters (see [2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md)).
- **not numeric** - text parameters (always last in a command) ignore base math entirely.

requirements.heading: Worked encodings
requirements.text: A field's value is `first_digit × base + second_digit` (and so on for wider fields). Digit values: `0`-`9` = 0-9, `A`-`Z` = 10-35, then (UltraNums only) `a`-`z` = 36-61, `#` = 62, `&` = 63.

requirements.text: | Value | 2-digit MegaNum | 2-digit UltraNum |

requirements.text: So the ubiquitous corpus line `!|fZKQO` is a 1280×960 world frame in MegaNums - and note that TeleGrafix's chosen frame fits 2-digit MegaNums with 15 to spare (1295 max). A constructed UltraNum equivalent would be `!|J1S|fK0F0` _(constructed example - see the caution below)_.

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: | Largest coordinate in either axis | Recommended encoding |

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: | ≤ 1,295 | 2-digit MegaNums (the default; what every TeleGrafix scene does) |

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: | 1,296 - 4,095 | 2-digit UltraNums (`J1S`) - same wire size, larger range - **or** 3-digit MegaNums via [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](#rip_set_coordinate_size) |

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: | 4,096 - 46,655 | 3-digit MegaNums, or 3-digit UltraNums (max 262,143, capped by the 32,767 world limit) |

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: | larger | wider coordinate size; keep total field width ≤ 5 digits (32-bit arithmetic limit per 2.00a4) |

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: UltraNums earn one byte per coordinate over 3-digit MegaNums in the 1,296-4,095 band - meaningful at 2,400 baud when a scene is thousands of drawing operations.

requirements.heading: Interoperability caution
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: Interoperability caution
requirements.text: **No UltraNum usage has been observed in the wild.** All 116 TeleGrafix demo scripts run `J10` MegaNums, and SyncTERM cannot parse UltraNums at all - its number reader (`parse_mega`, ripper.c:9107-9131) treats `a`-`z` as _case-insensitive base-36 digits_, so a base-64 scene would silently mis-decode rather than fail. MegaNums are the only wire-proven encoding; treat UltraNums as documented-but-unexercised.

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP §4.1; corpus._

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: Starting with the v2.0 specification of RIPscrip - carried unchanged into 3.x - the language is resolution independent through a "world coordinate system": you can alter the base coordinate system used to address the video's physical device coordinate system. Each coordinate system is called a "Coordinate Frame". There are two distinct levels of coordinate systems, from the lowest (least abstract) to the highest level (the drawing board):

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: 1. **DEVICE COORDINATE FRAME** - the resolution of the actual display device. This is not determined as part of the RIPscrip language itself, it is actually determined by the terminal - based upon whatever type of video hardware is present (and what mode the user has chosen).

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: 2. **[WORLD COORDINATE FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame)** - This is the master coordinate system. This is the global set of coordinates, set by [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) (wire opcode `f`). Ideally, it should be higher in dimensions than the Device Frame so that you do not lose resolution when "mapping" X/Y coordinates from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system. If the dimensions of the World Frame are the same as the Device Frame then the mapping operation between World and Device Frames are identical and can be skipped entirely since an X/Y coordinate in the World Frame directly corresponds to a pixel location in the Device Frame.

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: Per the white paper, the world coordinate system may be defined up to a maximum of **32,767 × 32,767** - "plenty of room to accommodate video hardware over the next several decades." (The 2.00a4 draft had said 65535×65535 _(v2.A4)_; the shipping figure is the signed-16-bit bound.) Since versions of the RIPscrip specification prior to v2.0 were based on a 640x350 resolution without any World Frame, the World Frame defaults to 640 across and 350 high for backward compatibility; the `$COMPAT$` text variable restores that whole 1.54 environment (see [1.0 Introduction](1.0-introduction.md#differences-from-154)).

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: A real 3.x example, from the RIPtel demo prologue:

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text:
```text
!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960
```

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: (comment and spelling TeleGrafix's own, ONLINE.RIP): `ZK` = 35×36+20 = **1280**, `QO` = 26×36+24 = **960**. The demos thus run in a 1280×960 world regardless of the user's actual screen mode. Alternate frames observed in the corpus: `HSDC` = 640×480, `HR9S` = 639×352, `HRDC` = 639×480. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 (the treatment carries into 3.x unchanged)._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Mathematics, unlike graphics, is abstract in nature. Graphics on the other hand, is very discrete in nature. A pixel in graphics is the smallest displayable element on a graphics screen (Picture Element). The corresponding concept in mathematics is a single point. A pixel has a discrete size and shape in graphics whereas in mathematics, a point is infinitely small and occupies no physical space in the cartesian coordinate system in which it exists.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: In graphics we use the concept of coordinates and points to specify where a pixel is located. If graphics were like mathematics where a pixel was infinitely small, a graphics monitor wouldn't show anything other than black because a pixel would be infinitely small surrounded by blackness. But this is not the case. Graphics hardware has to have pixels defined as discrete areas of the screen - addressable areas of the screen that can be set to a particular color. This is how we see things on the screen, as individual pixels of data used together to represent some kind of image.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Just like the point in mathematics, a line is infinitely thin, but has length. A line is composed of an infinite number of points between the beginning and ending locations of the line.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Relating these two distinctly different concepts to each other though doesn't always lend itself to a simple situation to understand. On the surface, a pixel's coordinate location appears to be the same thing as it is in mathematics. But, when you get into deeper issues of graphics theory this isn't truly the case because of the difference in sizes of a point compared to a pixel. In math, points don't have to be on even integer boundaries - they can be fractional. A point can be at (2.53,1.295), whereas in graphics, a pixel cannot be at a fractional location - there's no such thing as a part of a pixel!

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: A graphics screen is designed so that every pixel location on the screen has a unique location specified (in human terms) as an X/Y coordinate pair. This is called the Cartesian Coordinate System. It is by far one of the easiest ways of representing a coordinate in a two-dimensional world like a monitor. If you zoom in closely on a monitor and look at the layout of pixels and their relationships to coordinates, you might see something like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look at the previous diagram, you can see that there is a grid of pixels that is 24 pixels wide (the X direction) and 10 pixels high (the Y direction). Each of the squares is a black pixel. The pixels contain a "#" are considered white pixels. There are four pixels that are ON in this diagram, at locations (11,2), (12,2), (11,3) and (12,3). This is how graphics hardware addresses graphics pixels, by specifying an X/Y coordinate location for a pixel to turn it on or off (or more generally, to set it to a particular color).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the locations of the coordinates in the previous diagram, the X/Y coordinates address the physical pixel cells themselves. Each pixel cell is separated by infinitely thin lines - the pixel cells' borders so to speak. Now, each pixel is physically adjacent to the ones next to it and there are no gaps between them. This is the way graphics hardware works.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now that we've described the way graphics hardware addresses pixel locations, let's look at why it's not really the best way of describing graphics mathematically. For the hardware, this is the best way of handling things, but mathematically, it's not.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: The world of graphics hardware has many different facets. One graphics display device can often times display graphics at different resolutions. A typical video card on the IBM-PC can display graphics at 320x200, 640x350, 640x400, 640x480, 800x600, 1024x768 and even as high as 1280x1024 and higher. That's quite a bit of difference in pixel grids (like the one shown earlier). Not only can the number of pixels change horizontally and vertically, but when the resolutions get higher, the pixels get smaller and harder to see. When graphics hardware can achieve a resolution of infinity by infinity, then we will have achieved perfect sight (like what we see around us). But obviously, this will probably never happen in our lifetimes (or our great granchildren's for that matter).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: What would happen if you had a line drawn on a graphics screen from coordinates (0,0) to (639,349) at 640x350 resolution? You would have a nice little line on the screen that stretches from the upper-left corner to the lower-right corner. Now, if you drew the same line at 800x600 resolution? Your line would no longer go all the way to the bottom of the screen or to the far right of the screen. It would stop about 2/3'rds of the way down and over.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: The problems start to come up with mathematics and graphical representations when we try to make something look the same at one resolution as it does in another (resolution independence). Sure you can translate a coordinate in one resolution to some other coordinate in a different resolution. All you need to know are the dimensions of each resolution and a bit of algebra. But pixels aren't the same thickness! The line described previously could still be drawn properly to the lower-right of the screen, but it would appear a lot thinner. You could try drawing two lines offset by one pixel location and you would come "close" to the original thickness of the line at 640x350 resolution, but it wouldn't be a perfect match. A perfect match is a rare thing when dealing with different resolutions.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, on to the real issue at hand here: translation of coordinates. We won't worry about the size of pixels, but will concentrate on getting the locations of points correct at different resolutions. Let's say you have a screen at 640x350 resolution with two filled rectangles drawn on it. The first rectangle is drawn from (2,1) to (4,3) and the second one is drawn from (5,1) to (7,3) like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, you notice that both rectangles are right next to each other. There are no gaps between them. Now, if you tried to draw these same two rectangles on a graphics screen that was 1280x700 pixels in size, and tried to make it appear in the exact same location and size on the monitor, you would have to translate the corners of the rectangles to the new resolution and re-plot the rectangles. Now, 640x2 is 1280 and 350x2 is 700 so our new resolution is exactly twice as large in both the X and Y directions (this is RARELY the case!). So, in order to translate our original coordinates to this resolution we simply multiply the numbers by 2. Pretty simple. Our previous rectangles in their old untranslated state and the newly translated ones would be:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | Untranslated  | Translated      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, let's plot these two rectangles on our new graphics screen at the newly translated coordinates:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: What happened? We now have a black line in between the two rectangles. That's definitely not what we wanted to happen. Why did this happen? It's partly because of the nature of graphics hardware in the way they address pixels, and partly the way we humans think of pixels mathematically from a programming standpoint. What we need is a better mathematical representation of pixels and graphics coordinates so that when we translate coordinates these things don't happen.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: As we mentioned earlier, the lines on the above diagram represent the borders around each pixel. Each of these lines, like their mathematical counterparts, are infinitely thin. The only thing in the above diagram that has any size (or area) physically are the pixels themselves. Since the boundary lines around the pixels are defining the area that the pixel will occupy, it makes sense that we should think of those lines as the actual coordinates. If we think of the areas in between the pixels as the actual coordinates, we can think of pixels as the areas in between coordinates that are filled in with color. So, if we said to draw a filled in rectangle like we did earlier, we would actually be saying "fill in this rectangle's interior". Just like coloring books as a child, you have to stay inside the lines (or at least we're supposed to). Think about pixels as spots between the lines that get filled in with color just like a coloring book - the only difference is, a pixel cannot go outside the lines (don't you wish you were a pixel when you were younger?).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Using this new way of thinking of graphics is not very difficult, it just seems a bit odd -especially if you've been working with graphics for awhile. To draw the previous two rectangles properly the coordinates for them would have to be changed somewhat - like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **(old method)**

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | Untranslated  | Translated      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **(new method)**

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | UNTRANSLATED  | TRANSLATED      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Notice that the untranslated rectangles' coordinates are almost the same. In fact, the upper-left coordinates haven't changed at all. The only coordinates that have changed are the lower-right coordinates, and only by one pixel location. Now, if we draw these two rectangles using our new mathematical model for graphics, we would get the following (in both resolution examples:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the two graphs above you may notice a subtle difference in the numbering of the coordinates. The numbers are all there, but instead of labeling the cells themselves with coordinates, we have labeled the lines in between as the coordinates. When we say to draw a rectangle from (2,1) to (5,4) we are saying to draw a filled in area "between" coordinate lines 2 and 5 in the X direction and 1 and 4 in the Y direction. If you look closely at the upper left diagram, you will notice that is exactly what we have done. Now look closely at the upper right diagram. There are no gaps between the rectangles now. Also if you look at the translated coordinates, the right edge of the first rectangle is at X coordinate 10, and the left edge of the second rectangle is also at X coordinate 10. But they don't overlap each other. That's the part about this new way of thinking about things that gives people the hardest time.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: So far so good. Let's look at another example - one which draws the same two rectangles but this time, let's not fill them in. The diagram below shows the two at both example resolutions:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Not what you thought would happen, was it? This example illustrates a key point in our mathematical model of graphics: that there is a difference between filled objects and outlined objects. Filled objects fill everything inside an enclosed area whereas an outline (one or more lines) uses pixels to approximate an infinitely thin line. When lines and points are plotted on the video device, they are "rounded up" to the next highest pixel location. So, a point at (4,2) would not be on the intersecting lines at (4,2), it would be a pixel activated between 4 and 5 on the X axis and 2 and 3 on the Y axis. Look at the upper right diagram to convince yourself this is the case. Filled-in areas on the other hand, do not round up to the next highest pixel locations. They always fill in an area in-between the boundary lines. This means that in a filled-in rectangle, the right and bottom edges are "off by one" so to speak.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: To better illustrate these two different situations, we will draw a filled-in rectangle and a non-filled rectangle both using the same dimensions at the same resolution, then we will superimpose them on top of each other to better show the differences;

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Notice that the two rectangles are not the exact same size. Both the left and top edges are at the exact same locations, but in the case of the unfilled rectangle, the right and bottom edges are one pixel over and down. This shows that lines and points are rounded up to the next highest pixel location (the first pixel after the coordinate), but filled areas fill between the boundary lines. This seemingly odd way of doing things becomes extremely important when you deal with one image at different resolutions - as you saw with the case of translating two filled-in rectangles earlier from one resolution to another.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: In a very real sense, you could easily think about coordinates and graphics in two different ways. The way to think about them depends on the type of graphics operation being performed. If you are dealing with a fill operation of some kind, then you think about the drawing surface with coordinate lines "in between" the physical pixel cells. If you are dealing with a line drawing situation (or drawing points, circles, etc), then you can think of coordinates directly addressing the pixel cells themselves (just like when we began this conversation at the beginning of this section). When dealing with line drawing operations, there is no difference in mathematical models - there's only a difference when you get into filling areas in. Whichever method of thinking of things works best for you, use.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Other filled objects work the same way as do filled rectangles. For example, consider an unfilled polygon with the following vertices: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |          | X Pos | Y Pos |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 0 | 0     | 0     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 1 | 8     | 0     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 2 | 14    | 3     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 3 | 14    | 4     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 4 | 12    | 6     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 5 | 4     | 6     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 6 | 0     | 2     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: | Vertex 7 | 0     | 0     |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: With this polygon we would have a polygon that looks like the left diagram below. The right diagram is what it would look like if it were filled and had a border drawn at the same time (the different shaded blocks indicates which is border, fill-color, or both): _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Taking a second example. Let's consider an unfilled oval centered at (7,3) with a horizontal radius of 8 and a vertical radius of 4. The unfilled oval is depicted in the left diagram below. The diagram on the right is the same oval with the border drawn and also filled in. Notice how the border is drawn in relation to the filled-in interior and how it adheres to resolution independence. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the right diagram, you will notice that the oval isn't "balanced". This is because in this situation, the oval is centered about a particular point, but the filled oval is partially offset on an odd-boundary - the filled interior is 8 pixels to the left of the center point (inclusive), and 7 pixels to the right of the center point (inclusive). This is due to the resolution independent nature of filled regions. If you need to draw a perfectly smooth filled oval, draw one with a solid fill and with borders enabled, both with the same drawing and fill color. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **Practical summary:** for fills, think "coordinates between pixels"; for lines, points, and curves, think "coordinates address pixels" - the models only diverge for filled interiors. Filled polygons and curved regions follow the same fill-between-lines rule, with their borders (optional since 2.0, see [2.3 Shapes & Fills](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md)) rounding up like lines. _Evidence: 2.00a4 (the treatment carries into 3.x unchanged)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 (as the colliding draft letter `b`); HLP (`RIP_SetBaseMath`, plus `$BASEMATH$` variable); corpus (94 uses in 90 files; ONLINE.RIP inline comment "Set base math to MegaNums (base 36)") - not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: _Sets the base math for most RIPscrip parameters_

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `J`           |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `base_math:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|J <base_math>` **Example:** `!|J10`

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (MegaNums only)

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: This command sets the Base Math used extensively throughout the RIPscrip language. By default, the RIPscrip language uses Base-36 math for all of its numeric parameters. This number can be changed to accomodate larger values for numeric parameters. For example, a two digit base-36 number can hold a number from 0-1295. A two digit Base-64 number can hold a number from 0-4095 which is considerably larger.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: This can be used when you set the World Coordinate Frame to larger coordinates, even larger than 1024x1024. Altering the Base Math of the parameters gives you the ability to handle larger numbers without expanding the size (byte-wise) of parameters throughout the language (see [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](#rip_set_coordinate_size)).

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: **NOTE:** This command ALWAYS uses base-36 (MegaNum) math for its parameter. The reason for this is that this is a universal command, and the Base Math may not be known at the moment the command is received.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: When a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command is received, the base math is reset to Base-36 (MegaNum) values. If a scene is received after the Reset Windows command and it uses Base Math other than Base-36, then you MUST send a RIP_SET_BASE_MATH command immediately after the RIP_RESET_WINDOWS command.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: The valid settings at this time are:

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text:
- Base-36 (`10` meganum)
- Base-64 (`1S` meganum)

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: If an illegal Set Base Math command is received (an illegal base math setting), RIPscrip will default to MegaNums.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: **`J` is the confirmed wire opcode.** The RIPtel corpus settles it: 90 of 116 files open with the prologue `!|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO`, and ONLINE.RIP annotates `J10` inline as "Set base math to MegaNums (base 36)". The shipping 3.0 driver's command inventory confirms the name (`RIP_SetBaseMath`). _Evidence: corpus; HLP._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: > **Editor's note - the draft `b` collision:** the 2.00 ALPHA 4 draft assigned level-0 `b` to **both** this command and [RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_extended_text_window) - an unshippable collision, never resolved in any published document. The shipping 3.0 driver resolved it by moving RIP_SET_BASE_MATH to level-0 **`J`** (so the draft's format `!|b <base_math>` became `!|J <base_math>`), leaving `b` to the extended text window - exactly as SyncTERM's descriptor table also has it. This reference documents `J` as the 3.x opcode throughout; the draft position is preserved in the [2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math).

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (`RIP_SetCoordinateSize`, plus `$COORDSIZE$` variable; "Invalid coordinate size", and "Invalid coordinate size in environment header segment" for the scene-header form); corpus (94 uses in 90 files) - not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: _Sets the number of bytes used for XY coordinates_

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `n`                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `byte_size:1 res:3` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|n <byte_size> <res>` **Example:** `!|n2000`

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: This command alters the number of bytes that will be expected for all subsequent X or Y parameters in RIPscrip. By default, all X or Y parameters are two bytes in length as denoted syntax-wise as x:XY or y:XY in the specification. This command allows you to alter this size. In 1.x versions of RIPscrip, the maximum size of a parameter was in the X direction and the maximum value was 639. This could safely be represented in two meganum digits. In 2.0 of RIPscrip and beyond, we introduce a world coordinate system into the specification which allows you to use a much higher resolution for your drawing environment. This facilitates resolution independence. To provide for future expandability when ultra-high resolution devices might exist, the possibility of an X or Y coordinate exceeding 4095 might occur. Since this is the largest value that can be accomodated in a 2-byte UltraNum, we offer an option that provides for extensibility.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: Using this parameter to expand the byte size beyond 2 will make a RIPscrip file bigger. This is because every X/Y coordinate will be expanded in size by a certain number of bytes, and since these are the fundamental values in any graphical environment, it will result in larger RIPscrip files. In practice, this command should be used with caution. When situations permit, do not use this command, or use it with a byte size of 2 (the default). This will keep files from ever getting larger than they would be by default.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: Valid settings are from 2-5. If any other values are specified, then a value of 2 will be assumed. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: A [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command will reset the coordinate size back to two byte wide parameters.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: **NOTE:** The `<res>` parameter is reserved and should be set to "000" for future expansion by TeleGrafix.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE
requirements.text: The standard corpus prologue sends `!|n2000` - byte size 2, reserved `000` - annotated in TELPORT.FN as "Set X/Y coordinate size to 2 bytes". No corpus scene ever uses a size other than 2; a 2-digit MegaNum (0-1295) comfortably addresses the 1280×960 world frame. Commands whose coordinate fields obey this setting are marked `:XY` in the command entries. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: 1.3 World View & Virtual Canvas
requirements.text: Drawing happens in [world coordinates](../../glossary.md): the world frame is the logical space, the terminal maps it onto whatever physical resolution it runs at, and the current [drawing port](../../glossary.md)'s [viewport](../../glossary.md) clips what is drawn and sets its origin - the [screen](../../glossary.md) is simply port #0.

requirements.heading: 1.3 World View & Virtual Canvas
requirements.text: _The 1.54 model this generalizes - a single fixed 640×350 graphics window with a clipping viewport - is [1.3 in the v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md); a 1.54 scene runs unchanged under 3.x because the defaults reproduce that environment exactly._

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: Historical/provenance scaffolding, explanatory recommendation or worked 640x350 physical-device example; selected v3 physical canvases are the three approved 4:3 tiers, tested against independently derived corresponding ratios.

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: A drawing port is an area where graphics can be drawn. At any moment there is exactly one **current drawing port** - the port that receives graphical drawing operations. Ports come in two types:

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text:
1. **Screen (visual) drawing ports** - rectangular regions of the user's actual screen. Drawing to a screen port appears immediately. Screen ports divide the display into separate drawing areas that can be switched between at will.
2. **Offscreen bitmap drawing ports** (also called **clipboard ports**) - drawing surfaces that are not part of the visible screen. Graphics drawn to an offscreen port are invisible until copied to a screen port. Offscreen ports are used to compose scenes out of sight and reveal them whole, to cache bitmaps loaded from disk, to save screen regions under dialog boxes, and to drive transition animation.

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver additionally distinguishes **snapshot ports** - offscreen ports created by capturing screen contents - in its error strings ("No mouse/button fields on offscreen drawing ports"). _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: Ports live in a 36-slot [data table](7.1-data-tables.md), entries numbered 0-35. **Port 0 is always the screen** - it is the full size of the display, exists at all times, and cannot be created, deleted, or redefined (confirmed verbatim by the 3.0.7 driver's error strings "Can't delete graphics port #0" and "Can't create drawing port #0"); ports 1-35 are user-definable ("The given port number is invalid (1-35 only)"). Mouse fields, clickable buttons, text windows, and resident query expressions are screen-only and may not be placed on an offscreen port. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: Each port has its own coordinate origin - (0,0) is the upper-left corner of the port - and its own remembered drawing state, and every port has an associated **viewport**: a clipping rectangle inside the port that defines its drawing limits and shifts the drawing origin to its own upper-left corner. Anything drawn beyond the viewport's edge is truncated (clipped). By default a port's viewport is the full size of the port. So a point at (50,50) inside a viewport that starts at (40,40) inside a port that starts at (25,25) on the screen lands at screen position (25+40+50, 25+40+50) = (115,115). _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The Port Model at a Glance
The Port Model at a Glance
requirements.text: In TeleGrafix's own 3.x material the port system is the workhorse: the RIPtel demo corpus contains **9,104 uses of `2C` (RIP_PORT_COPY)** - almost all in the WIPE00-WIPE24 "wipe" transition library, which composes the next scene in an offscreen port and reveals it with sequences of narrow port-to-screen copies. Defining, deleting, switching, and copying between ports - and the port-copy scaling and viewport rules - are documented in [7.0 Drawing Ports](7.0-drawing-ports.md). _Evidence: corpus (WIPE00.FN-WIPE24.FN); HLP._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `f`                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x_dim:XY y_dim:XY` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|f <x_dim> <y_dim>` **Example:** `!|fZKQO`

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: This command sets the dimensions of the World Coordinate Frame. This Frame is the Global Coordinate Space of the RIPscrip drawing screen. It is not the exact size of the Device Frame - that is a lower level coordinate system. With this frame, you can "map" your scenes into something, say a 1024x1024 grid and let the terminal worry about mapping it into whatever device coordinates it is using (eg, 640x350, 800x600, etc). Any coordinates used for setting viewports or other such things will be specified in World Frame Coordinates. Actual drawing primitives will use the current Drawing Frame's coordinates - another level of coordinate mapping. This allows you to do things like draw full screen images inside a tinier window, leaving additional drawing space on the screen for other images.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: The actual Device Coordinate Frame is not specified in the RIPscrip language anywhere - it is handled entirely by the remote terminal, because only it knows the device coordinates of the environment that it is running under (although the host can query these values from the terminal).

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: The `<x_dim>` parameter is how wide the drawing area is in logical coordinates. The `<y_dim>` parameter is how tall the drawing area is in logical coordinates.
requirements.reason: Coordinate-frame dimensions, limit and ratio arithmetic only; host opcodes, reset orchestration and port/viewport translations remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: Per the white paper, the World Coordinate Frame may be defined up to a maximum of **32,767 × 32,767** - see [World Coordinate Systems in 1.2](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#world-coordinate-systems). _Evidence: WP._
requirements.reason: Coordinate-frame dimensions, limit and ratio arithmetic only; host opcodes, reset orchestration and port/viewport translations remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME
requirements.text: This command is the single biggest semantic change of the 2.0/3.x era: it redefines the logical coordinate space away from 1.54's fixed 640×350, making every subsequent coordinate frame-relative. It closes the standard corpus prologue in over 100 files as `!|fZKQO` - `ZK`/`QO` decode to **1280×960**, the square-pixel MegaNum world frame recommended by the 2.00a4 [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) discussion. Alternate observed frames: `HSDC` = 640×480, `HR9S` = 639×352, `HRDC` = 639×480 (BLUEFADE.FN works at 640×350 and TELPORT.FN's comments then "reset our environment back to 1280x960 world coordinates"). ONLINE.RIP demonstrates the driver's argument-parsing tolerance with an inline trailing comment: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960` _(sic)_. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Translating Device to World Coordinates
requirements.text: If we solve the above equations for Xw and Yw, we get the inverse equations - translations from Device Coordinates to World Coordinates:

requirements.heading: Precision of translation
requirements.text: If the World Coordinates are larger than the Device Coordinates, then when you translate World Coordinates to Device Coordinates, there will be pixel-perfect translation. This means that translation will be unambiguous - they will convert to pixel coordinates without there being any discrepency. For example, if your Device Coordinates are 640x350 and your World Coordinates are 1280x700, then a Point in World Coordinate space at (0,0) and (1,0) will both translate to the Device Coordinates (0,0) and (0,0) respectively. This is because the World Coordinate space is twice as large as the Device Coordinate space. If on the other hand the Device Coordinates were 1280x700 and the World Coordinate space were 640x350, then the World Points (0,0) and (1,0) would translate to (0,0) and (2,0) respectively. Notice that in the World Coordinates, the pixels were adjacent. But in the Device Coordinates, they are separated by a one pixel gap.
requirements.reason: Coordinate-frame dimensions, limit and ratio arithmetic only; host opcodes, reset orchestration and port/viewport translations remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Precision of translation
requirements.text: In summary, World Coordinates should always be equal to or greather than the size of the Device Coordinate Frame, otherwise disparity will exist in the translations. Since coordinate translation will almost ALWAYS be from World -> Device coordinates, everything will be fine if the World Frame has a larger resolution than the Device Frame. The same holds true for the inverse equations to translate from Device to World coordinates. If the World Coordinate Frame is larger than the Device Coordinate Frame, then any point that is translated from Device -> World Coordinates (a Mouse X/Y location for example), might not translate over precisely - skipping over pixel spaces in the World Frame - this is simply because of the precision of translation and cannot be overcome mathematically since a Mouse Pointer's location is pixel based - it doesn't have any finer locations than on pixel boundary locations (there's no such thing as a fractional pixel location in graphics hardware - only mathematically).
requirements.reason: Historical/provenance scaffolding, explanatory recommendation or worked 640x350 physical-device example; selected v3 physical canvases are the three approved 4:3 tiers, tested against independently derived corresponding ratios.

requirements.heading: Precision of translation
requirements.text: To maintain backward compatibility with previous versions of the RIPscrip specification, after a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](#rip_reset_windows) command is received, the World Coordinate Frame is defined as having the dimensions 640x350 until reset by a RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME or [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) command.

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: _Define the size & location of the Graphics Window_

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `v`                       |

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY` |

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Port, Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: This command defines the (X,Y) pixel boundaries of the RIPscrip graphics window, which will contain all RIPscrip graphics output. ASCII/ANSI text will be displayed in the current TTY window defined by the [RIP_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_text_window) command. (x0,y0) defines the upper-left corner of the graphics viewport, and (x1,y1) defines the lower-right corner (inclusive). The viewport may be deactivated, so RIPscrip graphics commands are ignored, by setting all parameters to zero (0).

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: The viewport is physically bound to the current [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). In other words when this command is executed, it will modify the viewport for the current drawing port. This in effect, modifies the clipping rectangle for that port. If any of the viewport coordinates would extend beyond the boundaries of the drawing port, they will be adjusted to fit inside the port. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: Graphics displayed in the viewport are "truncated" at this rectangular border, meaning if a circle would normally extend outside one of the borders, it will be chopped, only displaying the portion of the circle that is contained inside the viewport boundaries.

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: Coordinates that specify the boundary of the Graphics Viewport are specified in World Coordinates. The interior area of the Viewport is then considered the Drawing Frame. The Drawing Coordinate frame are set to the same size/dimension as the World Coordinate Frame area that the viewport inhabits. For example, if you define a viewport from (100,100) to (299,299) in World Coordinates, then your Drawing Frame will be a drawing area with a resolution of 200x200 logical drawing pixels. In other words, when you set a viewport, you immediately have a 1:1 mapping of logical drawing pixels to World Coordinate Pixels. If you wish to change the X/Y Drawing Frame resolution to some other value, use the RIP_SET_DRAWING_FRAME command after setting the viewport. If you draw anything before executing this command, then the privimitives will be drawing things in the current Drawing Frame's coordinates (a sub-set of the World Coordinates). The Drawing Frame's coordinates do not take on another mapping until you actually set them with a RIP_SET_DRAWING_FRAME command. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: To re-activate a viewport that was previously deactivated, either send a correctly configured RIP_SET_VIEWPORT command, or issue a query command with a `$AVP$` [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md) (Activate ViewPort). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_VIEWPORT
requirements.text: _[Editor's note: the `RIP_SET_DRAWING_FRAME` command referred to in the v2.A0 paragraph above was dropped before the ALPHA 4 draft - no entry for it exists anywhere in the specification, and no trace of it appears in the 3.x evidence (HLP inventory, corpus, or SyncTERM). In practice the viewport's 1:1 world-coordinate mapping described above is the only drawing-frame behavior defined.]_
