requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: | 1 | Maintain image aspect ratio - This will keep the image maintained in size no matter what the size of the display region is. If the region isn't perfectly proportioned in relation to the actual bitmap, then areas of the display region above and below the image will be blacked out (a margin), or possibly left and right depending on proportions of the bitmap. This will yield a visually accurate representation of the image. _(v2.A0)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: | 2 | Delete image definition when complete. This is only useful for images received via RIP*ENTER_BLOCK_MODE or via a UU-Encoded RIPscrip data block for text-only transfer. When the image is rendered on the screen, it's definition and/or local disk file is deleted automatically upon completion of the drawing process. *(v2.A1)\_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: | 4 | Do not clear the image area to the current background color before viewing the image. _(v2.A3)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: | 8 | Commit the color palette of the image (if any) to the actual video hardware/color lookup table. This is typically only of use when using the image style with GIF files. This flag is ignored with JPEGs. When active, any color palette in the image file to be displayed is used to alter the current video color system to make the image show up as close to the original image as possible. _(v2.A4)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: > **Editor's note:** flag 8 is paper-only in practice - it targets palette-carrying GIF files, and GIF was dropped over LZW licensing before any 3.x client shipped a decoder ([6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md#file-roles)). The flag is documented here as the ALPHA 4 draft defined it. _Evidence: 2.00a4 (flag definition); WP (GIF dropped)._

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: If no RIP*IMAGE_STYLE command is processed before a JPEG image is to be displayed, then the image area is defined to be the full size of the viewport in whatever port is currently active. When a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) or a [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) command is received (ie, the environment is reset), then the image area is also reset to the maximum size of the current viewport. *(v2.A3)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: The example (N2*TITLE.RIP) sets flag 4 - don't clear the area first - for its inset newspaper photo. Corpus uses also appear in the truncated 12-character form `!|1i00009F6Q0004` with the reserved block omitted, which the shipping driver's truncation-tolerant parser accepts. \_Evidence: corpus (N2_TITLE.RIP).*

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: [Mouse fields](../../glossary.md) - host-defined rectangular hot regions that transmit a [host command](../../glossary.md) when clicked - the commands that delete them, and control of the mouse pointer shape.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: _The 1.54 record is [4.1 in the v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.1-mouse-fields.md); the 2.0 record is [4.2 in the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md), which added world-coordinate placement, the region-selective [RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS](#rip_kill_enclosed_mouse_fields), and [RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR](#rip_set_mouse_cursor)._

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: Two global rules apply to all mouse regions (fields and buttons alike):

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text:
- Up to 128 mouse fields, 128 mouse buttons, or any combination may exist simultaneously, but combined their total number cannot exceed 128 - they share the mouse field [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#mouse-field-table). _(v1.54)_
- When the user clicks the mouse on the screen, all mouse regions (whether mouse fields or mouse buttons) are scanned from most recent to the least recent ("last in, first out"): if regions overlap, the newest one wins the click. _(v1.54, revised v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: Mouse fields exist only on the screen (port #0) - they cannot be placed on offscreen [drawing ports](7.0-drawing-ports.md). The corpus confirms both rules operate as documented in the shipping 3.0 driver. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: _Defines a rectangular hot mouse field_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `M`                                                    |

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `num:2 x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY clk:1 clr:1 res:5 text` |

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1M <num> <x0><y0><x1><y1> <clk><clr><res><text>` **Example:** `!|1M000G7Y8ICC1000000ID=2:$-=RETURN=>NEWSPAPR.RIP$$>TWEATHER.RIP$`

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Viewport, Port (NO; screen ports only), Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse)) · HLP (`RIP_Mouse`; `$FIELDID$` variable, mouse-field entry/exit queries) · corpus (100 uses in 31 files) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16381)

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: This command ties together three things:

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text:
- A region on the screen
- A mouse-click event
- A string of text to be transmitted by the terminal.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: This command defines a rectangular region on the screen that functions as a "hot" mouse area. If the user clicks the [left] mouse button while pointing inside the region, then the terminal must transmit the `<text>` string to the Host. The (x0,y0) parameter MUST be the upper-left corner, and (x1,y1) MUST be the lower-right corner of the region.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<num>` parameter used to be used in the older RIPscrip v1.0 specification but is now obsolete. For upwards compatibility, it should be set to "00". _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<clk>` parameter, if 1, indicates that the region should be visibly inverted while the mouse button is down. This offers visual feedback. If `<clk>` is 0, the region will not be inverted while clicked.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<clr>` parameter, if 1, will physically zoom the text window to full screen size and clear the screen. This is useful if the `<text>` parameter instructs the host to enter an area of the System that doesn't support RIPscrip graphics.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<text>` parameter is a Host command that gets sent when the field is clicked. You may use a caret (^) or a backquote (`` ` ``) to represent control characters, (e.g., ^M for carriage return, `` `G ``, ^C, etc.). Mouse fields may use Data text variables, active text variables, pick lists, control characters and local file playback directives. At no time are templates permitted in simple mouse fields. See the section on [host commands](5.0-host-commands.md) for more details about these types of features of RIPscrip. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: Mouse fields are always created relative to port #0 (the screen port). Under no circumstances are mouse fields allowed in offscreen drawing ports - you can't have a clickable mouse area in a region that cannot be clicked (ie, off the screen). If the current drawing port is an offscreen port, or even a port other than port #0, then the mouse field is defined relative to screen port #0 for the purposes of defining its position. The same applies to mouse-based buttons (see the [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) command). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: Mouse fields that extend partially outside of a viewport are truncated to fit inside the viewport. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: When this command is stored in-memory, it is converted to global screen coordinates (for internal storage only). This makes it so that if you have mouse regions defined in multiple different viewports, that each field will be properly inverted at the right location regardless of the currently defined viewport. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: NOTE: All Mouse Fields are scanned in "last in, first out" order. This means that the last-most received Mouse Field will be the first one scanned for a mouse click. You are limited to a maximum of 128 Mouse Regions or Mouse Buttons (128 total). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text: The 3.x corpus reveals two undocumented extensions to the `<text>` parameter. Both live at the host-command layer - they are documented in full in chapter 5 and only summarized here:

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text:
- **`ID=n:` prefix** - assigns a numbered mouse-field identity, readable back through the `$FIELDID$` [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md) and used by the `.MSE` overlay scenes' entry/exit queries to drive hover status lines and cursor changes (the example above, from NEWSPAPR.RIP's navigation, is field ID 2). The prefix is not transmitted to the host. The mechanism - and RIPtel's canonical nine-field menu built on it - is documented in [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md#mouse-field-identities---idn). _Evidence: HLP (`$FIELDID$` - "current mouse field ID"); corpus (NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.MNU/MENU.MSE)._
- **Inline conditionals and macros** - `<<if $RETURN$!="">>$<<RETURN>>$<<else>>$NULL$<<endif>>` as a host command (BUTTONS.RIP), and [`$GOTOURL(WEBURL)$`](5.0-host-commands.md#launching-web-urls---gotourlname) launching a web URL from a variable (TELLISTS.MNU/.MSE - 1997-era web integration). The conditional/macro layer is [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md). _Evidence: corpus (BUTTONS.RIP, TELLISTS.MNU, TELLISTS.MSE)._

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text: Hover (entry/exit) behavior is not part of this command itself: the corpus wires deferred [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) modes 5/6 to mouse-field _entry/exit_ events - a 3.x extension of the documented click modes - to run `.MSE` overlay status-line updates and `$MCURSOR(n)$` pointer changes. _Evidence: HLP ("mouse-field entry/exit queries"); corpus (MENU.MSE) - mode numbering (hypothesis)._

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: _Destroys all previously defined hot mouse regions_

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `K`      |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | \<none\> |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1K` **Example:** `!|1K`

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (N/A) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_mouse_fields)) · HLP (`RIP_KillMouseFields`; also the `$MKILL$` variable) · corpus (8 uses in 8 files) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16370)

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: This command will "forget" all Mouse Regions. Use it at the beginning of each Scene, so that one scene's Mouse Regions don't get used in another.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: The corpus's TELKILL.FN ("Kill all mouse fields and entry/exit queries") wraps it as a reusable subroutine scene. _Evidence: corpus (TELKILL.FN)._

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: _Destroys any Mouse Fields inside a region_

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `k`                               |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY flags:4` |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Fill Style (see below), Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_enclosed_mouse_fields)) · HLP (`RIP_KillEnclosedMouseFields`) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: This command will destroy any Mouse Fields or Mouse Active Buttons that are contained inside the given rectangle or that intersect the rectangle. The exact operation of this function is dependent on the setting of the `<flags>` parameter. The `<flags>` parameter can combine any of the following flags to determine the exact mode of operation:

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **Region Specific Flags**

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | Flags | Description                                              |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 1     | Kill only fields completely contained (non-intersecting) |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 2     | Kill only fields that intersect bounding rectangle       |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 4     | Kill fields entirely outside bounding rectangle          |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: > If 1, 2 and 4 are not present, then NO fields are deleted. One of these flags must be supplied for any mouse fields to be deleted.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **What Types of Fields not to Destroy**

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | Flags | Description                              |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 8     | Don't destroy simple Mouse Fields        |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 16    | Don't destroy active Mouse Button fields |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: > If 8 and 16 are not present, then all types of mouse fields are destroyed.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **What to do With the Affected Region(s)**

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | Flags | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 32 | Clear the affected field(s) to black (color 0) |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 64 | Fill the affected field(s) with current fill color and fill pattern (64 overides 32 in the case that both of 32 and 64 are present). |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 128 | Perform the 32/64 operations on the whole bounding rectangle (based on Region Specific Flags). |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: > If 128 is omitted but 32 or 64 are used, then the mouse field's affected are cleared with the appropriate method. If 128 is present as well, then instead of clearing the individual mouse fields with the given method, the entire region specified by the Region Specific Flags is affected (ie, the entire interior of the bounding rectangle is cleared, etc). If 32, 64 and 128 are omitted, then the affected region/fields are left on the screen visually, but their mouse field definitions are destroyed internally. If 128 is used, but 32 and 64 are omitted then nothing is done visually either.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: The demos always clear all fields at once with [RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS](#rip_kill_mouse_fields) instead. _Evidence: corpus (absence)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: _Sets the mouse cursor (pointer) to various shapes_

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `c`                    |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `cursor_style:2 res:4` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1c <cursor_style> <res>` **Example:** `!|1c06`

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_set_mouse_cursor)) · HLP (`RIP_SetMouseCursor`; also the `$MCURSOR(n)$` variable) · corpus (2 uses in FXSHWIMG.FN) - not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: This command allows you to alter the current mouse cursor shape that is shown on the screen. This feature lets you change the cursor to another shape to give the user of the terminal an idea that something is going on. For example, changing the cursor to the shape of an hourglass or a watch could give the idea that they should wait for a moment because something is going on.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: The `<cursor_style>` parameter is an ID number that specifies which cursor style should be activated. The possible values for this parameter are: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | Style | Description                                    |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 00    | Standard "left-leaning" arrow cursor (default) |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 01    | Wrist watch cursor                             |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 02    | Cross-hair cursor                              |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 03    | I-bar cursor (for text editing)                |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 04    | Pointing finger cursor                         |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 05    | Hand held up cursor                            |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 06    | Hourglass cursor                               |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: When a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) or a [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) command is executed, the mouse cursor is automatically reset to the default, standard pointer cursor.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: FXSHWIMG.FN brackets its slow JPEG display with `!|1c06` / `!|1c00` - hourglass on, arrow back - omitting the reserved digits entirely, which the shipping driver's truncation-tolerant parser accepts. Most corpus cursor changes go through the `$MCURSOR(n)$` variable inside [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) commands instead ([5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md)), typically wired to field entry/exit for hover pointer changes. _Evidence: corpus (FXSHWIMG.FN, DEMO-01.COL, MENU.FN)._

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: [Buttons](../../glossary.md) - styled interactive controls with plain, icon (BMP), or clipboard faces, optional [hot-icon](../../glossary.md) pressed states (`.BMH`), special effects (bevel, chisel, recess, sunken), labels, hotkeys, and radio/check-box grouping. A style is defined once ([RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style)) and then instantiated by [RIP_BUTTON](#rip_button) commands; up to 36 styles live in the button style [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#button-style-table) and are switched with [RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_switch_button_style).

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: Reference tables: [Label Orientation](#label-orientation) · [Button Types](#button-types) · [Size & Color Parameters](#size-and-color-parameters) · [Flags Field 1](#flags-field-1) · [Font Metrics & Descenders](#font-metrics-and-descenders) · [Chisel Effect Insets](#chisel-effect-insets) · [Flags Field 2](#flags-field-2)

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: _The 1.54 record is [4.2 in the v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.2-buttons.md); the 2.0 record is [4.3 in the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md), whose changes were `.BMP`/`.BMH` faces, world-coordinate placement, the `<other_port>` clipboard-port parameter, and style slots._

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: _Button style definition_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: | **Command** | `B` |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `wid:XY hgt:XY orient:2 flags:4 size:2 dfore:2 dback:2 bright:2 dark:2 surface:2 grp_no:2 flags2:2 uline_col:2 corner_col:2 other_port:1 res:5` |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1B <wid> <hgt> <orient> <flags> <bevsize> <dfore> <dback> <bright> <dark> <surface> <grp_no> <flags2> <uline_col> <corner_col> <other_port> <res>` **Example:** `!|1B0000020PVS080F000F080700000F07000000`

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style)) · HLP (`RIP_ButtonStyle`; limits - label ≤255 chars, hotkey ≤255, groups 0-35, types "plain, icon or snapshot") · corpus (47 uses in 18 files) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:15015)

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This RIPscrip command is probably one of the most complex in the entire protocol. It defines how subsequent [RIP_BUTTON](#rip_button) commands will be interpreted. The purpose of this command is to define what a Button is and how they operate. Buttons can have many different configurations, flags, and styles. With the diversity of modes that the Button can take on, complexity is a necessary evil.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: There are 36 separate button style slots that can be defined simultaneously. This command allows you to alter the current button style slot. This button style slot is used by the RIP*BUTTON command to define buttons of particular types. Button style slots can be used to avoid retransmitting button styles over and over again. *(v2.A4)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This command does not actually do anything visibly on the screen. Simply put, this creates an internal definition for the Button mode which will be used with RIP_BUTTON commands after the definition is created.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: TeleGrafix left the positional crib for its 36-character argument block as a comment in the corpus's SHOWFONT.FN:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text:
```text
!|! wwhhooffffssffbbBBddssgg22uuccprrrrr
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: HLP's "snapshot" button type corresponds to the 2.00a4 clipboard button. _Evidence: corpus (SHOWFONT.FN); HLP._

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: Every Button can have an optional text label. It can appear in several different locations compared to the Button itself. This is specified in the `<orient>` parameter. The actual text of the label is not specified with this command, it is specified when you actually create a Button (see RIP_BUTTON below). The value that `<orient>` can be is as follows:

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | Value | Description of Orientation                |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 00    | Display label above button                |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 01    | Display label to the left of button       |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 02    | Display label in the center of the button |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 03    | Display label to the right of button      |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 04    | Display label beneath the button          |

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: There are three basic "types" of Buttons. There are Icon buttons, Clipboard buttons and Plain buttons. Each of these differ in the way that they create the button's image. A description of each type is as follows: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **ICON BUTTON (flag 128)** - An Icon Button means that the actual image of the button will be created by loading a bitmap icon image from the disk and load it at the given locatino. Any special effects (see below) can be applied to the Icon to further enhance the image. The filename for the Icon is supplied with the RIP*BUTTON command, as is the Icon's upper left X/Y coordinate. Icon Buttons are always stamped in COPY mode. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **CLIPBOARD BUTTON (flag 1)** - A clipboard button uses the clipboard port contents for the base image of the button. If no `<other_port>` is defined (ie, port #0), then the specific port that is used for the source image is determined by the clipboard pointer. If the clipboard pointer isn't defined, then the RIP*BUTTON commandsd that follow are ignored. If the `<other_port>` is from 1-35, then this specifies a previously defined port. This port will be the source of the bitmap image of the button. The entire contents of the port's viewport will be the image used for any subsequent RIP_BUTTON commands. If the given port doesn't exist, then it the RIP_BUTTON command(s) are ignored. Any special effects can be applied to this image to further enhance the overall button's image. *(v2.A3)\_

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **PLAIN BUTTON (flag 256)** - A plain button is exactly that, plain. No special graphics are used to create the button. The entire button region is simply filled-in with a solid colored rectangle using the `<surface>` color. Any special effects can be further applied to enhance the button's appearance. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<hgt>` and `<wid>` parameters represent the fixed height and width of the Button (applies only to Plain Buttons). If both values are greater than zero, then this will represent the actual size of the Button (its dimensions are not specified by the RIP_BUTTON command). If both of these are set to zero, then the actual RIP_BUTTON command will specify the size of the particular Button (dynamic sizing).

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<bevsize>` parameter is only used if the BEVEL FLAG (flag 512) is specified. When active, this parameter will determine how many pixels thick the bevel should be. This may be any value greater or equal to zero. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: There are a large number of flag values that can be combined to achieve a great many effects. There are two flag parameters for the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command, `<flags>` and `<flags2>`. They are detailed in the two tables that follow in this Section. You may combine any of the flags in the first table together simply by adding the "Value" of each one together and representing that number as a MegaNum.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<dfore>` and `<dback>` parameters are used with the text label. The `<dfore>` parameter is the foreground color for the text. It is always used to determine the color of the text label. The `<dback>` color is the color of the dropshadow (if any). This parameter is only used when you have specified the "Dropshadow" flag in the `<flags>` parameter (see below).

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: NOTE: There are seven (7) color parameters in this command. These parameters are ALWAYS used in Color Map mode. Direct RGB Color Mode cannot be used for these parameters. With Color Map mode, you have up to 256 separate color combinations possible for each color, providing you with a great deal of flexibility. The color parameters always use the Base Math set by the global Base Math setting. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<bright>`, `<dark>` and `<surface>` parameters are used with Plain Buttons and with the Special Effects styles (see `<flags>` below). These colors represent the highlighted color, the shadowed color, and the regular surface color that is used in Special Effects. Typical color combinations for these colors might be White, Dark-Gray and Light-Gray respectively for a "chiseled steel" appearance. Each of these values can contain a two-digit value representing any valid color code that may be used in the [RIP_COLOR](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_color) command.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: In addition to the special effects colors, are two additional colors that can be used, `<uline_color>` which is used for the color of the underline (in the text label), and `<corner_color>` which is used to display the colors of corners for things like the Bevel, Recess, etc.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<grp_no>` parameter determines which Button Group subsequent RIP_BUTTON commands will be associated with. Button Groups are used to maintain groups of Buttons for things like Radio Buttons and/or Checkbox Buttons. See the section on the BUTTON COMMAND for more information on these modes, and what Button Groups can offer. This value can range anywhere from 0-Z (i.e., 0-35). You should not mix Checkbox and Radio buttons in the same group. -- unpredictable things may happen if you do.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: Some `<flags>` are mutually exclusive. For example, you can only have one of the "Plain", "Icon", or "Clipboard" flags chosen at once. To better assist you in determining which values can be combined with each other, the right-most five columns in the next two tables explain if the specific flag can be used under a specific condition. For example, you cannot choose the "Hot Icon" flag if you are dealing with a Clipboard Button. Another example is that you cannot underline the hotkey character in the label if it is not a Mouse Button.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: The Icon Button, Clipboard button and Plain flags have already been discussed. Following, will be more discussion of the various flags used in the preceding table: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS INVERTABLE (flag 2)** - This means that the button will be inverted when clicked. This flag is only useful when combined with the "Button is a Mouse Button - flag 1024) flag. Even if the button has special effects, those will be inverted as well as they are considered part of the button - all except for the Recessed effect. The recessed effect is NEVER considered part of the actual button image, and will never be part of the mouse field, button's image or anything - it is just extra graphics. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **RESET SCREEN AFTER BUTTON CLICK (flag 4)** - This flag is used when the button is considered a Mouse Button (flag 1024). What this means is that when the user clicks on the button, the screen will be reset exactly the same as a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command will do. The reset is performed before the host command is processed (if any). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY CHISEL SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 8)** - This displays a special effect on-top of the button image that gives the visual impression of an indented gutter just to the inside of the button's border. The amount of indentation varies depending on the size of the button. See below for a table of indentation values for the Chisel effect. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY RECESSED SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 16)** - This places a recessed one-pixel bevel around the exterior of the button. It is never considered part of the button's image. Its purpose is to give the button a more 3D look by making it appear that the button is "poking through" a hole in a dialog box. This effect is accomplished by placing a black outline (one pixel wide) around the exterior of the button's image (including bevel, etc), then placing a one-pixel wide inverted bevel around the black outline. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DROPSHADOW THE LABEL IF ANY (flag 32)** - This flag will instruct RIPscrip to place a dropshadowed version of the text label one pixel to the right and one pixel lower than the original label. This is accomplished by drawing the label first in the `<dback>` color, then drawing the label offset up-left in the `<dfore>`. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **AUTO-STAMP IMAGE INTO CLIPBOARD SLOT (flag 64)** - This option is also known as "Auto-Clip". What this means is right after the first button's image is rendered (including any special effects), it is automatically copied into another port specified by the `<other_port>` parameter. If that port is defined as port #0, then this mode is treated like a [RIP_GET_IMAGE](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_get_image) command, copying the image onto some clipboard port, by determining the clipboard pointer and establishing an offscreen bitmap port located at the first unused port number. If the `<other_port>` parameter is set to a value from 1-35, then a specific port number is used; that port is deleted (if it's in use) then re-defined. If the `<other_port>` parameter specifies the same port as the currently active drawing port, or if the clipboard pointer points to the current drawing port, then auto-clip mode is ignored. The Recessed special effect is not considered part of the button image for this flag and is not made part of the clipboard image. After the image is copied into a clipboard port, the label is drawn (this is so that the label is not placed into a clipboard port), then a number of flags in the current Button Style definition are altered. Specifically, the Icon and Plain flags are disabled, and Clipboard button enabled (thus making any subsequent buttons use the resultant Clipboard button image for their button's representation). In addition, the chisel, bevel, auto-clip and sunken flags are disabled. The final result is a Clipboard button with no special effects other than the Recessed effect (if any). This is most often used with Icon Buttons where every subsequent button uses the same Icon over and over again - the net result of this is less "disk usage" whenever a button is created; in addition, buttons will draw faster too. If this option is used, then the parameter `<other_port>` is used to determine which clipboard port to use for the stored image. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS AN ICON BUTTON (flag 128)** - See previous discussions on button types above. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS A PLAIN BUTTON (flag 256)** - See previous discussions on button types above. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY BEVEL SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 512)** - When this flag is active, a bevel will be drawn `<size>` pixels thick on the outside of the base image of the button. This makes the button that many pixels wider and taller in each direction. See the RIP*BUTTON for a more detailed description of the affects of the button's final size. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS A MOUSE BUTTON (flag 1024)** - When this flag is enabled, the button becomes a clickable mouse region. When this option is in use, the Invert flag and several others are available (see the preceding chart). When a button is a non-mouse button, then it is only used to draw a dialog box or an elaborate "static graphic" image of something that "looks" like a button. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **UNDERLINE HOT-KEYS IN LABEL (flag 2048)** - When this flag is active, the first occurence of the hot-key character in the button's label will be underlined using the `<uline_col>` color. Special care must be taken when underlining the character, taking into consideration if the character has a segment that goes below the "baseline" of the font. Consult the following section to determine what ASCII characters have these "descenders". Characters with descenders have the underline drawn slightly lower than for characters without them. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **MAKE ICON BUTTON USE HOT ICONS (flag 4096)** - A Hot Icon is a button that has an alternative image when the button is "depressed". Normally, when a button is an Icon button, some form of Icon File is used to create the image of the button (eg, EMAIL.BMP). When the Hot Icon flag is in use, whenever that button is depressed, rather than using the normal Icon File for the button's image, a different Icon File is used for the button's image. The filename would be the same filename as the original Icon, but with an extension of .BMH instead of .BMP. When Hot Icon is in use, the alternative Icon is stamped in COPY mode. If the file does not exist, then the original Icon's image is used, but pasted in NOT mode for the duration of the depression. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **ADJ. VERTICAL CENTERING OF LABEL (flag 8192)** - Some Labels may appear non-centered vertically when drawn using some fonts that are rather large. With this in mind, you have the option to adjust the vertical centering. What this does is take into consideration the height of any descenders of the label and calculate those into the overall height of the label before centering. If this flag is not used, then the descenders are not taken into consideration when the vertical centering is calculated. See the Font Metric tables below for more detailed information on font sizes and their associated metrics. This command has no effect if the Label orientation is LEFT or RIGHT of the button. It only applies to an orientation of TOP, BOTTOM or CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON BELONGS TO A RADIO GROUP (flag 16384)** - When this flag is used, then any buttons defined in this button `<group_no>` are considered to be radio buttons where only one of the buttons can be clicked (selected) at any particular time. If a button is not a radio button or a checkbox button, then the "selected" flag of the RIP*BUTTON command is ignored. When a Radio Button is clicked, any other radio button in that button group that is selected is automatically de-selected and the current one selected. Any host command is processed at the time of the button click. If a Radio Button is drawn initally as selected, then that host command is processed at the time of its initial drawing. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md) for a more complete description of Radio Buttons and how they interact with their Button Group and with each other. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY SUNKEN SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 32768)** - When this option is enabled, a one-pixel inverted bevel is drawn exactly one pixel to the inside of the base image of the button. This and the chisel effect are the only two special effects which physically "overwrite" portions of the base button image. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: Following is a more complete description of the flags described in the `<flags2>` parameter: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS IN A CHECK BOX GROUP (flag 1)** - When this flag is selected, then the button `<group_no>` is considered a Check-box group. When in this mode, the Radio Group flag is not accessible - A Button Group can be a Radio Button, a Check-box button or neither, but not more than one at the same time. A Check-box button group is a group of buttons where each button in the group can be either ON or OFF in any combination. In this way, more than one button in the group can be clicked at the same time. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md) for a complete discussion of how the Host Commands are processed for Check-Box buttons. If a check-box button is drawn as "pre-selected", then the Host Command is processed immediately upon inital drawing of the button (when it is received). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **HIGHLIGHT HOTKEY CHARACTER (flag 2)** - When this flag is active, then the first occurence of the hotkey character in the label will be hilighted using the `<uline_col>` color. This gives the user a visual impression of what keystroke they need to type in order to activate the button without the mouse. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **EXPLODE (ZOOM OUT WHEN CLICKED) (flag 4)** - This optional flag is designed to "zoom out" from the button when the user clicks on it. What is generally done is a dotted rectangle is drawn initially around the button and it is repeatedly redrawn over itself in XOR mode, constantly getting larger and larger until it hits the full size of the screen. This gives the visual impression that the button is zooming out to another screen. Each time another frame of the zooming rectangle is drawn, the previous rectangle on the inside of the new one is erased by XOR drawing the same rectangle over itself again. This option does not need to be supported in order to be considered a RIPscrip terminal, although it would be nice. In other words, this is not a "make or break" feature. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **LEFT JUSTIFY LABEL (TOP/CTR/BTM) (flag 8)** - If this option is enabled, then any TOP, CENTER or BOTTOM label orientations will be left justified to the left edge of the button. The exact indentation of the label from the interior of the button's base image depends on whether the chisel effect is active. If chisel is OFF, then the indentation is 10 pixel. If chisel is ON, then the indentation is 20 pixels. This option can be combined with the Adjust Vertical Centering flag only if the label orientation is CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **RIGHT JUSTIFY LABEL (TOP/CTR/BTM) (flag 16)** - If this option is enabled, then any TOP, CENTER or BOTTOM label orientations will be right justified to the right edge of the button. The exact indentation of the label from the interior of the button's base image depends on whether the chisel effect is active. If chisel is OFF, then the indentation is 10 pixel. If chisel is ON, then the indentation is 20 pixels. This option can be combined with the Adjust Vertical Centering flag only if the label orientation is CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **DON'T FILL-IN BUTTON INTERIOR** - If this option is enabled and the button is a Plain Button, then the interior of the Button will not be filled in with the surface color. By default, any plain button will have its interior filled in with the surface color. Use this option if you don't want the button face to be drawn. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **FILL-IN INTERIOR IN FILL PATTERN** - If this option is enabled in conjunction with a plain button, then the interior of the button that would normally be filled in with the surface color will instead, use the current Fill Color and Fill Pattern to fill in the interior. This allows for patterned button faces. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: This command physically creates a new Button using a previously defined [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style) in the current button style. You may have at most 128 different Mouse Buttons (you may have any number of non-Mouse Buttons). The `<slot>` parameter determines which button style slot is used to determine how this button appears. _(v2.A1)_ The ALPHA 4 draft removed the explicit `<slot>` parameters in favor of the current-style model. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<x0>` and `<y0>` parameters for this command designate the upper-left corner of the Button. This (X,Y) location may not be the actual "absolute" corner position of the Button, as it may be adjusted via the Special Effects functions that are part of the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command (see above).

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<x1>` and `<y1>` parameters are only used for Plain Buttons when you have not specified a specific Height and Width in the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command. These parameters are used in Dynamically Sized Buttons. If the Height and Width in the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE are non-zero, then these two parameters are set to zero.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<hotkey>` parameter is only used with Mouse Buttons. It is the ASCII code for the keystroke that will activate this Button. It is represented as a two-digit MegaNum. If this character exists in the text label, and the Underline flag or hilight hotkey flag is enabled in the RIP*BUTTON_STYLE, then the character will be underlined in the label. Control codes are allowable, and a value of 255 (decimal) corresponds to "any" key. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<flags>` parameter provides several different functions for each button. The possible "combinatorial" flags for this parameter are listed in the following table. Note that these values may be combined together (by adding their values) to arrive at the final flag parameter's value.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | Value | Description                                   |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | 1     | Draw button as already selected               |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | 2     | Button is "default" when \<ENTER\> is pressed |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Using a flag of 1 means that the Button is already "selected". By selected, we mean that it is already clicked and should be initially drawn as clicked. This is typically used for Radio Buttons and/or Check Boxes. This only affects the image. The Host Command WILL NOT be automatically sent to the host when a selected Button is drawn. If this parameter is set to 0, then the Button will be drawn in normal, unselected mode.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<text>` parameter for this command is somewhat different than those found in previously described RIPscrip commands. All other RIPscrip commands only have one text parameter. This command requires anywhere from 0-3 text parameters. The way RIPscrip accomplishes this is by separating each block in the `<text>` parameter with the delimiter `<>`. This text parameter delimiter is not needed before the first text block, but is necessary between the 1st and 2nd blocks, and the 2nd and 3rd blocks. Here is an example of a typical text parameter for this command:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text:
```text
ICONFILE.BMP<>TEXT LABEL<>HOST COMMAND
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The actual syntax of this text parameter is as follows:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text:
```text
[icon-file][[<>text-label][<>host-command]]
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The block described as ICONFILE.BMP is actually the Icon Filename that will be used for the Button if it is an Icon Button. If it is not an Icon Button, then this block will read `<>` all by itself (a "null" block). _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Note that we actually specified a file extension of ".BMP" for our icon filename. You shouldn't explicitly specify a filename extension like this if it is the default extension of the filename. The reason for this is that some platforms don't use file extensions and their use is not really appropriate. When in doubt, don't specify a file extension. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The .BMP file extension does not need to be included as part of the filename. If omitted, it will automatically be appended to the filename. If an extension is provided, it will be used verbatim. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The "TEXT LABEL" block is actually the text that will be used to descriptively label the Button. You may also specify a "null" block for no label (i.e., `<>`).

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The final block of the `<text>` parameter is the Host Command. This block contains any text that should be sent to the Host after this Button is clicked. This may contain any Control Characters, Pick-List definitions, Text Variables or Template Definitions. This block might be "segmented" into multiple Host Command segments. See [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md) for additional information on these Host Command features.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: When this command is stored in-memory, it is converted to global screen coordinates (for internal storage only). This makes it so that if you have mouse button regions defined in multiple different viewports, that each field will be properly inverted at the right location regardless of the currently defined viewport. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: NOTE: All Mouse Fields are scanned in "last in, first out" order. This means that the last-most received Mouse Button will be the first one scanned for a mouse click. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Not all of the blocks in the `<text>` parameter need to be specified. Here are examples of the valid combinations of text blocks:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | Parameter Example       | Description of the Text Parameter           |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>label<>host_cmd` | Specify all three blocks                    |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>label<>host_cmd`     | 2 blocks specified; no icon                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>label<>`         | 2 blocks specified; no host command         |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>label`           | 2 blocks specified; no host command         |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<><>host_cmd`          | 1 block specified; no icon or label         |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>label<>`             | 1 block specified; no icon or host command  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>label`               | 1 block specified; no icon or host command  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<><>`              | 1 block specified; no label or host command |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>`                | 1 block specified; no label or host command |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon`                  | 1 block specified; no label or host command |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<><><>`                | A blank text parameter; all blocks omitted  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<><>`                  | A blank text parameter; all blocks omitted  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>`                    | A blank text parameter; all blocks omitted  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Under RIPscrip 1.54 and earlier versions, button icon filenames ended with .ICN for normal icons, and .HIC for "Hot IcoN". Under 2.0 and later, these file extensions are different. For normal button icons, the extension .BMP is used for a standard bitmap, and .BMH is used for a "hot bitmap". _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: When a button is displayed that uses an icon/bitmap, special care must be taken when dealing with hot bitmaps. If the flag is present in the button style indicating to use hot icons, then when the button is displayed as selected then the hot bitmap (.BMH) file's image is used to display the button. If that file doesn't exist, then the normal bitmap button is displayed in an inverted state. If neither of these files are present, then the RIP*BUTTON command is ignored. *(v2.A3)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: If the host command string of the button cannot be parsed properly, then the button is completely ignored. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: NOTE: The `<res>` parameter is reserved for future use by TeleGrafix Communications, Inc.. It should be set to 0 for compatibility with future releases.

requirements.heading: The shipped 3.x button aesthetic
requirements.text: The 3.x corpus shows how TeleGrafix itself built buttons: rather than 1.54-style chiseled plain buttons, scenes stamp **bitmap skins** with [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) (TELBUT.BMP, RADIONEW.BMP, CHECKBOX.BMP) and lay `1U` buttons or [`1M` mouse fields](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse) over them; the corresponding `.BMH` files on disk are the pre-rendered **highlight-state** variants automatically shown while a hot-icon button is depressed (they are never named in any script - pairing is by filename convention; see [6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md#bmh---button-highlight-variants)). `1B` + `1U` with empty `<><>` blocks also serve as pure chisel-frame decorations. The example above is a plain radio-group demo button whose host command is empty - its behavior comes from the button-style flags. _Evidence: corpus (ICONS/\*.BMH pairs; BUTTONS.RIP, TELDEMOS.MNU)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: _Switches to a new button style_

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `B`            |

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `bstyle_num:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|2B <bstyle_num>` **Example:** `!|2B04`

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md#rip_switch_button_style)) · HLP (`RIP_SwitchButtonStyle`; button-style slots 0-35, `$SBS$`/`$RBS$` backup variables) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This command physically switches the currently active button style. Any subsequent button operations will use this new button style.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: You are allowed up to 36 separate button styles to switch between. Possible button style slot numbers are from 0-35 (0-Z).

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: When a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) or a proper [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) command is executed, then all unprotected button style slots are reset to the default button style. Also, the current button style is reset to button style number 0.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: The demos simply re-send [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style) before each button group instead of switching slots. _Evidence: corpus (absence)._

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: Speaker tone generation - waveform-style sounds produced by the terminal itself, triggered through Active [Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md) anywhere text variables are allowed; each variable's definition includes the exact `sound()`/`delay()` recipe so every terminal produces the same effect.

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: A terminal that does not implement a particular sound should still recognize the variable and do nothing (see the implementer note in [5.1](5.1-text-variables.md)).

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: _This is the 1.54 sound capability ([4.3 in the v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.3-tone-and-sound-generation.md)) carried forward through 2.0 ([4.4 in the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md)) into the 3.0 engine. Digitized audio **files** (`.WAV`) are a separate capability - see [4.5 Audio Files](4.5-audio-files.md) for the [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio) command and [5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md) for the `$)FILE.WAV$` host-command trigger. The summary table of all variables is in [9.1 Text Variable Reference](9.1-text-variable-reference.md)._

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (tone-command error strings; RIPTEL.HLP variable tables); SyncTERM (ripper.c:8235 `rv_sound`)._

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: These text variables generate different kinds of sounds. _(v2.A4)_ SyncTERM implements the default (parameterless) behaviors, two of them with source comments reading `// Literally in the spec.` - independent confirmation that the 2.00a4 recipes below describe the shipping behavior. _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:8235-8283)._

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver demonstrably contains this tone-generation family: its error strings validate tone commands with **frequency, duration, and increment sweep** parameters ("start frequency greater than stop", zero increment/duration errors), and RIPTEL.HLP's variable tables document the named sounds; `$RESET(SOUND)$` resets the sound subsystem ([5.1](5.1-text-variables.md#reset)). No wire-level opcode for direct tone commands has been recovered from the corpus _(the demos ship no audio at all)_. All sound variables are _actions_: they expand to an empty string and play a PC-speaker effect. _Evidence: HLP (tone-command error strings; RIPTEL.HLP variable tables); corpus (absence)._

requirements.text: **Format:** `$BEEP(frequency,length)$`

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $BEEP$

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: This Active Text Variable beeps the terminal, producing a Ctrl-G sound. No parameters are required. If none are provided then the frequency is assumed to be 1000 Hertz and the length of time that it should play is 75 milliseconds. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: This command allows you to specify no parameters (default settings), only one parameter (the frequency), or both parameters (frequency and length/duration). Under no circumstances will values for any of the two parameters above 65535 be permitted. If values above these limits are encountered then the variable is not processed. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: Note that this text variable has a 75 millisecond delay after the beep is complete where no sound is playing. Stringing multiple beeps together will have a noticable gap between the sounds. To play continuous tones at different frequencies, use multiple [`$T$`](#t) variables (see below). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: The C source code to play this sound is:

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text:
```c
sound(freq);     // the Hertz frequency to play
delay(length);   // millisecond delay
nosound();       // turn the sound off
delay(75);       // millisecond delay
```

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$BEEP(1000,75)$` ... equivalent to `$BEEP$` **Returns:** nothing

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: This Active Text Variable produces a sound like firing your energy weapons in a game. Now you too can blast away with the best of them. Trivia question: What does phaser stand for? See [`$REVPHASER$`](#revphaser) for the answers.

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: This command doesn't require any parameters. If none are specified then the START is assumed to be 2500 Hertz. STOP is assumed to be 50 Hertz, INC is assumed to be 20 Hertz increments and TIME is assumed to be 2 milliseconds. START must be greater than STOP and INC must be greater than zero. If none of these conditions are met then the defaults are used for the sound effect. _(v2.A1)_

Under no circumstances will values for any of the four parameters above 65535 be permitted. If values above these limits are encountered then the variable is not processed. _(v2.A4)_

$PHASER$

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: This Active Text Variable produces an audible sound. Both parameters are required. The \<freq\> parameter determines the frequency in Hertz and the \<length\> parameter determines the duration of the tone in milliseconds. frequency is assumed to be 1000 Hertz and the length of time that it should play is 75 milliseconds.

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: Digitized audio files: Microsoft **WAVE** (`.WAV`) PCM audio, played in the background while graphics and command processing continue - triggered from the command stream with [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](#rip_play_audio) or at the host-command layer with the `$)FILE.WAV$` playback prefix ([5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md#local-audio-playback---filewav)), and distinct from the terminal's own speaker-tone generation ([4.4 Tone & Sound Generation](4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md)), which needs no files at all.

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: _The 2.0 record is [4.5 in the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.5-audio-files.md); the file-role view is [6.1 Content File Roles](6.1-content-file-roles.md#wav-audio); byte-level RIFF/PCM layout and playback semantics are in the [v2.0 audio techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.4-audio.md)._

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: > **Editor's note - provenance:** WAV audio is not a 3.x innovation. RIP_PLAY_AUDIO entered the 2.0 specification at ALPHA 3 ("Added the RIP_PLAY_AUDIO command to playback a WAVE file" - 2.00a4 changelog) and **shipped** in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (January 1995): its manual introduces "digitized sound, in the form of .WAV files" (RIPTERM.DOC §4.3) with an Audio Setup screen for 19 sound boards (Sound Blaster, Pro Audio Spectrum, Gravis, etc.) and a `-A` command-line switch to disable digitized audio (RIPTERM.DOC §2.3), and the install carries HMI "Sound Operating System" drivers and a `RIPTERM.WAV` - both preserved (see the [RIPterm 2.30 audio assets](../../2.0/assets/audio/README.md)). TeleGrafix's December 1995 "RIP-2 Internet Multimedia" press release advertised the same "digital WAV sound". Like several other "3.x" features, it belongs to the RIPterm 2.30 product era that 3.x inherits (see the [revision history](1.0-introduction.md#revision-history)).

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: RIPscrip permits the support of digitized audio to be played in the background whild graphics and other operations are being performed. This includes playing sounds while graphical commands are being received from the host (without interruption).

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: The format of audio data used by RIPscrip is formally defined as straight audio data in the Microsoft WAVE file format. When dealing with host systems and downloading digitized audio data, or being told to play back audio data, RIPscrip will assume that you are working with WAVE files. For example, you might be told to playback a file named SOUND.WAV. If you are not internally supporting the actual WAVE format, but some other format, then you need to translate the name of the file to the correct name in your environment (if necessary) and perform the playback.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: When dealing with the [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) command, you need to be careful if you're not dealing with true WAVE files. The RIP_FILE_QUERY command is used to "detect" if a particular file is present on the target system and if so, if it is the right date/time and file size as the file on the host. The file on the host will be in WAVE format so if you're translating the files as they're received, you need to translate the RIP_FILE_QUERY information returned to the host so that it thinks that the file you have on your local hard disk is actually a WAVE file (ie, translate the file size to a WAVE equivalent). If the sizes and, or the time/date don't match, the host could download a new file to you (via the [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) command) thinking that your's is out of date.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: If you receive a WAVE file via the RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE command, or by some other meanss, and you're dealing with anther digitized audio file format, it is up to you to translate that WAVE file to your destination format. Consequently, if you are requested to send a WAVE file to the host system, and the host system is requesting a .WAV file, then you must translate your file to WAVE format before sending it.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: A Microsoft WAVE file is actually a normal "Pulse Code Modulation" digitized audio file stored with a bit of header information to identify whether it is stereo, 16-bit, 8-bit, etc, and other pieces of critical information for the decoding of the data. See the "Microsoft Windows Programmer's Reference Guide" for more specific information on the internal format of WAVE files.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A3._

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: _Play a local digitized audio file on the terminal_

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `w`              |

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `res:4 filename` |

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1w <res> <filename>` **Example:** `!|1w0000filename.wav`

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** none **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio)) · HLP (`RIP_PlayAudio`; the `$)FILE.WAV$` macro, `AUDIO=TRUE` in RIPscrip.ini, DLL export `RIP_AudioSupport`) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: This command will physically start a local .WAV file to play back on the user's remote terminal. The audio file must already exist in the user's hard disk in the same location as their bitmapped icons. If the file doesn't exist, then this command does nothing. If you specify the `<filename>` parameter as `$OFF$` then you will in effect be shutting off any currnetly running sound file. If a sound is already playing when this command is received, the older file that was playing will be terminated in place for the new file. You may use [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) to transfer audio files to the user's computer for subsequent playback.

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: NOTE: The `<res>` parameter is for future expansion. For compatibility with future relases of RIPscrip, it should be set to "0000".

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: The `$)FILE.WAV$` host-command prefix is not a separate audio system - it is the macro-layer way of invoking this same playback engine; the command-stream vs macro-layer comparison is in [5.3](5.3-local-playback.md#playback-prefixes-vs-dedicated-commands).

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver plainly supports the command - audio configuration, tone-command error strings, and the DLL entry points all appear in the HLP material - but the demo corpus ships no audio files and never issues it. Playback is effectively **single-channel**, fire-and-forget, last-command-wins: no evidence in any recovered source - spec, help strings, or corpus - shows mixing of simultaneous sounds or any way for the host to monitor playback status. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: Stopping, resets, and capability negotiation
requirements.text:
- **Stopping playback** - issue [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](#rip_play_audio) with `$OFF$` as the filename, or the [`$RESET(SOUND)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#reset) text variable, which aborts any playing digitized sound immediately (the DLL string table names a dedicated `resetKeywordSOUND` handler). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
- **Reset interaction** - a [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) with flag 2048 ("clears and stops any playing sound/music") silences audio as part of a scene reset; the soft-reset flag combination includes it. A plain [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) does not mention audio - hosts that need silence on reset should use the header flags or `$RESET(SOUND)$`. During a [`$D(time)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#d) delay, sound-related activity continues while everything else pauses. The 3.0 engine additionally tracks audio as a headerable object class in its [scene header segments](7.1-data-tables.md#audio-new-in-3x). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (header-segment error strings)._
- **Terminal-side switch** - the RIPtel installer creates the master toggle **`AUDIO=TRUE`** in the `[CONFIG]` section of `RIPscrip.ini`; the driver also exposes a `RIP_AudioSupport` client-API entry point. _Evidence: HLP._
- **Capability negotiation** - before relying on audio, query [`$IFS(WAV)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs): the terminal answers `1` if it can play WAVE files, `0` if not. `$IFS(LIST, _AUDIO)$` lists every audio format the terminal supports. The `$IFS$` processor is present in the 3.0 DLL's variable table. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
- **Delivery and housekeeping** - hosts deliver `.WAV` files with [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) (or a UU-encoded block), check freshness with [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query), and clean up with [`$FILEDEL$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel); audio files live alongside the icon files in the [connection directory](../../glossary.md)/default-directory family - see [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: The **Host Command Language (HCL)**, as the RIPscrip 3.0 White Paper names it - the action language that mouse regions, buttons, hotkeys and query expressions speak back to the host, divided into five areas: control characters, pop-up picklists, local playback directives, template directives, and text variables. A [host command](../../glossary.md) is, at its simplest, raw text transmitted to the host when a button or mouse field is clicked; every HCL directive is something the terminal interprets _before_ (or instead of) transmitting.

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP; 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: The other four HCL areas: [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md) · [pop-up picklists](5.4-popup-lists.md) · [local playback directives](5.3-local-playback.md) (`$>`, `$<`, `$(`, `$)`) · [template directives](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md)

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: _The 2.0 record this generation inherits is [5.0 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.0-host-commands.md) (1.54 lineage in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/5.0-host-commands.md)); the flowed-text/overflow machinery the HCL pagination variables drive is the [Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md)._

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11884-12001); HLP._

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text: A host-command string may be attached to:

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text:
- **Buttons** (`1U`) - the command block of the Text Parameter segment, executed when the button is clicked. Only buttons may contain [template directives](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md).
- **Mouse fields** (`1M`) - the host command executed when the field is clicked.
- **Queries** (`1` + ESC) - the query text itself is a host-command string, executed or deferred per the mode digit (below); full entry at [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query).
- **Keystroke macros / hotkeys** - hotkey-triggered buttons execute their command block exactly as if clicked.

requirements.heading: What Can Go Where
requirements.text: The 2.00a4 "what can go where" chart carries forward unchanged in the evidence:

requirements.heading: What Can Go Where
requirements.text: | Context | Templates | Data Text Vars | Active Text Vars | Pick Lists | Ctrl Chars | Local Playback |
