Now, which of these three templates is the currently active one? None of them! A template definition doesn't become the active template until that button containing its definition is clicked (selected). What this means is, you can have a bunch of buttons all belonging to the same Button Group with their own respective template definitions, but only the template relating to the most recently clicked button will be the currently active template for that group.

requirements.heading: Basic Template Mechanics
requirements.text: There are two ways of activating a template:

requirements.heading: Basic Template Mechanics
requirements.text:
1. Draw a button as "pre-selected" - in other words, the button is drawn pre-clicked immediately when it is received by the terminal. When this happens, the Host Command for that button is processed immediately and if a template definition exists in that host command, it is acted upon immediately thus making that template the currently active template for that Group.
2. The user clicks on a button containing a template definition. If a template is already active in that group, it is overwritten by the newly activated template.

requirements.heading: Basic Template Mechanics
requirements.text: In either case when templates are defined, nothing is actually transmitted to the BBS unless the Command Block contains some Direct Host Command sub-block(s) like this:

requirements.heading: Basic Template Mechanics
requirements.text:
```text
[5:]Template definition[]hello world^m
```

requirements.heading: Basic Template Mechanics
requirements.text: If this button were clicked, then Group number 5 would have the template activated with the template text "Template definition". Then the Direct Host Command `hello world^m` would be transmitted to the BBS. In this example, we see how a single host command can do multiple things - in this case, it defined a template in group #5 AND transmitted something to the BBS!

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11736-11800)._

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Radio Buttons are a "type" of button group. Only one button in that group can be active (clicked) at any one time. If a button that is not active is clicked, any other buttons in that group that ARE clicked are de-selected and the one that is being clicked is selected. If that newly clicked button has a Host Command, it is processed. If it has a template definition, it too is processed, overwriting the currently defined template for the specified group. Since Radio Buttons can only have one currently active button in a single given Radio Group, similarly you can only have one template active for that group at any given moment.

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Check Box Buttons are another "type" of button group. Unlike Radio Buttons, Check Box buttons can have zero or more buttons active (clicked) at any one time. If a check box button group has ten buttons defined in it, zero, five or all ten of those buttons can be active simultaneously. Their respective Host Commands are all processed when the buttons are individually clicked. Now what about templates? Since you can only have one template defined in a group at any given moment, how do check box buttons accomplish this multiple-template concept? Whenever a check box button is clicked (or unclicked), the template for that group is re-calculated. Any buttons in that group that have template definitions are scanned, and any check box buttons in that group that are selected have their template definitions concatenated together (strung together) end on end. The result is one large template which is built up from the template definitions of each selected check box button. SyncTERM's `process_template_definition` (`ripper.c:11736-11800`) implements exactly this - when the defining button belongs to a radio or check-box group, it concatenates the `template_cmd` of every selected button in the group, in creation order.

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Let's take a couple simple examples step-by-step to see how templates are maintained internally.

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 1 - RADIO BUTTON TEMPLATES**

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Let's say you have four buttons in Button Group #3, and that button group is defined as a Radio Button group. Here are the host command definitions for each of those buttons in this example:

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Button #1:   [3:]ABCD
Button #2:   [3:]EFGH
Button #3:   [3:]IJKL
Button #4:   [3:]MNOP
```

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Now, if none of the buttons are clicked, then template group #3 is blank. If button #1 is clicked, the template for group #3 would be defined as "ABCD". Now, if button #4 is clicked, what would the template definition for group #3 be? That's right, "MNOP". Notice how only one of the given templates is active at any given moment.

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 2 - CHECK BOX TEMPLATES**

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Now let's explore the slightly more complex world of check box templates. As stated previously, check box templates can be strung along together to make a larger template - template construction of sorts. Let's say you have a Button Group #2 defined as a check box group with 7 buttons defined in it. Each of the buttons are initially drawn as "unselected", or unclicked (inactive). Here are the button host command definitions for each of the 7 buttons:

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Button #1:   [2:]Apples^m
Button #2:   [2:]Oranges^m
Button #3:   [2:]Cherries^m
Button #4:   [2:]Grapes^m
Button #5:   [2:]Pears^m
Button #6:   [2:]Banannas^m
Button #7:   [2:]Lemons^m
```

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: Now, if all 7 buttons are not clicked, then template group #2 would be blank. Let's click on some buttons and see what the template will become as we change which buttons are clicked and which aren't:

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Button #3 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Cherries^m
Button #5 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Cherries^mPears^m
Button #3 clicked (OFF) ... Template:  Pears^m
Button #5 clicked (OFF) ... Template:  <blank>
Button #2 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Oranges^m
Button #1 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Apples^mOranges^m
Button #4 clicked (ON) .... Template:  Apples^mOranges^m
                                       Grapes^m
```

requirements.heading: Radio Buttons and Check-Box Templates
requirements.text: As you can see, the active template for a check box group is actually a combination of all selected buttons' templates, in ORDER OF DEFINITION, not in the order that they were clicked. Pay close attention to the end of the example where buttons were clicked in the order of 2, 1 then 4. If you notice the active template though, they are in 1, 2 then 4 order! They are in the order that the buttons were originally defined.

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11918-11923)._

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: There are two ways of using templates: Template Embedding and Template Chaining. Template embedding is a way of "inserting" a template inside another host command - you can insert the contents of an active template inside of a button's Direct Host Command. The direct host command is "expanded" around the inserted template and the contents of the specified template are made part of the direct host command.

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: Let's illustrate this with an example. Taking the check box example above which had a list of fruits as check box buttons, we will build a menu to take someone's order for fruit. Here is what the simple menu screen will look like:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: We will use two separate button groups. Group #0 will contain one button, the "Submit Order" button. Button Group #2 will be a check box button group containing our seven choices of fruits as in the preceding example. Here are the Host Command definitions for each of the eight buttons:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text:
```text
Group #0 (normal button - not a radio or check-box button)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     SUBMIT ORDER:   I wish to order $?2$ right now^m

Group #2 (check box button group)
─────────────────────────────────
     APPLES:    [2:]APPLES^m
     ORANGES:   [2:]ORANGES^m
     CHERRIES:  [2:]CHERRIES^m
     GRAPES:    [2:]GRAPES^m
     PEARS:     [2:]PEARS^m
     BANANNAS:  [2:]BANANNAS^m
     LEMONS:    [2:]LEMONS^m
```

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: Notice in the "Submit Order" button that there is a special code in the Direct Host Command, `$?2$`. This is a special variation of a [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md), used only in Template Embedding. It instructs the terminal to "insert template #2 here". The format of the template embedding code is:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: ...where "x" is the template identifier (0-Z) that is to be inserted. Now back to the example: if the user clicked on "APPLES", "CHERRIES", "PEARS" and "LEMONS" as in the menu shown above, then clicks on "Submit Order", the Submit Order button's host command reads:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text:
```text
I wish to order $?2$ right now^m
```

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: After template #2 is inserted where the embedding code is, the host command would look like this:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text:
```text
I wish to order APPLES^mCHERRIES^mPEARS^mLEMONS^m right now^m
```

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: And after the `^m`'s are converted to carriage returns the final host command would be like this:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text:
```text
I wish to order APPLES
CHERRIES
PEARS
LEMONS
right now
```

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: What if the user didn't click on any of the fruits, but did click on the Submit Order button? Well, since template #2 belongs to a group that is a Check Box group, which can have zero or more items selected simultaneously, the `$?2$` code would be expanded to a null string, or nothing, so the final host command would be:

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text:
```text
I wish to order  right now
```

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: If template #2 was associated with a Radio group which has to have one button clicked at all times, and none of the buttons were active, then the terminal would hilight all the radio buttons in group #2 and instruct the user to choose one first. This is done automatically by the terminal, you don't need to worry about Radio Buttons.

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: Just remember, Check Box buttons can legitimately have a blank template, but Radio Buttons cannot due to the very nature of the buttons.

requirements.heading: Embedded Templates - `$?N$`
requirements.text: The final host command after template embedding is limited to 4096 bytes of data. If a host command would grow beyond 4096 bytes due to embedding, it is truncated to exactly 4096 bytes.

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11949-11982)._

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: Template Chaining is the second form of using templates. Rather than inserting the contents of a template into a host command, like in embedding, template chaining feeds data into a template and then takes the result and transmits that to the BBS. In other words, Template Embedding inserts a template into a Host Command. In Template Chaining, a Host Command is inserted into a template (the exact opposite).

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: Template Chaining uses a similar insertion code to embedding but with a subtle difference - there is no template identifier. The code is:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: This is a "generic insertion code". It is used in the template definition itself, not in the Direct Host Command like the template embedding code was used. The actual data that replaces the `$?$` depends on the Direct Host Command that is "feeding" the template.

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: A template chaining operation is performed almost exactly like defining a template with a subtle difference: the colon (`:`) is omitted from the template definition like this:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[5]This is template chaining
[5:]This is template definition
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: What's the difference? In the case of the `[5:]`, a template for group #5 is defined. In the `[5]` example, the template chaining instruction is invoked on Template #5. The phrase "This is template chaining" will be fed into template number 5. If template number 5 has a generic insertion code `$?$` in it, then it will be replaced with the phrase "This is template chaining". The final result after the replacement will be a direct host command that will be transmitted to the BBS. Since template #5 doesn't have an insertion code, the phrase "This is template chaining" will be lost in the chaining process and the final host command would be "This is template definition".

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: Here are a couple examples of template chaining illustrating several ways that it may be used (we'll only show "active" template definitions):

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[3:]This is a plain old template
[4:]This template inserts $?$ here!
[5:]This has two insertion codes $?$ and $?$

[3]This text is lost in the chaining process
[4]SOMETHING
[5]HERE
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: This would be the result of the three chaining operations:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
3 ... This is a plain old template
4 ... This template inserts SOMETHING here!
5 ... This has two insertion codes HERE and HERE
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: There are three distinctly different situations in this example. The first shows a regular template without an insertion code being used in a chaining operation - the data that was fed into template #3 was lost because template #3 didn't have an insertion code. In the second example, a single insertion code is used and the word "SOMETHING" is inserted in place of the insertion code. The third example shows that an insertion code can be used more than once in a given template.

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: What if you tried to chain to a template that hasn't been activated yet (ie, a blank template)? If the template in question belongs to a radio group, then the terminal would instruct the user to click on one of the radio buttons to activate the template (he doesn't know that templates are involved of course). If it was a check box template, then the final host command would be nothing and in effect, nothing would be transmitted to the host. If the template in question belonged to a generic button group, then also nothing would get transmitted to the BBS.

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: In the preceding examples, only one template was used (chained-to). In reality, you can chain to multiple templates with ease. Just add the template identifiers for the templates you want to chain to in the order you wish to chain to, like this:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[1E3]This is a three-level chaining operation
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: The Host Command would be fed into template #1 first. After any replacements, the result of the template #1 chaining would be fed into template #E. After any replacements/insertions are performed on template #E, the final result is fed into template #3, and the final result of that chaining operation is sent to the BBS.

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: Here is an example of multiple template chaining calls:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[1:]red green $?$ blue
[E:]LOUD QUIET $?$ YELL
[3:]soft $?$ hard smooth gritty

[1E3](host command)
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: We can break this down conceptually into three separate chaining operations to illustrate what happens step-by-step:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[1E3](host command)
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: Results in:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[E3]red green (host command) blue
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: Resulting in:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
[3]LOUD QUIET red green (host command) blue YELL
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: And then finally:

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text:
```text
soft LOUD QUIET red green (host command) blue YELL hard smooth gritty
```

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: This last phrase is then sent to the BBS verbatim. Template chaining is useful for controlling HOW particular data is transmitted to the BBS, while template embedding is useful for controlling WHAT data is transmitted to the BBS. You can think of template chaining as a method of defining "commands" that will be sent to the BBS where the commands can be different depending on which buttons are clicked in that group. Template embedding on the other hand is often used for controlling the data parameters that are used with particular commands.

requirements.heading: Template Chaining - `[ABC]`
requirements.text: You are allowed up to 36 separate template chaining levels in one template chaining operation. After all chaining is completed, the final host command cannot exceed 4096 bytes. If a chaining operation would exceed that amount, it is truncated to exactly 4096 bytes.

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: Template Embedding and Template Chaining do not need to be separate methods. You can combine them if you wish - you can have embedded templates inside of template chains. This provides for utter flexibility in doing whatever you want.

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: Here are a couple of examples of combinations:

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 1**

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
[5:]EMBEDDED VALUE

[3:]Here is a $?$ and an $?5$

[3]CHAINED HOST COMMAND
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: This would result in:

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
Here is a CHAINED HOST COMMAND and an EMBEDDED VALUE
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 2**

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
[5:]EMBEDDED VALUE

[3:]Here is a $?$ and an $?5$
[4:]print("$?$")

[34]CHAINED HOST COMMAND
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: This would result in:

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
print("Here is a CHAINED HOST COMMAND and an EMBEDDED VALUE")
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 3**

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
[4:](hello)
[5:]ANOTHER $?5$ EMBEDDED $?4$ VALUE

[3:]Here is a $?$ and $?5$

[3]CHAINED COMMAND
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: This would result in:

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
Here is a CHAINED COMMAND and ANOTHER ANOTHER $?5$ EMBEDDED $?4$
VALUE EMBEDDED (hello) VALUE
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: Taking this one step-by-step:

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
Step #1:   Here is a CHAINED COMMAND and $?5$

Step #2:   Here is a CHAINED COMMAND and ANOTHER $?5$
           EMBEDDED $?4$ VALUE

Step #3:   Here is a CHAINED COMMAND and ANOTHER ANOTHER
           $?5$ EMBEDDED $?4$ VALUE EMBEDDED (hello) VALUE

     <end of processing>
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 4**

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: This would result in:

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text:
```text
print("print("HELLO (silly) WORLD")^m")^m
```

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: Example #1 shows a situation with a single chaining operation and a single embedding operation done at the same time. Example #2 shows a more complex situation where multiple levels of template chaining are going on while embedding is also being used.

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: Example #3 is somewhat different though. Why weren't the embedded template codes expanded at the lowest level of template #5? If you look closely at template #5, it has an insertion code instructing the system to insert template #5 (itself) in the middle of the template. This is legal, but only because an embedded template inside an embedded template cannot have any more embedding performed on it. In other words, you are allowed up to two levels of embedded templates, but the lowest level (2nd) cannot have any insertion codes, text variables, control characters or pick-list definitions in it - if it does, they will be treated as "raw" text instead of host command directives.

requirements.heading: Advanced Template Concepts
requirements.text: Example #4 shows a more involved Template Chaining operation in which the same template is chained to more than once in a given operation. This is allowable for extra flexibility, although in the real world will probably not be used much.

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: In any template definition or host command, you can have [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md), [pick lists](5.4-popup-lists.md) or control characters anywhere. You can freely use them in a Direct Host Command, in a template chain and in embedded templates. They do get a bit odd though in how they interact with Embedded Templates - but only if you have an embedded template within an embedded template. Which host-command features may appear where is summarized in [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md#what-can-go-where).

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Recall from the previous discussion: at the lowest level of the embedding, there is no processing done on the string of text. This is to prevent endless loops and combinatorial explosion of data and CPU time. Text variables, pick lists and control characters WILL be processed at the first level of an embedded template, but not at the second level.

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Here are some examples that better illustrate text variables:

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 1**

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
[3:]The date is $DATE$ ... $?$

[3]HELLO
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Results in:

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
The date is 07/18/93 ... HELLO
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 2**

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
[3:]The date is $DATE$

HELLO THERE, $?3$
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Results in:

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
HELLO THERE, The date is 07/18/93
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 3**

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
[2:]The time is $TIME$^m
[3:]The date is $DATE$^m

HELLO THERE^m$?3$$?2$
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Results in:

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
HELLO THERE
The date is 07/18/93
The time is 03:43:32
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: **EXAMPLE 4**

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
[1:]The day is $DOW$^m

[2:]The time is $TIME$^m
[3:]The date is $DATE$^m$?1$^m

HELLO THERE^m($?3$)($?4$)($?1$)
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Results in:

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
HELLO THERE
(The date is 07/18/93)
The day is $DOW$^m
(The time is 03:43:32)
(The day is Sunday)
```

requirements.heading: Host Command Language and Templates
requirements.text: Notice how the `$?1$` embedded template used in template #3 does not get processed - it is just inserted raw.

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text: Template definitions may contain text variables, pick lists, control characters, and template insertion codes. When do these special "directives" get processed? The answer is when the template gets USED, not when it becomes ACTIVE! To better illustrate this, let's look at a simple example.

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text: Let's say you have three radio buttons (group #2) on the screen and another button (group #0) which uses the template for the radio button group. Here's the host command definitions for each of these four buttons:

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Group #2 - Radio Button Group
─────────────────────────────
     Button #1:  [2:]It's a pretty day at $TIME$
     Button #2:  [2:]It's a rainy day at $TIME$
     Button #3:  [2:]It's a hazy day at $TIME$

Group #0 - Ordinary button group
────────────────────────────────
     Button #4:  Today's forecast:^m$?2$
```

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text: Now, let's say that none of the radio buttons are drawn as "selected" for starters. At 11:45:03 in the morning, the user clicks on button #2 indicating it's a rainy day. The active template for group #2 would be defined as:

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text:
```text
It's a rainy day at $TIME$
```

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text: At 11:46:37 he clicks on the Forecast button. The host command sent to the BBS would be:

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Today's forecast:
It's a rainy day at 11:46:37
```

requirements.heading: Processing of Templates
requirements.text: Notice that the time that is inserted in place of `$TIME$` is the time that the user clicked on the Forecast button, NOT the time he clicked on the "rainy day" button which activated the proper template. This illustrates that text variables, pick lists, and control characters are not "processed" until they are referenced (used) by some other button or template in an active Host Command situation.

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text: Remember that a single Host Command can be segmented into multiple "Command Blocks" by separating them with the delimiter `[]`. Here's a real-world example of a host command broken down into several command blocks:

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
[3:]Template Definition[4]Template chaining[]BBS TEXT
```

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text: If you look carefully at the above host command, three distinct things are happening. First, template #3 is defined with the text "Template Definition". Secondly, the phrase "Template chaining" is chained (fed) into template #4 (whatever that one is) and the final result of the chaining operation is sent to the BBS. Finally, the last command block is processed which happens to be a Direct Host Command, so the text "BBS TEXT" will be transmitted to the Host as well.

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text: If a host command doesn't have one of the command block delimiters like a template definition (eg, `[3:]`), or a template chain directive (eg, `[3]`), or a Direct Host Command Directive (eg, `[]`), then the Host Command is, by default, considered to be a Direct Host Command. The following are all considered Direct Host Commands and they all do the exact same thing:

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
HELLO^mWORLD^m
HELLO^m[]WORLD^m
[]HELLO^mWORLD^m
[]HELLO^m[]WORLD^m
```

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text: Here are some more examples of Command Blocks using the previous example as a foundation, but this time we throw in another command block. Again, all four of these examples do the exact same thing:

requirements.heading: Command Block Segmentation and Templates
requirements.text:
```text
HELLO^mWORLD^m[3:]Template Definition
HELLO^m[]WORLD^m[3:]Template Definition
[]HELLO^mWORLD^m[3:]Template Definition
[]HELLO^m[]WORLD^m[3:]Template Definition
```

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: If you think about Command Blocks, you might be inclined to think that figuring out which template definition block of a command block to activate might get insane. It could! Look at the following set of three Radio Button definitions:

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Button #1:  [3:]Hello world[3:]This is Pluto
Button #2:  [3:]Hello world[3:]This is Saturn
Button #3:  [3:]Hello world[3:]This is Jupiter
```

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: What happens if button #2 is clicked, thus activating that template? What template command block is used to create the final, active template? The answer is the last one! The text that becomes the actual active template for template #3 would be this:

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
This is Saturn
```

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: If a Host Command references this template as in the following example, you will see that the secondary template definition is the one that is actually in use:

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
I'm a martian singing in the rain^m$?3$
```

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: Resulting in:

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
I'm a martian singing in the rain
This is Saturn
```

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: In short, Command Blocks are processed in all situations, and if a discrepancy exists where two or more template definitions in the same Host String correspond to the same template group, the last definition is the one that becomes active. This applies even if you are dealing with Check Box buttons. In the above example of the martian, if Buttons #1, 2 and 3 were Check Box Buttons instead, the "Hello World" template definitions would still be lost and would NOT get concatenated together to create the final Host Command. If buttons #1 and #3 are clicked, then template #3 would be:

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
This is PlutoThis is Jupiter
```

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text: It would NOT be:

requirements.heading: Command Blocks, Radio and Check Box Templates
requirements.text:
```text
Hello worldThis is PlutoHello worldThis is Jupiter
```

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (MENU.DEF, MENU.MNU, MENU.MSE, MENU.ENT); SyncTERM absent._

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text: **New in this generation.** Beyond the slot templates, the RIPtel corpus reveals a second, entirely undocumented expansion mechanism: `<<NAME>>` expands to the value of the text variable `NAME` - anywhere in a command's argument text, including _inside_ a `$…$` reference. No surveyed non-TeleGrafix implementation supports it.

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text: The demo's menu system is built on it. A `.DEF` configuration file sets plain variables with the [set-syntax](5.0-host-commands.md#setting--reading-user-variables-from-host-commands):

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1^[0000$-=LAB2=Demos$
!|1^[0000$-=CMD2=>TELDEMOS.FN$
!|1^[0000$=-MSG2=Demonstrations of RIPscrip graphics$
```

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text: and the _generic_ menu scenes consume them by macro:

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1b3Y7YCCAY0000000000TELBUT.BMP|@809U<<LAB1>>       (button label text)
!|1M003W7YCEAW1000000ID=1:$<<CMD1>>$                 (host command, composed inside $...$)
!|@HSKA$&MSG<<FIELDID>>$                             (macro composing a variable NAME)
```

requirements.heading: The 3.x Macro Layer - `<<NAME>>`
requirements.text: The second line is the striking one: `$<<CMD1>>$` expands `<<CMD1>>` to `>TELDEMOS.FN` _first_, yielding `$>TELDEMOS.FN$` - a [local playback directive](5.3-local-playback.md) assembled at run time. The third composes a variable _name_ from the built-in `$FIELDID$`, then dereferences it with `$&…$` (see [Mouse-Field Identities](5.0-host-commands.md#mouse-field-identities---idn)). One `.MSE` overlay and one `.MNU` screen thus serve every menu in the product; only the tiny `.DEF` files differ. Expansion evidently happens before `$…$` parsing _(hypothesis on the exact evaluation order)_.

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (BUTTONS.RIP, TELDEMOS.RET, MENU.RET, SPECLEFX.RIP, FXSHWIMG.FN); SyncTERM absent._

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: **New in this generation.** The same `<<…>>` bracket introduces conditionals, evaluated before the containing command executes. Keywords are case-insensitive (`<<IF>>` and `<<if>>` both appear). The observed grammar:

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text:
```text
<<IF expr>> text <<ELSEIF expr>> text <<ELSE>> text <<ENDIF>>
```

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: with expressions built from `$…$` values, quoted string literals, the comparison operators `=` `!=` `<`, the connectives `AND` / `OR`, and parentheses. All from shipping TeleGrafix scripts:

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: **Choosing a background by color depth** - the most common idiom, appearing as the _filename argument_ of a `1R` ([RIP_READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene)):

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1R00000000<<IF $COLORS$<"256">>BLUEBACK.FN<<ELSE>>BLUEFADE.FN<<ENDIF>>
```

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: **A computed "Back" button** - as a mouse-field host command:

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1M000M0B37121000000ID=1:<<if $RETURN$!="">>$<<RETURN>>$<<else>>$NULL$<<endif>>
```

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: If a return scene was recorded (`$-=RETURN=>NEWSPAPR.RIP$`), play it; otherwise do nothing (`$NULL$`).

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: **Compound conditions** - connectives and parentheses (TELDEMOS.RET, MENU.RET):

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text:
```text
<<IF $NO_WIPES$="" OR $NO_WIPES$="NONE">>$>TELPORT.FN$<<ELSE>>$RESET$<<ENDIF>>
<<IF $TGMENU_WIPES$="1" and ($NO_WIPES$="" or $NO_WIPES$="NONE")>>$>WIPE01.FN$<<else>>$NULL$<<ENDIF>>
```

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: **The slideshow idiom** - the Special Effects demo's image cycler, rotating the same JPEGs that N2_PHOTO.RIP's newspaper gallery displays. The display subroutine FXSHWIMG.FN seeds the rotation on first use, testing whether a variable exists at all via `$INUSE(TV,name)$` (`TV` = the text-variable object class; returns `0`/`1`):

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1p0000<<IF $INUSE(TV,NEXT_IMG)$="0">>$-=NEXT_IMG=ASTRO.JPG$<<ENDIF>>$&NEXT_IMG$
```

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: and the "Next Image" button (SPECLEFX.RIP) advances it - a multi-branch `<<ELSEIF>>` spread over continued lines (`\` at line end continues the command):

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1U4GCUA2E60000<>Next Image<>\
<<IF $NEXT_IMG$="ASTRO.JPG">>$-=NEXT_IMG=JUPITER.JPG$\
<<ELSEIF $NEXT_IMG$="JUPITER.JPG">>$-=NEXT_IMG=BEACH2.JPG$\
<<ELSE>>$-=NEXT_IMG=ASTRO.JPG$\
<<ENDIF>>\
$>FXSHWIMG.FN$
```

requirements.heading: Inline Conditionals - `<<IF>> … <<ELSEIF>> … <<ELSE>> … <<ENDIF>>`
requirements.text: State machine, existence test, silent assignment, computed playback: a complete client-side program in five lines of button command. The matching cleanup is `$RESET(TV,NO_WIPES)$`, deleting a variable by name.

requirements.heading: Comparison Semantics
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; editorial analysis._

requirements.heading: Comparison Semantics
requirements.text: Operands are string-valued, and `$COLORS$<"256"` is the only ordering comparison observed. For the values that occur in practice (`16` vs `256` vs `65536`) lexical and numeric comparison happen to agree, so the corpus cannot distinguish which the driver performs - treat `<` on numbers other than these as unverified _(hypothesis)_. Equality against `""` tests emptiness/undefinedness and is used interchangeably with `="NONE"` sentinels by TeleGrafix's own scripts.

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: Local playback directives instruct the terminal to process a file _already on the user's disk_ instead of pulling content over the modem - the client/server heart of the [Host Command Language](5.0-host-commands.md), which the White Paper singles out as the way "to simulate menus on an online service locally, thus making it so that you don't have to transmit hardly anything over the modem." They are prefix [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md), usable from within any host command or query.

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP; 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: All four playback forms share one shape: `$`, a one-character prefix, the filename, `$`. RIPtel searches for the named file in the current host's [connection directory](../../glossary.md) first, then in `ICONS\`, then along the user-configured Search Path (which allowed CD-ROM-resident resources for games) - the [file override](../../glossary.md) lookup order detailed in [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#lookup-order-file-override). _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: | Directive     | Media                             | Example           |

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: | `$>FILE.RIP$` | RIPscrip scene (or any text file) | `$>NEWSPAPR.RIP$` |

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: | `$)FILE.WAV$` | Digitized audio                   | `$)TRAIN.WAV$`    |

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: | `$<FILE.BMP$` | Bitmap image                      | `$<BRICK.BMP$`    |

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: | `$(FILE.JPG$` | JPEG photograph                   | `$(ASTRO.JPG$`    |

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: The bracket mnemonic is deliberate, and inherited from 2.0: angle brackets (`>`, `<`) mark the _low-level_ playback primitives (raw RIPscrip, raw bitmap), while the parentheses (`)`, `(`) mark the _higher-level_ media objects (audio, compressed photos). _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: 5.3 Local File Playback
requirements.text: _The 2.0 record this carries forward is [5.3 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.3-local-playback.md); 1.54 had only `$>file$`, in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/5.3-local-playback.md)._

requirements.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; SyncTERM (ripper.c:7967-7970); corpus (DEMO-01.COL, TELCMDS.FN)._

requirements.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
requirements.text: You can re-play a `.RIP` file that you have locally on your hard disk from any place that allows text variables. After the initial dollar sign (`$`), enter the greater-than symbol (`>`) followed by the filename (with or without the `.RIP` extension), then ending in another dollar sign (`$`). Several examples:

requirements.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
requirements.text:
```text
$>MYFILE.RIP$
$>FILE1$
$>FILE1.RIP$$>FILE2.RIP$$>FILE3$
```

requirements.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
requirements.text: The file replays as if it had arrived from the host - with one critical difference: **the data is echoed locally only, never sent to the host**. If the file is a RIPscrip scene, its graphics draw and any mouse fields it defines are created, which is how pop-up dialogs and entire menu systems run without host traffic. The file need not be RIPscrip at all - any text file, ANSI screen, or (in 3.x) flowed article text is legal; see the [Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md) for the non-RIPscrip case.

requirements.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
requirements.text: SyncTERM implements the form as a special case checked _before_ text-variable lookup: a leading `>` routes the remainder to `rip_play_scene` (`ripper.c:7967-7970`).

requirements.heading: Local Scene Playback - `$>FILE.RIP$`
requirements.text: The RIPtel corpus leans on this directive harder than on any other: 34 distinct `$>file$` forms chain the whole demo together - `$>WIPE00.FN$` transition "subroutines", `$>newspapr.rip$` navigation, and the `$<<RETURN>>$` computed-return idiom described under [Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#the-3x-macro-layer---name). Filenames are case-insensitive in practice (`$>newspapr.rip$` and `$>NEWSPAPR.RIP$` both appear).

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text: `$)FILENAME$` plays a local digitized audio file - Microsoft WAVE format as far as the wire is concerned; a terminal using another native format must translate. The file extension itself is unimportant:

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text:
```text
$)AUDIOFILE.FIL$
$)TRAIN.WAV$
```

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text: The macro form is the HCL twin of the `1w` ([RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio)) command, and the same playback model applies:

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text:
- Audio plays **in the background, asynchronously** - graphics keep drawing and host data keeps arriving while sound plays.
- There is a **single playback channel**: starting a new file terminates whatever is currently playing.
- The reserved filename `$OFF$` (i.e. `1w` with filename `$OFF$`) silences the current sound.
- If the file does not exist locally, the directive does nothing; hosts deliver audio files ahead of time via block transfer ([6.2](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md)).

requirements.heading: Local Audio Playback - `$)FILE.WAV$`
requirements.text: See [4.5 Audio Files](4.5-audio-files.md) for the audio format details. Note that RIPtel 3.1's install sets `AUDIO=TRUE` in `RIPSCRIP.INI` and its help advertises "background digitized audio," but the demo corpus itself ships no `.WAV` files and never issues an audio command - the demos are silent. _Evidence: corpus; HLP._

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text: `$<FILENAME.BMP$` places a local bitmap (`.BMP`) file onto the screen through the current **image style** (`1i`, [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style)): the bitmap is displayed inside the current image settings and adheres to them. This mode of displaying a BMP file is the only method for showing a BMP via the image-style settings. If no image style definition has been recorded, the bitmap is shown at the maximum size of the current viewport - scaled to fill it entirely.

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text: For the purposes of universality, the bitmap is shown using the current screen's color palette and "auto-dithering" mode. RIPTEL.HLP is explicit that the full flexibility of `RIP_LoadBitmap` (palette modes, clipping options - [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap)) is _not_ available from the macro form; use the wire command when you need it. This directive is provided as a simple method of showing a bitmapped image from within a host command:

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text:
```text
$<FILENAME.BMP$
```

requirements.heading: Local Bitmap Playback - `$<FILE.BMP$`
requirements.text: Note that this uses the less-than sign, unlike the greater-than sign used for local RIPscrip playback - the opposite angle-bracket marks it as a low-level primitive playback, per the bracket mnemonic above.

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; corpus (N2_PHOTO.RIP)._

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text: `$(FILENAME.JPG$` displays a compressed photographic image the same way - through the current image style, or full-viewport when none is recorded. The JPEG file is considered a higher-level object than a raw bitmap, so it uses the parenthesis prefix instead of the angle bracket. JPEG is the only supported photo format in the 3.0 driver:

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text:
```text
$(MYFILE.JPG$
```

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text: A companion action variable positions the _next_ image without redefining a style on the wire:

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text:
```text
$IMGSTYLE(cur,x0,y0,x1,y1)$
```

requirements.heading: Local JPEG Playback - `$(FILE.JPG$`
requirements.text: where `cur` selects the current screen port. The demo corpus displays its sixteen JPEGs through the wire commands (`1i` + `1p`) rather than the macro form, but the macro and `$IMGSTYLE$` are documented in RIPtel's help as the host-command route to the same machinery.

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: **`$>file.rip$` - scene playback from a mouse field.** A mouse field whose host command is nothing but a playback variable displays a locally stored dialog scene when clicked - nothing is sent to the host:

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: Clicking the region replays `HELPBOX.RIP` from the connection directory (or the default `ICONS\` directory, or the search path). If `HELPBOX.RIP` itself defines mouse fields - say an "OK" button whose host command is `$PCB$` to paste back the screen area saved earlier - the pop-up is fully interactive without any host round-trip. _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: The shipping corpus does exactly this at production scale - a DEMO-01.COL mouse field records a return scene, then plays the weather page, all locally:

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text:
```text
!|1M000G7Y8ICC1000000ID=2:$-=RETURN=>NEWSPAPR.RIP$$>TWEATHER.RIP$
```

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (DEMO-01.COL)._

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: **`$(file.JPG$` - image display from a button.** A button that shows a locally cached photograph inside the current image area when clicked:

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text:
```text
!|1U0A0A00003200<>View photo<>$(SUNSET.JPG$
```

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: The image scales into the image area exactly as if the host had issued [RIP_IMAGE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image) - but with no transmission cost, because `SUNSET.JPG` was delivered earlier by block mode. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: **`$)FILE.WAV$` - audio playback from a host command.** A host command (or portion of one) that starts background audio:

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text:
```text
$)TRAIN.WAV$Now boarding^m
```

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: The terminal starts `TRAIN.WAV` playing in the background and transmits `Now boarding` plus a carriage return to the host. Stopping playback (`$OFF$` semantics) belongs to [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio) - see [4.5 Audio Files](4.5-audio-files.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: **Chained playback.** Several files can be replayed back-to-back from one command, as in `$>FILE1.RIP$$>FILE2.RIP$$>FILE3$` - useful for assembling a scene from locally cached parts. The corpus's `.RET` return scripts chain a transition wipe and a destination scene the same way (`$>WIPE01.FN$` … `$>TELPORT.FN$`). _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus (TELDEMOS.RET, MENU.RET)._

requirements.heading: Worked examples per prefix
requirements.text: **Computed playback (3.x).** With the [macro layer](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#the-3x-macro-layer---name), the filename itself can be assembled at run time: `$<<CMD1>>$` expands `<<CMD1>>` to `>TELDEMOS.FN` first, yielding the playback directive `$>TELDEMOS.FN$` - the mechanism behind RIPtel's generic menu scenes. _Evidence: corpus (MENU.MSE)._

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: Same media, different invocation path: the chapter-4 commands live in the RIPscrip **command stream** (the host draws _now_, mid-scene), while the playback prefixes live at the **host-command/macro layer** (the action fires later, when a button or mouse field is clicked, or when a query is processed). The prefix forms also deliberately trade flexibility for brevity - fixed display settings where the commands take parameters.

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: | Media | Command-stream command | Host-command prefix | Differences |

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: | RIPscrip scene | [RIP_READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene) | `$>file.rip$` | Same playback engine; the prefix form is the only one usable from a click |

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: | BMP bitmap | [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) / [RIP_LOAD_ICON](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_icon) | `$<file.BMP$` | The prefix displays via the image-style area with auto-dithering and the current palette only; the commands offer position, scaling, put modes, palette and transparency flags |

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: | JPEG image | [RIP_IMAGE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image) | `$(file.JPG$` | Both display via the current [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style) settings |

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: | WAV audio | [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio) | `$)FILE.WAV$` | Both start background playback; the command form also defines `$OFF$` to stop a running sound |

requirements.heading: Playback prefixes vs dedicated commands
requirements.text: The corpus shows both paths in production use, split exactly along this line: scene navigation and subroutines fire from clicks via `$>` (34 distinct forms) while mid-scene subroutine calls use `1R` (92 uses in 34 files), and the sixteen demo JPEGs display via the wire commands (`1i` + `1p`) because they are drawn during scene playback, not on click. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
requirements.text: Pop-Up Pick Lists - host-defined selection lists that pop up on the terminal and splice the chosen entry's response into the [host command](5.0-host-commands.md) being built, legal anywhere a [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md) is. The mechanism carries into 3.x from 2.0 intact, with one 3.x extension: an optional pop-up position.

requirements.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11356-11635, 11936-11948)._

requirements.heading: 5.4 Pop-Up Lists
requirements.text: _The 2.0 record is [5.4 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.4-popup-lists.md) (1.54 lineage in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/5.4-popup-lists.md))._

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: Any place that you can use a text variable (Queries, Button and Mouse Field return strings, and Keystroke Macros), you can take advantage of a unique feature of RIPscrip - Pop-Up Pick Lists. A Pop-Up Pick List is simply a list that pops up allowing the user to choose from one of several available values. Whichever entry in the list is chosen will insert its associated response into the host command returned back to your host.

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: A list is created by putting the special list instructions inside two sets of parentheses, `((` and `))`. The list consists of an optional question followed by two colons (`::`), followed by one or more comma-separated list entries. For example, `((Send Email to?::Sysop,Cosysop,Joe))` says to pop up a list asking "Send Email to?", giving the choices of "Sysop", "Cosysop", and "Joe".

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: The full 3.x syntax, with every extension in place:

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text:
```text
((*x,y:Question::response@Description,response@Description,...))
```

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | Element | Meaning |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `((` … `))` | List delimiters |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `*` | Response required - the user cannot ESC out of the list |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `x,y:` | Pop-up position in [world coordinates](../../glossary.md); omit either value (keep the comma) to center on that axis _(new in 3.x - HLP)_ |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `Question` | Prompt text; if omitted, the default is `Choose one of the following:` |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `::` | Separates the question from the entries |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `response` | The text spliced into the host command when chosen |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `@Description` | Optional display text shown in the list instead of the response |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: | `~h~` or `_h_` | Hotkey markup around a character of the description; the first marked character is the active hotkey |

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: By default, if the user presses ESC instead of picking an entry in the list, then nothing is inserted into the text of the command. You can indicate that the user must pick an entry by putting an asterisk (`*`) at the beginning of the question - for example, `((*Send Mail to?::Sysop,Joe))` forces a choice of either Sysop or Joe.

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: In the previous examples, Sysop and Joe are the text responses that are inserted into your host command. They are also what is displayed in the listing. If you want to display something else in the listing instead of the return text, add an `@description` to the end of the entry. For example:

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text:
```text
((Send Mail To?::Sysop@Head Honcho,Cosysop,Joe))
```

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: ...would display a pop-up pick list of Head Honcho, Cosysop, and Joe.

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: One final feature allows you to specify a hotkey for each entry in the list. To highlight the first character of an entry (thus allowing that key to activate the entry), put a tilde (`~`) or an underline (`_`) before and after the keystroke: `_S_ysop` highlights the "S" in "Sysop". You can highlight more than one character, but only the first one will be the active hotkey. If you omit the second tilde or underline, then the remainder of the description will be highlighted.

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** If you use a tilde or an underline in the Text Response (not the description), those characters are inserted into your host command when it is transmitted to the host. You probably don't want to do this. Recommendation: only use hotkey features on list entries where you specify a description!

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: If you do not specify a question, then the list defaults to the question:

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text:
```text
Choose one of the following:
```

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: Rules carried forward from 2.0, all confirmed by RIPtel's help: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text:
- Up to **64 entries** per list _(v2.A1)_; in earlier revisions of RIPscrip, a maximum of 20 entries was allowed. If the total number of entries makes the picklist too tall to fit on the screen, it must handle some form of scrolling mechanism. _(v2.A1)_
- In RIPterm version 1.52 and earlier, the total length of a pick list was 256 bytes; in version 1.53 and later, this limit was increased to 1024 bytes. _(v1.53)_
- The characters `!`, `\` and `|` have special significance in the RIPscrip language; to use them in a _Text Response_ they must be escaped with a backslash (`!` becomes `\!`, `\` becomes `\\`, and `\|` for the vertical bar). The hotkey markers `~` and `_` **cannot** be escaped - if they exist in a Text Response they are returned to the host, but everything after them is underlined and the first character is treated as the hotkey. Put hotkeys in descriptions, not responses.
- If the user presses ESC on a non-required list, nothing is inserted.

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: Examples, from simplest to fullest:

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text:
```text
((Send E-Mail to?::Sysop,Joe,Mike))
((*Send E-Mail to?::Sysop@The Head Honcho,Joe,Mike@My Brother))
((::Sysop@_T_he Head Honcho,Joe,Mike@My _B_rother))
((*10,50:Order which fruit?::A@_A_pples,O@_O_ranges,C@_C_herries))
```

requirements.heading: Pop-Up Pick Lists
requirements.text: The last example uses the 3.x position extension - the list pops up at world coordinates (10, 50) rather than centered. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Recursion into the HCL
requirements.text: _Evidence: SyncTERM (ripper.c:11936-11948, 11890-11896)._

requirements.heading: Recursion into the HCL
requirements.text: The chosen response is not merely transmitted - it is **re-fed through the host-command interpreter**. A pick-list entry may therefore itself contain text variables, control characters, [playback directives](5.3-local-playback.md), or another pick list; SyncTERM implements exactly this (`do_popup`'s result recursing through `handle_command_str`), with recursion depth capped at 64. An entry prefixed `*` inside the option list forces that answer without user interaction - the mechanism SyncTERM uses to auto-answer forced choices. A menu that plays local scenes, a scene that pops another menu: pick lists plus `$>` playback form a small but genuinely programmable UI layer, years before such things were commonplace.

requirements.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 (mechanism; constructed example)._

requirements.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
requirements.text: Consider a [mouse field](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md) whose host command embeds a pick list:

requirements.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
requirements.text:
```text
!|1M0000122912340100000E((*Read which area?::MAIL@_M_ail,NEWS@_N_ews,FILES@_F_iles))^m
```

requirements.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
requirements.text: The flow when the user clicks the field:

requirements.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
requirements.text:
1. The terminal begins expanding the field's host command and encounters the `((…))` list definition.
2. A pop-up appears titled "Read which area?" listing **M**ail, **N**ews, **F**iles (hotkeys highlighted). The leading `*` means ESC is refused - the user must choose.
3. The user picks "News". The list expression is replaced by that entry's text response, `NEWS`.
4. Expansion continues - in 3.x, the response itself is re-fed through the interpreter (recursion above), so a response containing directives would execute them here. The trailing `^m` becomes a carriage return, and the terminal transmits `E NEWS` followed by CR to the host - which sees an ordinary command string and never knows a menu was involved.

requirements.heading: Worked example: definition and response flow
requirements.text: Nothing about the list persists after expansion; clicking the field again pops the list again.

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: The wire commands that exchange data and files with the host: text-variable query and definition, local scene playback from the command stream, file queries, timing control for local playback, block-mode file transfer, UU-encoded data blocks, capability negotiation and the multi-lingual groundwork.

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: **None of the level-3/level-9 commands on this page appears anywhere in the RIPtel demo corpus**: the demos are local scene files whose resources (bitmaps, JPEGs, fonts) already sit on disk, so nothing ever needs transferring or rate-limiting. All are nonetheless attested for 3.x - each is named in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory (one under a new name, noted below), and SyncTERM implements the block-mode transfer with a full protocol table. The query commands, by contrast, are the most heavily used commands in the corpus. _Evidence: HLP; corpus; SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: Capability negotiation in brief: query [`$IFS(keyword)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs) (Is Feature Supported) for a `1`/`0` answer on any feature - protocols (`$IFS(ZMODEM)$`), image formats (`$IFS(JPEG)$`), audio (`$IFS(WAV)$`), emulations, languages - or use its `LIST` directive to enumerate whole categories; query [`$TERMINFO(keyword)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#terminfo) for the terminal's name, vendor and version. These supersede the vendor codes of the [auto-sense response](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ansi-sequences-auto-sensing). Full variable inventory in the [Text Variable Reference](9.1-text-variable-reference.md). _(v2.A4)_ _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: _[Editor's note: the v2.A3 revision notes announce a `RIP_FILE_DELETE` command "to remove unneeded JPEG or WAVE files", but no command entry for it exists anywhere in the ALPHA 4 draft, and no such name appears in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory. The capability is nonetheless implemented - as a text variable rather than a command: `RIPSCRIP.HLP` carries the handler symbol `tvarProcFILEDEL`, whose `tvarProc` prefix marks a text-variable processor, and the literal `FILEDEL` is present in the shipping RIPterm 2.0, 2.20.01 and 2.30 executables. Use [`$FILEDEL(file,…)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel) (no wildcards, no paths) - the variable form is the 3.x mechanism. See [6.2](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#the-delivery-workflow) and the [2.0 errata](../../2.0/ripscrip/errata.md#rip_file_delete-was-announced-never-specified). *Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP.*]_

requirements.heading: 5.5 File Transfer & Queries
requirements.text: _The 2.0 record is [5.5 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md) (1.54 lineage in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/5.5-queries-and-advanced-commands.md)). RIP_SCROLL - formerly RIP_COPY_REGION - lives in [4.0 Icons & Bitmaps](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_scroll)._

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query)); HLP (`RIP_Query`; query OBJECT/OPTION keywords, resident queries); corpus (489 uses in 62 files); SyncTERM (ripper.c:14881, descriptor `1#3#++`)._

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: _Query the contents of a text variable_

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `Σ` (the Escape character, ASCII 27)   |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `mode:1 window_num:1 res:2 query_text` |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1<escape> <mode> <window_num> <res> <query_text>` **Example:** `!|1<escape>2Q00this is a query $COMMAND$^m`

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** [Base Math](../../glossary.md) (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** Σ is used to indicate the Escape character (ASCII 27 or ESC).

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: The Query Text Variable command instructs the terminal to immediately respond with some piece of information, whether statically stored, stored internally in RAM (dynamic information), or pre-defined text variables.

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: This command is unique in RIPscrip in the fact that the command character that is used is NOT a printable character. The escape character (ASCII 27) introduces this command as a measure of security: since the query command can query the terminal for critical (potentially private) information, you would not want a user to be able to query another user's terminal for something like his address information. Since most hosts do not allow the user to enter an escape character, this character is ideal for this purpose - using escape allows only the host (under most circumstances) to be in control of any queries.

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: The query text can contain control characters, pick-list definitions and text variables - see [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md) for these features.

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: Whether the information is transmitted instantly or not is dependent on the `<mode>` parameter, which determines when data queries are processed:

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | Mode | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | 0 | Process the query command NOW (upon receipt) |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | 1 | Process when mouse clicked in the current Graphics Viewport _(v2.A0)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | 2 | Process when mouse clicked in the current Text Window (any text variables that return X or Y mouse coordinates return TEXT coordinates, not graphics coordinates in this mode; these coordinates are two-digit values instead of the graphical four-digit values). _(v2.A0)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | 3 | Process when mouse clicked in the Graphics Viewport specified in the `<window_num>` parameter. If that viewport doesn't exist (hasn't been defined yet), then this query command is ignored. _(v2.A0)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: | 4 | Process when mouse clicked in the Text Window specified in the `<window_num>` parameter. Any text variables that return X or Y mouse coordinates return TEXT coordinates based on that window's MicroANSI text font sizes, not graphics coordinates in this mode. _(v2.A0)_ |

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: Modes 1-4 do not return the results of the query instantly - the query commands are processed when the user clicks the mouse in the text window or graphics viewport respectively. If the `<mode>` is 1 or 2, the current window/viewport is the area acted upon; modes 3 and 4 take the window number from the `<window_num>` parameter. If the associated window or viewport is not defined, the query command is ignored. These "queries after mouse clicks" are only acted upon if the user is clicking on something other than a Button or a Mouse Field. To disable a deferred query mode, issue the same command with the query string of `$OFF$`; providing a `<text>` parameter of anything other than `$OFF$` produces a revised (active) query command. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: If more than one query command can be acted upon (ie, multiple viewport queries and/or text window queries are found that the mouse was clicked inside of), then processing happens in a very specific order - all affected queries are processed, none are skipped: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text:
1. The port/viewport table is scanned from 0-35. If a query is found for a port that isn't deactivated, and the mouse was clicked inside that region (for screen ports only), then the query is processed and the next port/viewport is checked.
2. The text window table is scanned from 0-35. If a query is found for a text window that isn't deactivated, and the mouse was clicked inside that window's display area, then the query is processed and the next text window is checked.
3. If a "current viewport" query, otherwise known as a floating viewport query, is found and the mouse was clicked inside the current viewport, then the floating viewport query is processed.
4. If a "current text window" query, otherwise known as a floating text window query, is found and the mouse was clicked inside the text window's display area, then the floating text window query is processed.

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: When the user clicks the mouse down, all queries are checked against the point where the mouse was originally clicked. After all queries are processed, the mouse click is ignored until the user releases the mouse button. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: It should be mentioned that text window queries are performed before any viewport queries where resident queries are concerned. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: Some examples of query statements:

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text:
```text
                      ^m     Send a carriage return to the BBS now!
My name is $FULL_NAME$^m     Send text "My name is <insert-name-
                             here>" followed by a  carriage return
                             to the BBS.  The <insert-name-here>
                             will be replaced with whatever the
                             variable $FULL_NAME$ contains.
```

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** The `<res>` parameter is reserved for future use by TeleGrafix Communications, Inc. It should be set to 00 for compatibility with future releases.

requirements.heading: RIP_QUERY
requirements.text: **The 3.x record.** The corpus is saturated with the immediate form (mode 0) used as a _command executor_ rather than a data query: `$COMPAT$` (set 1.54-compatible environment), `$COFF$$DTW$` (cursor off + deactivate text window), `$D(1)$` (delay - 197 uses driving the wipe animations), `$MCURSOR(n)$`, `$SBAROFF$`, and conditional dispatch such as `!|1<ESC>0000<<IF $TGMENU_WIPES$="1">>$>WIPE01.FN$<<else>>$NULL$<<ENDIF>>` (see [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md)). Deferred modes 5/6 appear in the corpus wired to mouse-field _entry/exit_ status-line updates (`.MSE` overlays), a 3.x extension of the documented click modes - see [Query Deferral Modes](5.0-host-commands.md#query-deferral-modes). One authoring typo (CURVES.RIP's `|1<ESC>…` with no `!`) shows the shipping driver's tolerant introducer handling. _Evidence: corpus; HLP._

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) - flagged obsolete there already); HLP (`RIP_Define`; the DLL also exports `RIP_DefineTextVariable`); SyncTERM (ripper.c:15899) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: _Define a text variable_

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `D`                  |

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `flags:3 res:2 text` |

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1D <flags> <res> <text>` **Example:** `!|1D00700text_var,60:?question?default data`

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: This command is used to create a text variable on the Client (terminal) system. Simply put, a text variable is a piece of information assigned to an identifier that can either be saved to the terminal's [persistent variable store](../../glossary.md) (static variables) or kept in memory only (dynamic variables). Per the 2.00a4 draft, identifiers are 1-12 characters - any alphanumeric character and underscores (`_`), where neither an underscore nor a number can be the first character; RIPtel 3.1's help raises the name limit to 20 characters for the in-line variable syntax (see [5.0](5.0-host-commands.md#setting--reading-user-variables-from-host-commands)), while SyncTERM's reconstruction keeps 12. Values run to 255 characters; where and how persistent variables are stored is implementation-defined.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: The `<flags>` parameter combines three separate values into one MegaNum flag that determines how the variable definition will operate:

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: | Value | Description of Flag                   |

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: | 001   | Save variable to the persistent store |

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: | 002   | Cannot specify a blank response       |

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: | 004   | Non-interactive query                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: When a variable is flagged as persistent, it becomes a part of the Client system's actual configuration: the value is saved indefinitely until either changed or manually erased. You may choose not to allow the user to enter a blank response, requiring them to enter some piece of information for the variable.
