requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: The last flag determines whether the definition is interactive or not. An interactive definition will attempt to define the variable: if it already exists, the value pops up on the screen asking the user to confirm it is correct; if it does not exist, a similar pop-up box appears asking the user to enter data for the given variable. In a non-interactive situation, the Client system checks whether the variable exists. If it does, nothing happens (unless a default response is specified in this command, whereby the Client's variable is updated with the new information). If the value is not defined, the definition becomes interactive by default, since the user actually has to enter something anyway.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: The `<text>` parameter is segmented in nature, much like the [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) command's. Its syntax:

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text:
```text
variable-identifier[,field-width]:[?question-text?][default-value]
```

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: An example:

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text:
```text
FULL_NAME,30:?What is your full name?John Doe
```

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: The first section is the variable-identifier, immediately followed by an optional field-width (default 60; limit the values to 1-60). The colon (`:`) indicates that the identifier field is completed and that the remainder contains the question and/or the default response (if any) - with neither, the parameter reads `TEXT_VAR,width:` with no additional data. The question-text is specified between question marks (`?this is a question?`). The remainder is a default-value for the variable's contents; it may be omitted so that the user must enter his/her own value instead of some "canned response".

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** The `<res>` parameter is reserved for future use by TeleGrafix Communications, Inc. It should be set to 00 for compatibility with future releases.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: THIS COMMAND IS NOW OBSOLETE. USE THE SPECIALLY ENHANCED TEXT VARIABLE SYSTEM WITHIN QUERIES OR HOST COMMANDS TO PRODUCE THE SAME RESULTS AS THIS COMMAND AND MUCH MORE! _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE
requirements.text: The corpus confirms the succession: the demos define hundreds of variables exclusively through the `$-=NAME=value$` [set form](5.0-host-commands.md#setting--reading-user-variables-from-host-commands) and the `$[directives]NAME[@question][=default]$` prompt syntax, never `1D`. The host may also delete variables; RIPtel confirms with the prompt _"The host wants to delete the variable %s. Proceed?"_, and protected variables trigger a "Data Security Activated" message. _Evidence: corpus; HLP._

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene)); HLP (`RIP_ReadScene`; "Can't locate local RIPscrip scene file %s"; DLL export `RIP_PlaybackLocalRIPFile`); corpus (92 uses in 34 files); SyncTERM (ripper.c:16534)._

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: _Playback local .RIP file_

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `R`                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `res:8 filename...` |

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1R <res> <filename>` **Example:** `!|1R00000000testfile.rip`

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Draw Color, Back Color, Line Style, Fill Style, Write Mode, Font Style, Port (dependent on the contents of the source file), Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: This command instructs the remote terminal to playback a local `.RIP` file. The current execution of RIPscrip commands will be temporarily suspended and the contents of the designated RIP file will begin executing. Regardless of whether or not the current RIPscrip code coming across the modem is in the middle of a line or not, the RIP playback file will be assumed to start at the beginning of a line. Therefore, if a RIP_READ_SCENE command is located in a `.RIP` file, it must be the very last command on the line, followed by a carriage return instead of a command delimiter (`|`). This ensures that the loaded `.RIP` file will begin executing properly with the correct delimiters found in the correct places.

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: The RIP playback file can alter colors, fonts, or whatever. Once the playback of the file is complete, the remaining RIPscrip code that was temporarily suspended will resume execution. Any changes that appeared in the loaded playback file will remain in effect when the resumed code is processed - if you change a color or a font in the playback file and leave them changed, they remain in effect during the resumed execution.

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** The `<res>` parameter is reserved for future development by TeleGrafix. It should be set to "00000000" for compatibility with future releases.

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: **The 3.x record.** In the corpus this is the _subroutine call_ of an entire scene architecture - `.FN` function scenes, `.DEF` variable definitions, `.MSE` overlays - and it gains three undocumented argument forms: _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text:
- **Plain `.TXT` files**: `!|1R00000000DRAGON.TXT` inside an open `1e` column region flows the file's text into the columns, word-wrapped - it is _not_ parsed as RIPscrip. See [Flowing Whole Files](3.1-column-text-system.md#flowing-whole-files---1r-on-plain-text).
- **Overflow pages**: `!|1R00000000$OVERFLOW(1,CUR)$` re-reads the current page of a column stream's overflow buffer ([pagination](3.1-column-text-system.md#pagination---overflow-and-resetoverflow)).
- **Computed filenames**: `!|1R00000000<<IF $COLORS$<"256">>BLUEBACK.FN<<ELSE>>BLUEFADE.FN<<ENDIF>>` - the corpus's ubiquitous color-depth dispatch - and `$&MAIN_STORY$` variable dereferences (NEWSPAPR.RIP). See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#inline-conditionals---if--elseif--else--endif).

requirements.heading: RIP_READ_SCENE
requirements.text: The host-command twin of this command is the `$>FILE.RIP$` playback prefix - same engine, click-triggered - compared in [5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md#playback-prefixes-vs-dedicated-commands).

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query)); HLP (`RIP_FileQuery`); SyncTERM (ripper.c:16104) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: _Query existing information on a particular file_

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `F`                        |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `mode:2 res:4 filename...` |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1F <mode> <res> <filename>` **Example:** `!|1F010000testfile.icn`

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: This command queries the existence of a particular file, regardless of type. It is intended for host systems to determine if a particular icon or RIP file exists on the terminal's hard disk - the host side of the 3.x resource-caching story ([staleness check](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#the-delivery-workflow)). The `<mode>` parameter determines the command's response; the terminal sends the response to the host immediately upon execution.

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | Mode | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | 00 | Simply query the existence of the file. If it exists, a "1" is returned. Otherwise a "0" is returned to the Host (without a carriage return). |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | 01 | Same as 0, except a carriage return is added after the response. |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | 02 | Queries the existence of a file. If it does not exist, a "0" is returned to the Host followed by a carriage return. If it does exist, the returned text is a "1." followed by the file size (in decimal). The return sequence is terminated by a carriage return. An example of the returned text could be "1.20345". |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | 03 | Queries extended return information. If the file does not exist, a "0" is returned followed by a carriage return. If it does exist, the text returned to the Host is in the Format: `1.size.date.time <cr>`. An example of a return statement could be `1.20345.01/02/93.03:04:30<cr>` |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: | 04 | Queries extended return information. If the file does not exist, a "0" is returned followed by a carriage return. If it does exist, the text returned to the Host is in the Format: `1.filename.size.date.time <cr>`. An example of a return statement could be `1.MYFILE.RIP.20345.01/02/93.03:04:30 <cr>`. Note that the file extension adds another period into the return text. |

requirements.heading: RIP_FILE_QUERY
requirements.text: The self-contained demo corpus has no host to answer, so the command never appears there; SyncTERM implements it against its per-BBS cache directory. Which directories are searched, and where downloaded files land, is the connection-directory model of [6.2](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md). _Evidence: SyncTERM; HLP._

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_delay)) - not in the RIPSCRIP.HLP name inventory, not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: _Causes the Client Terminal to Pause_

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `D`              |

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `delay_period:4` |

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|3D <delay_period>` **Example:** `!|3D002D`

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: This command will cause the remote terminal to pause for `<delay_period>` number of "timer ticks". A Timer Tick is defined as being 1/60th of a second, so a delay period of 60 would be equal to one full second of delay.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: During the time period of the delay, the remote terminal should be queueing up any incoming RIPscrip code or raw text (if any) into some form of internal buffer to prevent character loss. After the delay period is complete, the data in that buffer (if any) should be processed immediately and the terminal should resume processing the incoming stream of data.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELAY
requirements.text: **The 3.x record** points to this command having been superseded by the text-variable form: the corpus performs all of its pacing - 197 occurrences - with `$D(1)$` inside [RIP_QUERY](#rip_query) commands (`!|1<ESC>0000$D(1)$`, the heartbeat of every wipe animation), and RIPSCRIP.HLP carries a `D` _variable_ processor (`tvarProc` list) but no `RIP_Delay` command name. See [5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md). _Evidence: corpus; HLP._

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_baud_emulation)); HLP (`RIP_BaudEmulation`; `$BAUDEMUL$` variable) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: _Set Baud Rate Emulation for Local RIP Playback_

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `e`          |

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `rate_val:4` |

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|3e <rate_val>` **Example:** `!|3e01UN`

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: This command sets the rate at which [local RIP file playback](5.3-local-playback.md) is performed. By default, local RIP playback is done at full speed, which is dependent on your CPU, hard disk speed and many other factors. With this command, you can set the speed at which the playback is performed so that it approximates a particular baud rate. The setting remains in effect even after a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command, so that a Reset command inside a local RIP file will not alter the playback speed in mid-stride. The setting remains in effect until changed explicitly by the user (if possible under the terminal software), or by the host via another RIP_BAUD_EMULATION command.

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: Typical settings for `<rate_val>` might be 300, 2400, 4800, 19200, etc. A value of 0 indicates that local playback should be performed at maximum speed (no baud rate emulation). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BAUD_EMULATION
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver keeps the feature (its `$BAUDEMUL$` variable reads the setting back), but the demos run at full speed and pace their animations with `$D(n)$` delays instead. _Evidence: HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode)); HLP (`RIP_EnterBlockMode`; "Invalid file transfer protocol number", upload confirmation "Upload file(s) '%s'?", DLL exports `RIP_GetBlockModeFilename`/`RIP_GetBlockModeTransferType`; RIPtel itself uses Zmodem for actual transfers); SyncTERM (ripper.c:17069; manual parse from 17150) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: _Enter block transfer mode with host_

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `Σ` (the Escape character, ASCII 27)             |

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `mode:1 proto:1 file_type:2 res:4 [filename] <>` |

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|9<escape> <mode> <proto> <file_type> <res> [filename] <>` **Example:** `!|9<escape>00010000ICONFILE.BMP<>`

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Port (in image or local-playback file types), Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: This command is used to auto-initiate any desired File Transfer Protocol. The `<filename>` parameter is optional on downloads, required for uploads, and if omitted must be replaced with a `<>` parameter (end of string).

requirements.heading: RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE
requirements.text: The `<mode>` parameter specifies upload or download: "1" for upload mode, "0" (zero) for download mode. A filename is required for uploads. If the user has Data Security enabled on the terminal, they are prompted to OK the upload before it proceeds (RIPtel asks "Upload file(s) '%s'?"). If the user does not authorize the upload, ten Ctrl-X's (ASCII 24 or CAN) are sent at one-tenth second intervals. The `<file_type>` parameter is ignored for uploads.

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: The `<proto>` parameter is the file transfer protocol specifier, merged here with SyncTERM's 3.0-era dispatch (ripper.c:17187-17300):

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | Value | Protocol | Filename Required? | SyncTERM |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 0 | Xmodem (checksum) | Yes | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 1 | Xmodem (CRC) | Yes | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 2 | Xmodem-1K | Yes | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 3 | Xmodem-1K (G) | Yes | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 4 | Kermit | Yes | **rejected** |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 5 | Ymodem (batch) | No | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 6 | Ymodem-G | No | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 7 | Zmodem (crash recovery) | No | supported |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 8 | Zmodem (no crash recovery) _(v2.A0)_ | No | - |

requirements.heading: Transfer Protocols
requirements.text: | 9 | Super Kermit _(v2.A4)_ | No | - |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: The `<file_type>` parameter determines what type of files are to be received during the block transfer:

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | Value | Description of Block Transfer Contents                         |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | 0     | RIP file sequence (display it)                                 |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | 1     | Generic file sequence (store files for future use) _(v2.A0)_   |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | 2     | BMP file sequence (store them in proper directories) _(v2.A1)_ |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | 3     | Image file sequence (display it) _(v2.A0)_                     |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | 4     | COMPOSITE DYNAMIC file sequence (batch protocols only)         |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: | 5     | ACTIVE DYNAMIC file sequence (batch protocols only)            |

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: Whether the `<filename>` is specified or not, this command must have a `<>` sequence after the filename (even if there is none). With a filename, using Xmodem/CRC:

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text:
```text
!|9<escape>01020000filename.icn<>
```

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: Without a filename, using Zmodem:

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: In brief: type 0 plays the received RIP file back like any other local RIP file; type 1 stores generic files for future use with no processing; type 2 is identical to type 1 but designated for icon files (`.BMP`, `.BMH`, `.BMM`) - use type 1 instead, as type 2 might change in future revisions; type 3 displays received JPEG images through the current [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style) settings (full current-viewport size if none recorded); types 4 and 5 (batch protocols only) route each received file by its extension, storing it - and for ACTIVE DYNAMIC, also playing/displaying `.RIP` and `.JPG`/`.GIF` files on arrival. _(v2.A0)_ The full per-extension routing table, and where "the proper directory" is for every file type - the connection-directory model - are in [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#block-mode-routing---the-extension-table); files with unrecognized extensions are simply placed there with no further processing.

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** This command must be terminated with a carriage return. A vertical bar (`|`) command delimiter cannot be used to separate this command from a subsequent one on the same line. In other words, this command must be the last command on a line of text. The protocol must begin on the very next line.

requirements.heading: File Types
requirements.text: SyncTERM also sandboxes the command: filenames containing `\` are rejected, and received files land in a per-BBS `RIP` cache subdirectory rather than RIPterm's global icon directory. _Evidence: SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 ([v2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_begin_uuencode_block)); HLP (as **`RIP_BeginEncodedStream`** - the 3.0 name; "encoded stream" file types in the error strings) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: _Begin a generic UU-Encoded data block_

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `U`                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `file_type:2 res:8` |

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|9U <file_type> <res>` **Example:** `!|9U0200000000`

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Port (for displayable graphics sequences), Base Math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: This command must be the last RIPscrip command on the line of text. The very next line of text will be the beginning (header) information of a UU-Encoded data file block - a way to move binary resources (JPEGs, bitmaps, sounds) over text-only links. The header contains the filename associated with the binary UU-Encoded data; this information is decoded by the receiving terminal and the resulting file is stored on the terminal's hard disk to be processed depending on the `<file_type>` parameter, which is identical in nature and values to the parameter by the same name in the [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](#rip_enter_block_mode) command. The file that results from the UU-Encoded data block might be a JPEG file, BMP file, sound file, or could be just about anything.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: Immediately after the last line of UU-Encoded data, either raw text or RIPscrip code should begin. Some UU-Encoded data blocks have line-by-line CRC checking. If this mode is specified in the header of the UU-Encoded data block, then CRC checking on the lines should be performed as defined in the UU-Encoding specification. If a single CRC fails, the terminal should kill the partial file and ignore remaining UU-Encoded data until a RIPscrip or raw text block is encountered that it can then subsequently process.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver renamed the mechanism: RIPSCRIP.HLP's inventory lists it as `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`, and its error strings reference encoded-stream file types, confirming the feature survived into 3.x under the new name even though no shipped demo exercises it. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: The RIPscrip language itself is not tied to any particular language. However, there is a need to establish a means of determining and specifying what RIPscrip / text window fonts with special characters should be used, and what language should be used in the terminal software. It is up to the individual application to use whatever files it needs to support a particular language. RIPscrip provides a standardized way of specifying the language support to use: a character code for each of the languages supported. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: Currently, English is the only supported language in RIPscrip. For the purposes of multi-lingual extensibility, the convention was established in the 2.x draft: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: | Code | Description of Language |

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: | ENG  | English                 |

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: The means of setting the language is for the user to specify in the terminal, preferably in the dialing directory. This allows the user to select a different language for different systems. There is no ability for the host to specify to the terminal what language to use. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: International Support in RIPscrip
requirements.text: The means of finding out what languages the terminal supports is handled via the [`$IFS()$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs) text variable. For example, if the host were to query the terminal with a `$IFS(ENG)$`, the terminal would respond affirmatively. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: 6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files
requirements.text: Authoring-level conventions for 3.x script files: encoding and line endings, line length and continuation, comments and grouping, the script-container family, and the prologue/epilogue conventions of TeleGrafix's own 116 shipped RIPtel demo scripts.

requirements.heading: 6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files
requirements.text: _The 2.0 authoring conventions this page extends are in [6.0 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/6.0-writing-rip-files.md); the 3.0 engine inherits the 2.0 parser conventions documented in the [stream conventions techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/1.0-stream-conventions-delta.md)._

requirements.heading: What a .RIP file is
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._

requirements.heading: What a .RIP file is
requirements.text: A `.RIP` file is not a distinct binary format: it is a captured RIPscrip command stream - exactly the bytes a host would transmit - stored as a text file. Everything in [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md) applies verbatim to file content. A file can be transmitted by a host, replayed locally via the `$>file$` playback prefix ([5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md)), played back by [RIP_READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene), or delivered and auto-played through [block mode](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode).

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (116-file census - [script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md))._

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: All script extensions in the RIPtel corpus - `.RIP`, `.FN`, `.DEF`, `.MNU`, `.MSE`, `.RET`, `.ENT`, `.EXT`, `.COL` - are plain-ASCII RIPscrip command streams distinguished only by **role**, not by format. The corpus-attested roles:

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | Extension | Role |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.RIP` | A scene - the general-purpose script container |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.FN` | A "function" scene invoked as a subroutine via [RIP_READ_SCENE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_read_scene) or the `$>file$` playback prefix - the WIPE00-24 transition library, effects, and reusable setup blocks |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.DEF` | A variable-definition script (TELCMDS.DEF, MENU.DEF …) that seeds [text variables](../../glossary.md) for a scene group |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.MNU` | A menu scene (buttons, mouse fields, navigation) |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.MSE` | A mouse-field overlay scene wiring field entry/exit queries to status-line updates and cursor changes |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.ENT` / `.EXT` | Menu entry/exit transition stubs that save and restore the screen around a menu excursion ("Paste original screen image back" - see [7.2 Data Backup Areas](7.2-data-backup-areas.md)) |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.RET` | Return scenes replayed when control comes back from a linked demo (MENU.RET, TELCMDS.RET - invoked through RIP_READ_SCENE) |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: | `.COL` | A "column layout" scene built on the flowed-text column system, paired with raw-prose `.TXT` story files - see [3.1 Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md) |

requirements.heading: The script-container family
requirements.text: `.TXT` story files flowed into column regions are the one non-RIPscrip participant: inside an open column region they are word-wrapped as raw content, never parsed as commands ([3.1](3.1-column-text-system.md)). Playback search paths for all of these are covered in [5.3](5.3-local-playback.md) and [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md).

requirements.heading: Encoding and line endings
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18557-18580)._

requirements.heading: Encoding and line endings
requirements.text:
- **Line endings are CRLF** throughout the RIPtel corpus (the 1.54 spec said bare CR). They parse identically because CR dispatches the pending command while LF is unconditionally swallowed mid-command - see [1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md). Line endings are significant to the parser, so script files should be stored and transferred byte-exact - never re-wrapped or "normalized". Script files also contain **literal control bytes** - SOH (`0x01`) introducers and ESC (`0x1B`) command characters - so they are not safely editable in tools that strip or transcode control characters.
- Text content (graphics text, button labels, embedded raw text) is [CP437](../../glossary.md) - the code page of the BBS world, and the character set the 3.x client's MicroANSI terminal fonts render in full (all 256 glyphs; see [6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md)). There is no in-band encoding declaration. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus (FONTS/RIPscrip.maf glyph complement)._

requirements.heading: Line length and continuation
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 4-5, 13; corpus._

requirements.heading: Line length and continuation
requirements.text: Any command or line may be split with a backslash (`\`) immediately before the line break; continuation lines carry **no introducer** - they are bare argument bytes. Authoring practice:

requirements.heading: Line length and continuation
requirements.text:
- The split may land anywhere - mid-parameter, mid-number. The RIPtel corpus uses continuation for long vertex lists (POLYPOLY.RIP's RIP*FILL_POLYGON runs); the RIPterm 2.30 shipped corpus shows it as heavy production traffic (one palette-fade file is 1,024 physical lines of which 960 are continuations). \_Evidence: corpus (POLYPOLY.RIP); 2.00a4.*
- The 2.0-era 80-column discipline for command lines remains sound authoring advice - wrap for tool compatibility, but don't rely on readers enforcing any limit; terminals accept arbitrarily long lines. _(Inherited RIPterm 2.30-corpus observation - see the [v2.0 page](../../2.0/ripscrip/6.0-writing-rip-files.md).)_
- Watch trailing backslashes: an **odd** count means continuation, an **even** count means escaped literal backslashes. If you need a literal `\` at end-of-line, write `\\`; a continuation after a literal backslash needs `\\\`. _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 13; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18563-18576)._
- Multi-command lines are the norm - `|` chains commands on one line (`!|c0F|=00000001|S010F`), and the standard 3.x prologue is itself a four-command chain (below). Commands that must be last on their line (RIP*READ_SCENE, RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE) cannot be chained past. \_Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 4; corpus.*

requirements.heading: Escaping, comments and grouping
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 11, 14; corpus._

requirements.heading: Escaping, comments and grouping
requirements.text: Inside text parameters, `\!` → literal `!`, `\|` → literal `|`, `\\` → literal `\`; [host command](../../glossary.md) and text-variable metacharacters (`$`, `[`, `]`, `(`, `)`) are quoted with a backslash where they could be misread (`\$Name\$`) - see [1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md). At the file level:

requirements.heading: Escaping, comments and grouping
requirements.text:
- **Comments** - `!|!comment text` embeds a comment anywhere ([RIP_COMMENT](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_comment), _(v2.A2)_); everything from the `!` opcode to the next `|` or end of line is ignored, and the comment string is exempt from text-variable substitution. The RIPtel corpus contains **1,683 comment commands** (305 with prose): `!|command|! comment` chains are ubiquitous, and TeleGrafix's authors left positional field-layout cribs above complex commands (`!|! xxyyxxyycaffffccrrrrrrrr`). _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._
- **Trailing text after fixed-length arguments is tolerated** and used as inline commentary - the shipping driver stops reading once a command's fixed fields are consumed: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960` _(sic)_. Robust for the shipping driver, but not guaranteed by the language - prefer explicit `|!` comments. _Evidence: corpus (ONLINE.RIP)._
- **Grouping** - `!|(` … `!|)` bundles commands into logical groups for paint programs ([RIP_GROUP_BEGIN](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_group_begin)/[RIP_GROUP_END](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_group_end), _(v2.A2)_); terminals ignore them, and the 2.00a4 advice to strip groups from files placed online is consistent with their total absence from the shipping demo corpus. _Evidence: 2.00a4 - not in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory, not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._
- **UU-encoded data blocks** - a file (or stream) may embed raw binary content behind a [RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_begin_uuencode_block) command _(v2.A1)_; the 3.0 driver renamed the mechanism `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: Mixing ANSI, raw text and column content
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 6; corpus._

requirements.heading: Mixing ANSI, raw text and column content
requirements.text: Lines that do not begin with an introducer pass through to the current [text window](../../glossary.md) ([1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md)), so script files freely intermix RIPscrip with ANSI sequences and plain text. The flowed-text machinery extends the 2.0 modal wrinkle: after a text-region or column-region definition ([3.0](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md), [3.1](3.1-column-text-system.md)), raw lines are consumed as region/column content until a command line ends the block - the `.COL` scenes and their `.TXT` story files are built entirely on this.

requirements.heading: The SOH scene-start opener
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rule 12; corpus._

requirements.heading: The SOH scene-start opener
requirements.text: Ctrl-A (SOH, byte `0x01`) or Ctrl-B (STX, `0x02`) may replace the `!` introducer and - unlike `!` - are accepted anywhere in the stream, not just at line start ([1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md)). TeleGrafix's 2.2-era convention was to open a standalone scene file with `\x01|*` (SOH + [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows)); the 3.x corpus systematizes the SOH opener: **111 of 116 files begin their _first_ command line with SOH + `|`**, then use `!|` for every subsequent line - SOH apparently flags start-of-scene to the 3.0 stream parser, while `!|` remains the 1.54-compatible introducer. (Three files invert the pattern, nearly all-SOH; SOH mid-scene is legal and does appear, e.g. in DRAGON.RIP below.) Files that are deliberately non-destructive (wipes, fades, fragments) omit the `*` reset.

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (90+ files); HLP._

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: TeleGrafix never specified how a script file should begin or end, but their shipped 3.x scenes are consistent:

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: - **The standard prologue** opens 90+ of the 116 files: `!|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO` - pinning the scene's numeric conventions _before_ any coordinate-bearing command arrives (order matters). Decoded:

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | Piece | Command | Meaning |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | `!\|` | - | line introducer + command delimiter |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | `J10` | [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math) | [Base Math](../../glossary.md) ← 36 (`10` base-36 = 36): [MegaNums](../../glossary.md). The shipped opcode is level-0 `J`; the ALPHA 4 draft's `b` assignment collided with RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW - see the [1.2 note](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math) |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | `\|n2000` | [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size) | coordinates ← 2-digit fields |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | `\|M08` | [RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_set_color_mode) | 8-bit palette color mode |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text: | `\|fZKQO` | [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) | world frame ← 1280×960 (`ZK`=1280, `QO`=960) |

requirements.heading: Scene prologue and epilogue conventions
requirements.text:
- **Reset first** - standalone scenes open with the SOH reset opener (`\x01|*` or `!|*`), then the prologue; [RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_mouse_fields) (`!|1K`) clears stale fields so they cannot fire during the redraw (8 corpus files; TELKILL.FN wraps it as a reusable subroutine scene). _Evidence: corpus._
- **Query-command setup** - the demos do much of their scene setup through [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) terminal-control variables alongside the prologue: `$COFF$` (cursor off), `$DTW$` (deactivate text window), `$SBAROFF$` (hide status bar), `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$` (clear column-overflow state). _Evidence: corpus._
- **Scene header segments** - the 3.0 engine formalizes the 2.A1 [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) idea into structured header segments declaring the environment a scene expects (per-table flags, coordinate size, RGB bit count, revision code - see [1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md) and [7.1](7.1-data-tables.md#scene-header-segments-and-table-state)). No wire-format example has been recovered - the RIPtel demos use the explicit prologue commands instead - so the segment encoding remains undocumented _(hypothesis: a parameterized RIP_HEADER-style command, per the 2.A1 design)_. _Evidence: HLP._
- **State re-assertion** - authored streams re-assert unchanged state constantly (background color, write mode, fonts); state is inherited from whatever ran before, so well-behaved scenes re-establish everything they depend on. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._
- **Epilogue** - [RIP_NO_MORE](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_no_more) (`!|#`) marks scene end, activating mouse regions and queued clicks; nearly every RIPtel demo scene ends with one (287 uses in 95 of 116 files). The spec's advice to transmit three or more consecutively for noise immunity stands - the shipped RIPterm 2.30 scenes ended `!|#|#|#` - and terminals should also time out and assume NO*MORE if the stream goes quiet. \_Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus.*

requirements.heading: A real scene opening (DRAGON.RIP)
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (DRAGON.RIP; annotations editorial)._

requirements.heading: A real scene opening (DRAGON.RIP)
requirements.text:
```text
\x01|!                                    SOH scene-start + comment (no text)
!|*                                       RIP_RESET_WINDOWS - clean slate
!|1\x1b0000$-=NO_WIPES=Disabled$          query cmd sets variable NO_WIPES=Disabled
!|1\x1b0000$SBAROFF$                      hide the status bar
!|w0000000000                             RIP_TEXT_WINDOW - zero-size (off)
\x01|1\x1b0000$DTW$                       disable text window
\x01|1\x1b0000$COFF$                      cursor off
\x01|1\x1b0000$RESET(OVERFLOW)$           clear column-overflow state
\x01|n2000                                2-digit coordinates
\x01|M08                                  8-bit palette mode
\x01|W00                                  RIP_WRITE_MODE - COPY
\x01|fZKQO                                world frame 1280x960
\x01|2P10000ZKQO00030000                  RIP_DEFINE_PORT - offscreen port 1, 1280x960
\x01|J10                                  base math 36 (MegaNums)
\x01|1b0000HS0Y000G000000STRIP6.BMP       RIP_LOAD_BITMAP at (0,0), 640x34 region
\x01|c0F                                  draw color 15
```

requirements.heading: A real scene opening (DRAGON.RIP)
requirements.text: (`\x01` = SOH, `\x1b` = ESC; both are literal single bytes on the wire. Lines end CRLF. Note the mixed introducers - SOH mid-scene is legal - and `$…$` terminal-control variables doing setup work alongside drawing commands.)

requirements.heading: A minimal constructed scene
requirements.text: _(Constructed example - not from the corpus; commands and field widths follow this edition's command entries.)_

requirements.heading: A minimal constructed scene
requirements.text:
```text
!|*|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO                   reset + standard prologue
!|c0F|=00000001|S010F                     white pen, solid 1px line, solid fill
!|K05052S1U                               filled rectangle (5,5)-(100,66)
!|Y02000909                               font style: small stroked font, 9x9
!|@0F0PHello, RIPscrip 3.0                text at (15,25)
!|1b000000000000000000LOGO.BMP            bitmap at (0,0), unscaled
!|#                                       RIP_NO_MORE - scene complete
```

requirements.heading: Authoring-robustness notes from the corpus
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Authoring-robustness notes from the corpus
requirements.text: The shipping driver's parser is markedly tolerant, and shipped TeleGrafix files lean on that tolerance - a caution for authors targeting other terminals:

requirements.heading: Authoring-robustness notes from the corpus
requirements.text:
- **Typo tolerance is high.** A missing `!` introducer (`|1<ESC>0000$COMPAT$`, CURVES.RIP), separator lines `!|----` that accidentally parse as the `-` opcode with dash arguments (`-` reads as MegaNum 0), and bare `!|` no-op lines all pass through the shipping driver without visible failure. Robust parsers should degrade as gracefully; robust authors should not rely on it.
- **Truncated reserved fields are routinely omitted** (`!|2s002` for a documented 6-character argument block; `!|1c06` with no reserved digits). The documented practice remains to send reserved fields as zeros for forward compatibility.

requirements.heading: Naming and delivery
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Naming and delivery
requirements.text: Files referenced from commands and playback variables use bare DOS-style names - no path or sub-directory information (commands that take filenames reject paths). Extensions may be omitted where a command documents a default (`.RIP` for playback variables, `.BMP` for icon commands). Where files live on the terminal and how a host delivers them is covered in [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md).

requirements.heading: 6.1 Content File Roles
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 6.1 Content File Roles
requirements.text: The content files of the 3.x generation - what each file type is for and how commands reference it: images, three font systems, and the plain-text script containers. Roles live here; **byte-level layouts are implementer material** in the techspecs linked throughout.

requirements.heading: 6.1 Content File Roles
requirements.text: _Where the 2.0 edition documented essentially [one binary format](../../2.0/ripscrip/6.1-content-file-roles.md) (the BMP/DIB icon), the 3.x client ships a whole family._

requirements.heading: File roles
requirements.text: | Extension | Role | Evidence |

requirements.heading: File roles
requirements.text: | `.RIP` `.FN` `.COL` … | Plain-ASCII script containers - stored RIPscrip command streams distinguished only by role; the full family is in [6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files](6.0-writing-rip-files.md) | corpus |

requirements.heading: File roles
requirements.text: | `.BMP` | Primary bitmap format - [icons](../../glossary.md), button skins, backgrounds, wallpaper ([4.0 Icons & Bitmaps](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md)) | 2.00a4; WP; corpus |

requirements.text: | `.BMH` | Button-highlight BMP variant - the pressed/highlighted state of a same-named `.BMP` UI skin ([4.3 Buttons](4.3-buttons.md)) | corpus (ICONS/\*.BMH) |

requirements.text: | `.BMM` | An [icon mask](../../glossary.md): the AND-stamp companion raster for transparency - defined by the 2.x spec's extension tables; no `.BMM` files are known to have shipped, and the 3.x record adds no sighting | 2.00a4 |

requirements.text: | `.ICN` | Legacy 1.54 icons - read + converted only (below) | HLP |

requirements.heading: File roles

requirements.heading: File roles
requirements.text: Commands reference host-deliverable files by bare name - no path or sub-directory information is allowed. Default extensions are appended when omitted (`.BMP` for icon commands, `.RIP` for playback variables); an explicitly provided extension is used verbatim. _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: The 1.54 icon format - Borland `getimage()` memory dumps, documented in the [v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/6.1-content-file-roles.md) - is not a native 3.x format, but the 3.0 driver retains read support by _converting_ legacy icons to BMP on the fly: the DLL exports `RIP_ConvertIconToBmp` and carries the error strings "Can't convert RIP 1.54 Icon %s to 2.0 BMP format!" and "1.54 icon file %s has an invalid width". No `.ICN` files ship with RIPtel; hosts are expected to serve BMPs.

requirements.heading: Legacy `.ICN` icons (RIPscrip 1.54)
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP (RIPSCRIP.HLP error strings; RIPTEL.EXE export table)._

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: The 2.00a4 decision to adopt the Windows **Device-Independent Bitmap** stands in 3.x. The older 1.54 icon format was completely inadequate for resolution- and color-independent environments: it carried no color palette and no notion of pixel format. The DIB format accommodates monochrome (1-bit), 16-color (4-bit), 256-color (8-bit), and 24-bit uncompressed images, and stores palette information in the file so that color approximation or dithering can make the image appear correct in any color environment. Explicitly _not_ supported: RLE-compressed BMPs ("Can't show compressed bitmaps") and OS/2-style BMPs. Display options include stretching to any size, dithering, transparency, color-palette manipulation, and wallpapering.

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: BMPs are pervasive in the corpus (102 of the 234 files in RIPtel's `ICONS/`): backgrounds, button skins (via [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap)), and UI décor. Content creators normally never touch the bytes - icons are produced in a paint program, or captured on the terminal itself via [RIP_GET_IMAGE](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_get_image) + [RIP_WRITE_ICON](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_write_icon) (or per-port via [RIP_PORT_WRITE](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_port_write)). Implementers decoding or generating icon files should work from the [icon formats techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.0-icon-formats.md), whose header/color-table/pixel-block layout is unchanged in 3.x.

requirements.heading: Windows BMP / DIB
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP (§3.7.1); HLP ("Can't show compressed bitmaps"); corpus._

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - button-highlight variants
requirements.text: A `.BMH` file is a **plain Windows BMP** whose extension marks it as the _highlighted/pressed_ state of a same-named `.BMP` UI skin. RIPtel ships five pairs (BUTTON, CHECKBOX, RADIO, RADIOBUT, RADIONEW): each pair has identical dimensions, bit depth, and palette, differing only in pixel data (the `.BMH` shifted toward white/highlight tones). The client swaps the `.BMH` image in on hover/click for BMP-skinned buttons, checkboxes, and radio buttons; pairing is by filename convention - `.BMH` files are never named in any script ([4.3 Buttons](4.3-buttons.md)).

requirements.heading: `.BMH` - button-highlight variants
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (ICONS/\*.BMH byte comparison - see [binary triage §3](../../3.0/research/riptel-binary-formats.md))._

requirements.heading: JPEG (and GrayPEG)
requirements.text: JPEG remains the only compressed image format in shipping 3.x (GIF was dropped over LZW licensing; PNG was announced but never shipped - see the [white paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt)). All JPEGs are 24-bit; the white paper notes support for the **GrayPEG** grayscale variants. JPEG decoding is built into the driver (`jpegShow`, `LoadJPEGBuffer`, JPEG scaling-table error strings), images can be placed anywhere at any size, and progressive ("display while downloading") rendering was advertised but noted as not working in RIPtel 3.1. Seven JPEGs ship in the demo corpus, driven by [RIP_IMAGE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image) and the `$(file.JPG$` [playback prefix](5.3-local-playback.md). Byte-level decoder notes are in the [JPEG techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.1-jpeg-images.md).

requirements.heading: JPEG (and GrayPEG)
requirements.text: _Evidence: WP (§3.7.2, GrayPEG); HLP (jpeg_ strings; readme progressive-display note); corpus (N2*PHOTO.RIP, SPECLEFX.RIP).*

requirements.heading: `.WAV` audio
requirements.text: A digitized audio file, played in the background by [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](4.5-audio-files.md#rip_play_audio) or the `$)FILE.WAV$` playback prefix ([5.3](5.3-local-playback.md)), and stoppable with `$OFF$`. The 3.0 driver plainly supports audio (audio configuration, `AUDIO=TRUE` in RIPscrip.ini, the DLL export `RIP_AudioSupport`), but the demo corpus ships no audio files and never issues the command. Terminals that store audio in a translated local format must still answer [file queries](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md) as if the WAVE original were on disk. Format details: [audio techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.4-audio.md).

requirements.heading: `.WAV` audio
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: Fonts are **global client resources, never host-delivered per connection** - they resolve only from the client's font store (`FONTS\`), outside the [connection directory](../../glossary.md) model of [6.2](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md). The 3.x client ships three font systems plus a catalog file; creators select them by name/number through the font commands ([3.0 Text Output & Fonts](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md)):

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text:
- **`.RFF` outline fonts (Atech FastFont)** - the scalable outline-font system is a licensed third-party engine, Atech Software's "FastFont"; `.RFF` is evidently "RIPscrip FastFont", renamed from Atech's `.FF1`. Eight shipped faces (BRUSH, COBB, DEFAULT, DIXON, EUREKA, MARIN, OAKLAND, SYMBOL), 224 glyphs each (0x20-0xFF) on a 1000-units-per-em square, with **ten style variants per file** - base, `Th`in, `Cn` condensed, `Wd` wide, `Ex` expanded, plus hollow versions of all five - exactly the family-suffix names the corpus passes in extended-font-style commands ("Marin", "Cobb Th", …). RIPterm 2.30 (October 1997) shipped five of the families as byte-identical `.RFF` files - both generations are preserved in the [RIPterm 2.30 font assets](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md). _Evidence: corpus (FONTS/\*.RFF - [binary triage §1](../../3.0/research/riptel-binary-formats.md)); WP (§3.4.1)._
- **`atf.cfg`** - the FastFont engine's binary **catalog/cache**: a pre-scanned registry mapping style names to files so the rasterizer needn't open every font at startup. Machine-generated and safe to rebuild. _Evidence: corpus (FONTS/atf.cfg)._
- **`.maf` MicroANSI bitmap fonts** - `FONTS/RIPscrip.maf` holds the fixed-cell fonts used for ANSI/text-window emulation: six resolution records, each with five font-size subrecords of raw glyph bitmaps for the full 256-character (CP437) set - the per-resolution renderings behind the terminal text modes and the `$TWFONT$` "MicroANSI" font numbers ([1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md)). _Evidence: corpus (FONTS/RIPscrip.maf); HLP (MicroANSI font-loading error strings; MESSAGES.HLP text-mode list)._
- **`.CHR` Borland BGI stroked fonts** - the classic 1.54 vector "system font" set survives untouched: ten standard Borland BGI stroked-font files (BOLD, EURO, GOTH, LCOM, LITT, SANS, SCRI, SIMP, TRIP, TSCR). The format is Borland's, publicly documented, and unchanged; nothing RIPscrip-specific was added. _Evidence: 2.00a4 (system-font lineage); corpus (FONTS/\*.CHR); HLP ("BGI font" error strings)._

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: > _Editor's note:_ the FastFont format has full byte-level documentation under the earliest-version rule - the header, style-record, glyph-section, kerning, and `ATF.CFG` layouts live in the [v2.0 FastFont techspec](../../2.0/techspecs/3.2-fastfont-fonts.md), with the RIPtel-specific delta (the BRUSH/EUREKA/OAKLAND families and the regenerated `atf.cfg`) in the [v3.0 techspec](../techspecs/3.2-fastfont-additions.md). MicroANSI likewise: [v2.0 base](../../2.0/techspecs/3.3-microansi-fonts.md), [v3.0 `.maf` delta](../techspecs/3.3-microansi-maf-delta.md); the 1.54 stroked/bitmap lineage is in the [v1.54 techspecs](../../1.54/techspecs/3.1-bgi-stroked-fonts.md). Those pages supersede the research triage for format details.

requirements.heading: Fonts are not content files
requirements.text: > _Editor's note:_ the RIPtel install also contains client-internal binary files - resource containers and the variable database behind the [persistent variable store](../../glossary.md). These are implementation artifacts of one client, **not host-deliverable content and not specification surface**; they are decoded as research context in [`riptel-resource-containers.md`](../../3.0/research/riptel-resource-containers.md).

requirements.heading: 6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage
requirements.text: How a host gets content files onto the terminal and where they land: the query-then-download workflow, the block-mode extension routing table, RIPtel's per-bookmark host directory, the shared default icon directory, and the "file override" lookup order.

requirements.heading: 6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage
requirements.text: _The 2.0 model this carries forward is [6.2 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md) (1.54 lineage in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md))._

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: A well-behaved host delivers assets in two steps:

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text:
1. **Staleness check** - [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) asks whether a file already exists on the terminal's disk, and (modes 02-04) its size, date and time. The host compares the response against its own copy to decide whether a download is needed at all - the host side of the 3.x resource-caching story. Terminals that store audio in a translated local format must answer as if the WAVE original were on disk ([4.5](4.5-audio-files.md)). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (`RIP_FileQuery`); SyncTERM (ripper.c:16104) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, whose scenes are local and have no host to answer._
2. **Download** - [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) auto-initiates a file transfer (Xmodem variants, Kermit, Super Kermit, Ymodem, Ymodem-G, or Zmodem with or without crash recovery - protocol table in [5.5](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode)) with a file-type code telling the terminal what it is receiving - `.RIP` scenes to display or store, generic files, icons, or images to display on arrival. RIPtel itself uses Zmodem for its actual transfers. Over 7-bit-only links, [RIP_BEGIN_UUENCODE_BLOCK](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_begin_uuencode_block) embeds the same content as UU-encoded text _(v2.A1)_ - renamed `RIP_BeginEncodedStream` in the 3.0 driver. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (`RIP_EnterBlockMode`, `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`, DLL exports `RIP_GetBlockModeFilename`/`RIP_GetBlockModeTransferType`); SyncTERM (ripper.c:17069) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus._

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Once delivered, the host uses the assets by name - stamping icons, displaying images, playing audio, replaying scenes - with no further transmission cost, from the command stream (chapter 4) or from [host commands](../../glossary.md) via the playback prefixes ([5.3](5.3-local-playback.md)).

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Uploads work through the same block-mode command with mode 1; the user can be prompted to authorize them (RIPtel asks "Upload file(s) '%s'?"), and an unauthorized upload is refused with ten CAN (Ctrl-X) characters. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: Housekeeping: the [`$FILEDEL(file,…)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel) [text variable](../../glossary.md) lets the host delete files it created and no longer needs - no wildcards, no paths. The target "must be a filename that the host created, or downloaded to the terminal via RIP*ENTER_BLOCK_MODE or by some other means", and path information "will be ignored", so a host names a bare file and the terminal resolves it. \_Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP.* _(The v2.A3 revision notes also announced a `RIP_FILE_DELETE` command, but no entry for it exists in the ALPHA 4 draft and no such command name appears in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory - the variable form is the 3.x mechanism, implemented as `tvarProcFILEDEL`.)_

requirements.heading: The delivery workflow
requirements.text: > **Editor's note - implementation guidance, not specification.** No specification states which directory `$FILEDEL$` resolves against. Two of its own rules settle it in practice: deletion is limited to files _the host created_, and the host cannot supply a path. Since host deliveries land in the connection directory when one is configured, the safe reading is that `$FILEDEL$` should delete from the **connection directory only** and leave the shared default directory alone - files there may predate the session or belong to another host. This mirrors the lookup order in reverse: reads fall back from the connection directory to the shared default, but deletes should not. _(hypothesis)_ - inference from the spec's constraints and the storage model above; no shipping client has been examined to confirm it.

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: In the batch DYNAMIC file types, the terminal routes each received file by extension _(v2.A0)_:

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | Extension | COMPOSITE DYNAMIC (type 4) | ACTIVE DYNAMIC (type 5) |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | `RIP` | Store in proper directory | Store **and play back** locally |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | `BMP` | Place icon in proper directory | Place icon in proper directory |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | `BMH` | Place hot icon in proper directory | Place hot icon in proper directory |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | `BMM` | Place mask icon in proper directory | Place mask icon in proper directory |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | `JPG` | Store in proper directory | Store **and display** per image settings |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: | `GIF` _(v2.A4)_ | Store in proper directory | Store **and display** per image settings |

requirements.heading: Block-mode routing - the extension table
requirements.text: Files with any other extension are placed in the appropriate host directory with no further processing - which is how `.WAV` audio arrives, since it is absent from the table. "Proper directory" always resolves through the connection-directory model below, never through the user's ordinary download directory. (The `GIF` row is paper-only in 3.x - no shipped client decodes it; see [6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md).)

requirements.heading: Where files land
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP (RIPTEL.HLP "Host Directory", "Icon Search Path", "Download Directory"/"Upload Directory" topics - survey in the [techspec](../techspecs/4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md))._

requirements.heading: Where files land
requirements.text: The 3.x client carries the 2.0 storage model forward intact and renames its surface. Every host-deliverable media type still flows through **one directory family** - there is no separate audio, image, or scene directory:

requirements.heading: Where files land
requirements.text:
- The **default icon directory** (`ICONS\`) houses the whole host-deliverable media family: `.BMP`/`.BMH` icons (and legacy `.ICN`), `.JPG` images, `.WAV` sounds, and the script containers. RIPtel's installer creates `ICONS`, `FONTS`, and `Files` under the install root.
- Each **bookmark** (RIPtel's name for a dialing-directory entry) can name a per-host sub-directory - the **host directory**, the 3.x name for the connection directory (RIPterm 2.30's "System Dir", the 1.54 manual's DIR field) - configured in the bookmark editor's Advanced options. When one is specified, any icon, RIPscrip, sound, or image files sent by the host are automatically placed there. New bookmarks import their defaults from RIPtel's setup configuration, and auto-creation carries over from the DOS clients: "Many online services create their own host directories for you, without your knowledge."
- **New constraint in 3.x** - the host directory can only exist under the directory where the client is installed: "For security reasons, the host directory cannot exist in any arbitrary location on your hard drive." Directories the _host_ can populate are jailed under the install root; directories only the _user_ configures (the search path, below) may live anywhere. Implementations should preserve this property - host-influenced writes stay inside a client-owned sandbox.
- **New third lookup tier in 3.x** - the setup-level, user-configurable **icon search path**: extra directories consulted only after the two classic tiers fail, aimed at CD-ROM-distributed resource sets. Multiple directories are separated by semicolons (`C:\Windows;D:\;Icons\MyIcons`). The search path is **lookup-only** - host deliveries never write there.
- **Fonts are the exception** - stroked, outline and terminal fonts are global client resources resolved only from the font store (`FONTS\`), never per connection ([6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md)).
- **User file transfers stay outside the model** - ordinary Zmodem downloads land in a `Files` directory (with separate user-configurable download and upload directories), a different namespace from host-deliverable resources, exactly as in the 2.0 block-mode rule.

requirements.heading: Lookup order ("file override")
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP (RIPTEL.HLP "Host Directory" topic)._

requirements.heading: Lookup order ("file override")
requirements.text: When a command or playback variable references a file by name, the terminal searches the **host directory first**, then the default `ICONS\` directory, then the icon search path entries in order; first hit wins, and an error is reported only after all tiers fail. RIPTEL.HLP states the order outright: the client "will look for these kinds of files in that directory first. If the file cannot be found, then it checks the ICONS\ directory. If the file still cannot be found, then [it] checks any additional search directories that you have defined." The macro layer documents the same resolution order for the local-playback prefixes (`$>FILE.RIP$`, `$)FILE.WAV$`, `$<FILE.BMP$`, `$(FILE.JPG$` - [5.3](5.3-local-playback.md)).

requirements.heading: Lookup order ("file override")
requirements.text: The point of the scheme is unchanged from 2.0: same-named assets from different hosts do not collide - each host's `MENU.BMP` resolves to that host's own copy, while genuinely shared assets can live once in `ICONS\`. The RIPterm manuals call this behavior "file override". Commands never carry path information - filenames are bare DOS-style names, and the terminal decides where they resolve. (Modern implementations should also treat lookups as case-insensitive, as the DOS originals inherently were - see the [connection directory model techspec](../techspecs/4.0-connection-directory-model-delta.md).)

requirements.heading: Programmatic surface
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP ([help extraction §3, §5](../../3.0/research/riptel-help-extraction.md))._

requirements.heading: Programmatic surface
requirements.text: The directory model is reachable programmatically in 3.x, not just via configuration: the RIPscrip 3.0 function-name table includes **`RIP_SwitchDirectory`** among the wire commands - presumably switching the terminal's host/resource directory context - the client API exports `RIP_SetHostDirectory`/`RIP_GetHostDirectory`, and the text-variable processor list includes a `HOSTDIR` handler _(hypothesis: host-directory control)_. Wire-level semantics of `RIP_SwitchDirectory` are otherwise unrecovered - its opcode is unknown and no demo script in the RIPtel corpus exercises it.

requirements.heading: 7.0 Drawing Ports
requirements.text: [Drawing ports](../../glossary.md) - the fundamental drawing abstraction the 3.0 engine inherits from 2.0 and, by corpus evidence, the workhorse of shipped 3.x content: screen regions and offscreen (clipboard) surfaces, each with its own coordinate origin and [viewport](../../glossary.md).
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text: A drawing port is an area where graphics can be drawn. This is much like having a tablet of paper, where each page can be drawn to individually. However, just like a tablet of paper, only the piece of paper that is on the top of the tablet can be drawn to (the current piece of paper). The same concept applies to drawing ports. At any one moment in time, there is a "current drawing port". This current port is the one that will display graphical drawing operations when they are received.
requirements.reason: Device-pixel port ownership, origin/viewport, protection, lifecycle or copy behavior; wire parsing and world translation remain separately pending or blocked.

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text: There are two types of drawing ports:
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text:
1. A screen (visual) drawing port, and
2. An offscreen bitmap drawing port (also known as a "Clipboard Port").

requirements.heading: Drawing Ports - What Are They?
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver additionally distinguishes **snapshot ports** - offscreen ports created by capturing screen contents - in its error strings ("No mouse/button fields on offscreen drawing ports"). _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.text: A screen drawing port is the most commonly used form of drawing ports. A screen drawing port is a port that is somewhere on top of the screen. What this means is when a graphical drawing operation occurs, it is displayed in that port and subsequently to the screen immediately. Screen drawing ports are methods of dividing up the user's screen into separate regions, of which each can be thought of as completely separate drawing areas. You can switch between them pretty much at will to draw your graphics.
requirements.reason: Device-pixel port ownership, origin/viewport, protection, lifecycle or copy behavior; wire parsing and world translation remain separately pending or blocked.

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.text: Here is a typical example of one screen and how it can be divided up with multiple drawing ports:
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Screen Drawing Ports
requirements.text: As you can see, you have quite a bit of flexibility in placing your ports around on the screen. In this example, we have five ports defined on the screen. You might notice that port number 0 doesn't seem to have a rectangle associated with it. Actually, it does - it is the screen's boundary. Port number 0 is defined as the actual screen and cannot be redefined (you can alter its viewport though - see below for more details about viewports). Port 0 is always the full size of the screen. You can create your own screen ports, but port 0 is one that you cannot redefine the boundary of. This gives you the ability to always switch to port 0 to address the entire screen, but have the luxury of other ports when you only want to work with a portion of the screen.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: An offscreen bitmap port, otherwise known as a "clipboard port", is very much like a screen port, but it isn't actually a part of the screen. It is more like another screen that you cannot see, but one that you can still draw to. You might be asking yourself why something like this is part of RIPscrip? The answer is quite simple - they are extremely powerful! An offscreen port can be used for placing a piece of graphics data temporarily while you are showing a dialog box on the screen, only to restore the original graphics when the user clicks the "OK" button on the dialog box. The graphical data that was overwritten by the dialog box isn't deleted - it's been saved temporarily on a screen that you cannot see, but is restored to the screen when necessary. Another use of this might be if you had a very complicated scene to display, but you didn't want the user to see each little graphics operation until the entire scene was complete; switch to an offscreen bitmap port, draw your scene, then switch back to the screen and copy the offscreen port's graphics to your screen. Voila, the user sees the scene appear on his screen complete - not piecemeal!
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: There are numerous reasons why you would use offscreen ports; things like storing a bitmap that you just loaded from the hard disk onto an offscreen port so that when you paste it to the screen a large number of times, there isn't a large amount of disk activity on the user's machine. Another good example is in the situation of an online game where the screen is some kind of map, and one or more offscreen ports are used to hold small "icons", or bitmaps of game pieces. Simply copy the images from the offscreen port(s) to appropriate locations on the map and you've accomplished a rather complicated situation without adversely affecting the user's system with intense hard drive activity due to constantly loading bitmaps off the disk - the side effect, the game moves much more swiftly and with a lot less "jerkiness" due to the hard disk accesses.
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: Just like with screen drawing ports, you can select an offscreen bitmap port as the one which will receive graphical drawing operations. Selecting an offscreen port as the current port lets you draw simple graphics objects, photos and other such things to it. But remember, the graphics you draw to an offscreen port are of little value unless at some point you actually copy it to the screen so that the user can see it.
requirements.reason: Device-pixel port ownership, origin/viewport, protection, lifecycle or copy behavior; wire parsing and world translation remain separately pending or blocked.

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: Some things cannot be done to offscreen ports. For example, you cannot place a mouse field or a clickable button on an offscreen port. The reason for this is that the mouse only has any meaning to the screen - the environment that the user interacts with. How can the user click on a button that he can't see? He can't. You also cannot place [text windows](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) or assign resident query expressions to offscreen ports. The 3.0.7 driver enforces the rule with its own error string ("No mouse/button fields on offscreen drawing ports"). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Offscreen Drawing Ports (Clipboard Ports)
requirements.text: An offscreen port is most easily thought of as a graphics screen that you can't see. You can work with it to your heart's content, but the user can't see the contents of it until you copy the data to the screen. As long as you keep this one fundamental concept in mind, there should be no confusion about ports.

requirements.heading: The Port Table
requirements.text: Ports live in a 36-slot [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#drawing-port-table), entries numbered **0-35**:

requirements.heading: The Port Table
requirements.text:
- **Port 0 is always the screen.** It is the full size of the display, exists at all times, and cannot be created, deleted, or redefined - confirmed verbatim by the 3.0.7 driver's error strings "Can't delete graphics port #0" and "Can't create drawing port #0". You can always switch to port 0 to address the entire screen (its viewport may still be altered).
- **Ports 1-35** are user-definable - the driver rejects out-of-range numbers with "The given port number is invalid (1-35 only)". Each may be a screen sub-region or an offscreen bitmap.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: A port is a specific drawing area. No matter whether the port is a screen port or an offscreen bitmap port, it is still a drawing area, and as such, it has a legal number of horizontal and vertical pixels that can be drawn to. Every graphical drawing operation uses graphical coordinates with which they draw their image to the current port. For example, a circle needs to know the center point, and the radius of the circle in order to draw itself.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: Each port has what can be thought of as its own set of coordinates. Just like the screen where (0,0) is the upper-left corner of the screen, when a port is active (ie, current), (0,0) is the coordinate of the upper-left corner of the drawing port. If a port had a width of W and a height of H, then the lower-right coordinate would be (W-1,H-1). This holds true for all drawing ports, even offscreen bitmap ports.
requirements.reason: Device-pixel port ownership, origin/viewport, protection, lifecycle or copy behavior; wire parsing and world translation remain separately pending or blocked.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: As you can see, each port can be thought of as its own little drawing universe, with its own set of coordinates. This makes drawing things like graphs, or showing game map windows easy - without having to make extensive calculations in the host software to figure out where things need to be placed. This is considered "port relative" coordinates.

requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: Screen ports are defined as some location on the actual screen from the upper-left corner to the lower-right corner (in the current [world coordinate](../../glossary.md) system). From this information, the width and height of the port can be easily calculated, and the physical pixel dimensions are derived and remembered.
