requirements.heading: Ports and Coordinates
requirements.text: Offscreen ports are a bit different though. Since they're not part of the user's actual screen, they don't have this upper-left location on the screen. In this manner, an offscreen port is always thought of as having an upper-left corner of (0,0) and its lower-right corner as (W-1,H-1).

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: Each drawing port has an associated viewport, or clipping rectangle. A viewport is a rectangle inside the port that defines the drawing limits inside that port. It's similar in concept to a coloring book with invisible lines. You can draw all you want, but you can't go outside the lines. If any operation would extend beyond the edge of this clipping rectangle, it will be truncated. For example, if you have a drawing port that is 100x100 pixels in size, and you define the viewport to be from (25,25) to (74,74), you would have a 50x50 drawing area right in the center of the drawing port. If you then draw a circle in the exact center of the drawing port with a radius of 60 pixels, you would have pieces of the circle that extend beyond the top, left, bottom and right borders of the viewport. What you would see would be four arcs in each corner of the viewport as in the following example:

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: If you notice in the above diagram, the rectangle inside the port defines the viewport. The solid squares (█) denote pixels inside the viewport that would actually be drawn, and the shaded squares (░) show pixels that will not be drawn because they are outside the viewport.
requirements.reason: Historical evidence, descriptive introduction or diagram scaffolding; the normative port behavior is tracked separately.

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: You can alter the location and size of the viewport inside any given drawing port. By default, the viewport is set to the full size of the drawing port when the port is created. If you attempt to make the viewport go outside the actual port, it will be adjusted to fit so that it is completely within the port. If an attempt is made to define a viewport that is completely outside the boundary of its port, then the definition is ignored as an error condition. If the lower-right corner is outside the boundary of the port, then the lower-right corner of the newly defined viewport is set to the lower-right corner of the port itself.

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: Just like drawing ports, a viewport also "adjusts" drawing coordinates. When you alter the location of a viewport inside of a drawing port, the origin (0,0) for drawing operations relates to the upper-left corner of the viewport itself, not the actual underlying drawing port. All drawing operations pertain to a port's viewport, not the port itself. The port is considered the maximum limits for the viewport inside - just like the screen, you can only draw to areas inside the screen; the same applies to viewports and ports.

requirements.heading: Ports, Viewports and Graphical Operations
requirements.text: We've already discussed how a viewport "truncates" a graphical operation if it extends beyond the border of the port's viewport.

requirements.heading: Ports, Viewports and Graphical Operations
requirements.text: What if you're copying graphical data from one port to another? Graphics data can only be copied from one port to another in rectangular portions, and just like all other graphical operations, this kind of situation adheres to the viewports of both the source and the destination ports! Let's take an example where you are copying a rectangle of graphics from port 1 to port 2. For sake of clarity, we'll copy the entire viewport over (not a sub-area of the viewport). The following diagram shows what would happen if the two viewports aren't the exact same size (specifically, the source viewport is larger than the destination viewport):

The shaded squares (░) are graphics data from the source viewport that aren't copied to the destination. This shows how a viewport "truncates" graphical drawing operations, even when copying data from one port to another.

requirements.heading: Copying Data From One Port to Another
requirements.text: When you copy graphical data from one port to another (or to another location on the same port for that matter), you are duplicating the graphical contents of the source port onto the destination port. Whether the result is an exact replica of the original image or not is another matter. Whenever you copy a rectangle of data from one port to another, you need to specify a rectangle in the source port, and another one in the destination port. These two rectangles do not need to be the same pixel size. If they are different either in the width or height dimensions, then scaling of the source image will occur! For example, if the source image's rectangle doesn't have the same dimensions as the rectangle in the destination port, you could have a situation similar to the following:

If the two rectangles had the same width and height values, then our destination image would be pixel-for-pixel identical to the original (providing that the viewport of the destination port didn't truncate the image of course).

requirements.heading: Copying Data From One Port to Another
requirements.text: When copying rectangular pieces of data from one port to another, you have to be careful about viewports. If either the source or the destination rectangle are completely outside that port's viewport, then the copy operation isn't performed - nothing would be visible if it did happen, because either the source or the destination image wouldn't be visible inside the viewport.

requirements.text: Let's take another example but this time we will show scaling because this situation may not be intuitive. Let's assume that our source rectangle is twice as large as our destination rectangle both in the width and height dimensions. This means that our image will be reduced by 1/2. If the destination rectangle also had to be truncated, then the scaling is still performed. Under no circumstances will a vertical or horizontal "blank" zone be created during scaling. When you say "scale to fit", it does exactly what you told it to - it makes the graphics fit in the given area. Here is the diagram that shows this situation:

requirements.heading: Observed Usage in the 3.x Era
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (WIPE00.FN-WIPE24.FN); HLP._

requirements.heading: Observed Usage in the 3.x Era
requirements.text: The port system is the workhorse of TeleGrafix's own 3.x demo material. The RIPtel demo corpus contains **9,104 uses of `2C` (RIP_PORT_COPY)** - by far the most frequent command after RIP_LINE - almost all of them in the WIPE00-WIPE24 "wipe" transition library: each wipe composes the next scene in an offscreen port, then reveals it with a sequence of narrow port-to-screen copies to animate slides, splits, and dissolves. The supporting pattern (define port 1 full-screen, copy the screen into it, switch, draw, copy back) appears throughout the `.FN` function scenes, with TeleGrafix's own comments narrating it: "Create a port for the status line backup area, and copy the area where the status line will go into that drawing port."

requirements.heading: Observed Usage in the 3.x Era
requirements.text: The corpus uses only four level-2 port commands - `2P` (define), `2p` (delete), `2s` (switch), `2C` (copy) - confirming these as the practical core of the port system on the wire. (SyncTERM's `RIPSCRIP030001` mode implements **no level-2 commands at all** - the single largest gap between the open-source reconstruction and shipped 3.x content.)

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: This command physically defines a new graphical drawing port. The port can be either onscreen (a video port) or an offscreen bitmap port (a Clipboard Port). When defined, the newly created port becomes the current graphical drawing port (if the `<flags>` say to - see below).

requirements.text: If the `<port-num>` that you are trying to define is already defined, and the port isn't protected, it is redefined (ie, deleted then re-created using the new parameters). If the port is defined and protected, then the port definition operation will fail and the port will be switched back to the screen port (#0) as previously described.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<port-num>` parameter determines which entry in the master Port Table you wish to define. When working with ports, you need to be concerned about the port number you're working with - that's the location of the port, and that's how you access it when you need to switch ports - by port number. You are allowed up to 36 separate graphical ports (0-35 in decimal). Port #0 cannot be re-defined because it is always defined as the Screen Port. You can however, alter the viewport for Port #0 to make a sub-area on the screen to draw in (and clip). The viewport for Port #0 may also be deactivated as can the viewport on any other graphical Port. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: Device-pixel port ownership, origin/viewport, protection, lifecycle or copy behavior; wire parsing and world translation remain separately pending or blocked.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: To create a port, you need to specify the upper-left coordinate corner of the port and the lower-right coordinate of the rectangle bounding the port. The configuration of coordinates is different depending on the type of graphical port as declared by the `<flags>` parameter (see below). For Video Ports (onscreen ports), the `<x0>` and `<y0>` parameters define the upper-left corner of the port on the video screen, and the `<x1>` and `<y1>` values define the lower-right corner of the port. Together, they define the pixel width and height of the port (this adheres to global world coordinate systems). For Clipboard Ports (offscreen bitmap ports), you cannot have an upper-left corner - so the `<x0>` and `<y0>` parameters must be set to zero.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: Once defined, the viewport for the given port is defined as the size of the port itself (you may change it with a [RIP_VIEWPORT](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) command later if you wish). This makes it so that the entire port may be drawn into. If you need to define a sub-area of the port as a clipping boundary, modify the viewport for that graphical port.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<flags>` parameter for this command allows you to make some important distinctions to the port. The possible port flags are OR'd together to create one final number where each bit represents some flag value. The possible flag values and what they mean are described as follows:

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: | 1 | Port is an offscreen (Clipboard) port. When this flag is specified, the `<x0>` and `<y0>` parameter are assumed to be zero (even if they aren't set to 0, they are treated as if they were). When a port is declared as a Clipboard Port, all graphical operations are performed to an offscreen bitmap port and do not appear on the screen (without you specifically using a port copy operation). If this flag is omitted, then the port is treated as a Video Port and any graphics drawn to the port will show up on the screen immediately (providing the viewport for this port isn't deactivated). |

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_PORT
requirements.text: This command physically changes whichever port is currently active. You may specify a port number from 0-35 (36 ports total). If the designated port doesn't exist, then the port is automatically switched to port #0 (the screen's port). This has the side-effect that when the operation fails (ie, the destination port doesn't exist), all subsequent graphics operations would be sent to the screen which would give you a visual impression that something is very wrong.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: This command physically deletes one or more graphical ports. The exact port depends on the `<port_num>` parameter. If the port number specified is between 1-35, then the given port is deleted (providing of course that it is unprotected). If you attempt to delete a protected port, then this command will fail. If you attempt to delete port #0 (the screen port), then you will be activating a special case of this command - all unprotected ports from 1-35 are automatically deleted. This is a good garbage collection command mode when you want to start with a new slate of ports without the overhead of sending many delete port commands.
requirements.reason: Device-pixel port ownership, origin/viewport, protection, lifecycle or copy behavior; wire parsing and world translation remain separately pending or blocked.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<dest_port>` parameter defines the port number that will be switched to after the delete operation is finished. Typically, this will be set to port #0 (switch to screen port), but it need not be. If the destination port is undefined, then it will automatically switch to port #0. If you instruct this command to delete all ports, then the destination port may or may not be set to the screen port - it all depends on whether or not the destination port both exists, and is protected - remember, a protected port cannot be deleted with this command without first being unprotected. So, if you delete all ports and switch to another port that isn't port #0, and that port is protected, then that protected port is selected as the new active port. If however, that port doesn't exist (ie, it did exist at the beginning of this command, but wasn't protected), then the screen port #0 will be selected.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** The `<res>` parameter is reserved for future use and should be set to "00" for future compatibility with later RIPscrip revisions.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: The example, from NEWPORT.FN ("Make sure port #1 is deleted before continuing"), removes port 1 and returns to the screen; MAKEPORT.FN's `!|2p00` ("Delete all ports (screen is unaffected)") is the garbage-collection special case in the wild, with trailing reserved digits omitted - tolerated by the shipping parser. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_COPY
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** viewport, port, base math (current setting)

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_COPY
requirements.text: This command copies graphics data from one port to another (or possibly even the same port). The area copied is a rectangular area based on the (sx0,sy0)..(sx1,sy1) parameters in the `<source_port>` and the (dx0,dy0)..(dx1,dy1) parameters in the `<dest_port>`. The `<source_port>` and `<dest_port>` parameters specify which port numbers are to be used for the source and destination respectively. They may be set to the same port number which signifies that a bit-blit operation is to occur from one location of the current port to another. Both the source and destination ports are specified as port numbers from 0-35. If either port doesn't exist (or is deactivated) then this command will do nothing.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_COPY
requirements.text: The source port parameters (sx0,sy0)..(sx1,sy1) define the upper-left and lower-right corners of the rectangle in the source port that is to be the source image data. If all four parameters are set to zero, then the entire source port's viewport is used as the image. These parameters determine the portion of the source port that is to be used to copy to the destination port. The image data is taken from within the port's currently defined viewport. If the (sx1,sy1) parameters takes the image out of the bounds of the source port's viewport, then the values are adjusted to make it fit inside the viewport.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_COPY
requirements.text: The destination port parameters (dx0,dy0)..(dx1,dy1) define the destination rectangle in the destination port that will receive the graphical data. The (dx0,dy0) parameters define the upper-left corner of the destination location of the bitmap data. If the (dx1,dy1) parameters are set to zero, then the image is copied from the source port verbatim - with the exact same pixel dimensions as the source image rectangle. If these two values are not set to zero, then scaling of the source image may be performed. Whether or not scaling is performed depends on one fact - does the physical pixel size (height and width) of the source image rectangle exactly match the pixel size (height and width) of the destination port rectangle? If the pixel dimensions match exactly, then no scaling is performed on the rectangle. However, if the pixel size in either the vertical or horizontal directions are different, then the image is scaled to fit in the desired rectangle. When we talk about "pixel size", we are referring to the low-level device pixel size of the image. This means that we take into account world coordinate translation and viewport coordinate translations first, then compare the raw pixel sizes of the source and destination rectangles. If they differ, then we perform scaling of the bitmap. Otherwise we copy it over verbatim. If the destination rectangle coordinates are set all to zeros, then the image is placed at (0,0) in the destination port's viewport and the image will fill the entire port's viewport.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_COPY
requirements.text: By use count this is _the_ RIPscrip 3.x command: the WIPE00-24.FN transition library is almost nothing but port-copy animation, sliding successive slices of a pre-rendered offscreen scene onto the screen. The example line, from a wipe, copies the slice of offscreen port 1 from x = `XC` (1200) to `ZK` (1280), full height `QO` (960), onto screen port 0 at (0,0)-(72,960) in COPY mode - one frame of a right-to-left push (reserved digits omitted, as the shipping driver tolerates). Between the wipes and the `.MSE` status-line backups ("Copy the screen image to the port"), 46 of the 116 corpus files depend on it. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: This command physically takes the contents of the specific graphics port and writes it to a disk-based bitmap file (eg, a .BMP file) - the port-generation counterpart of [RIP_WRITE_ICON](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_write_icon). The specific area of the given port that is written to the disk is based on the (x0,y0)..(x1,y1) parameters. If all of these parameters are set to zeros, then the entire port's viewport is written to the desired bitmap file. If the (x1,y1) parameters are set to zero, then the lower-right corner of the image is taken to be the lower-right corner of the port's viewport. The (x0,y0) parameters determine the upper-left corner of the image's location in the given graphics port. You could use any of the following three variations:

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: | X0 | Y0 | X1 | Y1 | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | Grab the entire port's viewport for the image to be saved. |

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: | 25 | 25 | 0 | 0 | Grab the image area from (25,25) to the lower-right of the port's viewport as the image data to be saved. |

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: | 25 | 25 | 100 | 100 | Save the image data from (25,25) to (100,100) in the given graphics port to the destination bitmap file. |

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_WRITE
requirements.text: The `<port_num>` parameter determines which graphics port is to be the source of the image data. If that port is undefined, or the X/Y parameters place the graphics data off the port's viewport, then this command is ignored. If the (x0,y0) parameters fall inside the port's viewport, but the (x1,y1) parameters do not, then the lower-left corner is adjusted appropriately (as if the user specified (0,0) as the lower-left corner - see above).

requirements.heading: 7.1 Data Tables
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 7.1 Data Tables
requirements.text: Data tables - the mechanism, inherited from 2.0 and confirmed throughout the 3.0.7 driver's error strings, that turns nearly every piece of drawing state into a numbered, switchable, protectable table entry: six general tables of 36 entries each, plus the special 128-entry mouse field table.

requirements.heading: 7.1 Data Tables
requirements.text: _The switch commands live with their subject matter - [RIP_SWITCH_PORT](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_switch_port) in 7.0, [RIP_SWITCH_PALETTE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_switch_palette) in 2.0, [RIP_SWITCH_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_switch_text_window) in 1.4, [RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_switch_button_style) in 4.3 - while the graphical-style and environment switches are documented here._

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: RIPscrip 2.0 was different from its previous versions architecturally on a number of levels, and one of the key fundamental differences - the data table - carries into 3.x unchanged. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: A data table is a table of information used in RIPscrip. Data tables may be the color palette table (where each table entry is a complete color palette definition), graphical style tables, button style tables, [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md) tables, text window definition tables, mouse field tables, or environment data tables. Some data tables have an entry that is "currently active". This might be the currently active text window in the text window data table, or the currently active color palette in the palette data table. Every data table has one or more entries in it, in which each entry is a specific piece of data. Data table entries can be "in use" and/or protected (see below). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: Data can be moved from one table entry to another (in effect, making a copy of one table entry to another); this doesn't apply to all data tables (eg, mouse field data table). Also, most tables' entries can be protected so that the contents of a particular entry cannot be modified or deleted until either an unprotect entry function is executed, or a hard reset is performed (a hard reset completely resets the entire RIPscrip environment to ground zero). Again the mouse field data table cannot have individual entries protected. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: Host commands manipulate tables through the [`$CUR$`](5.1-text-variables.md#cur), [`$COPY$`](5.1-text-variables.md#copy), [`$PROT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#prot), [`$UNPROT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#unprot), [`$ISPROT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#isprot) and [`$INUSE$`](5.1-text-variables.md#inuse) [text variables](../../glossary.md).

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver's error strings confirm the table architecture directly: every general table has **36 entries, numbered 0-35** ("Invalid … entry number (0-35)", "Invalid button group number (>35)"), entries can be PROTECTed and unprotected, and data can be copied from one entry to another. Entry contents survive until overwritten, cleared by a reset, or removed by a hard reset. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Entry 0 - the Common Modifiable Entry
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Entry 0 - the Common Modifiable Entry
requirements.text: Entry 0 of each table is special: it is the always-present working entry that **cannot be deleted or protected**. The driver enforces this per table - "Cannot protect current text window slot when it is #0", "Can't protect environment data table entry #0", "Can't protect graphics style data table entry zero", "Can't protect color palette zero", and for ports, "Can't delete graphics port #0". Entry 0 is thus the common, freely modifiable entry every scene can rely on; protection is reserved for entries 1-35.

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: There are six different data tables for general data storage: the drawing port table, color palette table, graphical style table, text window table, the button style table and the RIPscrip environment data table. There are backup areas for these data tables so you can make complete backup copies for re-use later after some operation is performed (eg, executing a dialog box, running a door, etc). There are actually more data backup areas than there are data tables - see [7.2 Data Backup Areas](7.2-data-backup-areas.md). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: The `RIP_Switch*` command family in the 3.0 command inventory covers the switchable tables (`RIP_SwitchButtonStyle`, `RIP_SwitchEnvironment`, `RIP_SwitchPalette`, `RIP_SwitchPort`, `RIP_SwitchStyle`, `RIP_SwitchTextWindow` - plus `RIP_SwitchDirectory`, which belongs to the [storage model](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#programmatic-surface) rather than a drawing table; its wire opcode is unknown). _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: The general table groups are described in more detail as follows: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: One of the most fundamental aspects of the language is the concept of a [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). Any drawing of graphics occurs inside a drawing port. There may be up to 36 ports [defined](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_define_port) simultaneously. Port number 0 is always defined as the screen. Its dimensions are that of the screen. The remaining 35 ports may be sub-sections of the screen or may be offscreen memory drawing ports (ie, clipboard ports). At any one moment in time, only one port may be the current port - the port that will receive graphical drawing operations. If the current port is an offscreen clipboard port, then any drawing operations will not appear on the screen. The only way that those graphics can be viewed by the user is if the contents of the port are copied to a screen port. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: All ports, when defined, are defined using the current [world coordinate](../../glossary.md) system. From those coordinates, the port's actual physical pixel dimensions are determined and those dimensions are remembered by the port. Any graphical operation that bypasses the viewport system pays close attention to coordinates and the boundaries of the drawing port. If any coordinate would go outside of the port, it is adjusted to fit inside. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: Each port entry remembers its own drawing state - the full list is in [7.0](7.0-drawing-ports.md#the-port-table). The entire drawing port data table also keeps track of the "current viewport" query expression (otherwise known as a floating viewport query). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: In RIPscrip there is a graphical color palette. The color palette is a group of 256 separate color RGB values, also known as a color lookup table. This color palette is used to map a particular color number to some combination of red, green and blue color components. For example, color 0 is usually black (no red, green or blue), and color 255 is typically white (full intensity red, green and blue). This color palette is normally written directly into the video hardware of your computer to activate the colors. So when you try to draw in color 255, you see a white line appear on the screen. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: 36 independently owned 256-color palettes, one current selection, indexed-pixel cycling and complete palette-table snapshots/restoration including current/defined/protection state. Backup slots/stack, wire/variable handling and reset lifecycle remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: Up to 36 separate color palettes may be held at once. Only one entry in the color palette table may be current at any one moment in time. An entry in the color palette table is a complete 256 color palette. When you switch from one color palette entry to another, the colors on the screen will typically change instantly. This gives you the ability to quickly and easily switch from one color scheme to another without sending a large amount of information to the terminal every time you wish to switch color schemes. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: 36 independently owned 256-color palettes, one current selection, indexed-pixel cycling and complete palette-table snapshots/restoration including current/defined/protection state. Backup slots/stack, wire/variable handling and reset lifecycle remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: The language allows for two forms of color modes, color palette mapping mode (the default) and direct RGB color encoding - see [2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md). Under 24-bit configurations, a real hardware color palette is not possible; the palette is used as an RGB lookup table for subsequent drawing, and switching palettes will not change colors already on the screen. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: When a normal reset operation is performed, all unprotected palette entries are reset to bootup default color palette values. A "hard reset" will reset the entire color palette data table to default values. _(v2.A4)_ The 3.0.7 driver caps palette indices at 0-255 and enforces the per-command limits described in [2.0](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md). _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: Upstream #16 must reconcile palette reset in-use status or contradictory port current/entry-copy descriptions before observable table/variable behavior can be completed.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: There are 36 separate graphical style table entries. Initially, number 0 is current and is initialized to default values. A graphical style entry defines a number of currently active graphical attributes (each entry has all of these):

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text:
- Current drawing color
- Current background drawing color
- Current fill pattern number (or user-defined fill pattern)
- Current fill color
- Current line pattern number (or user-defined line pattern)
- Line pattern odd drawing rule (see [RIP_LINE_STYLE](2.1-lines.md#rip_line_style))
- Current mouse cursor style number
- Current font number (or font name for extended fonts)
- Current font size, orientation and horizontal/vertical alignment
- Current write mode (raster/transfer operation)
- Current color mode (palette or direct RGB)

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: With the ability of having multiple graphical style entries defined simultaneously, you can setup an entire graphical environment, then with a single command, switch to a completely different configuration in only a couple of bytes of RIPscrip code. This can greatly reduce the amount of RIPscrip code that needs to be transmitted after the style data table entries are initially setup. See [Protected Data Table Entries](#protected-data-table-entries) below for even more powerful aspects of the data table systems. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: Button style data table entries contain a complete button style definition as defined by a [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) command. Having multiple button style slots defined at the same time allows you to have many commonly used button styles defined at once, so that you can simply reference an already defined button style rather than having to transmit a rather lengthy button style command each and every time you wish to define a button.

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver additionally fixes button semantics via its error strings: button types are **plain, icon, or snapshot**; labels and hotkey codes are limited to 255; button groups are numbered 0-35. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: A [text window](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) is simply a region on the screen where raw, non-RIPscrip text is routed once it is received from the host. Initially, the text window is full screen, using the MicroANSI font #2 (80x25) - different from 1.54, whose initial setting was font #0 (80x43); 80x25 is more aesthetically pleasing to most people so it was made the default. A text window typically supports ANSI and VT-102 screen control codes. Each of the 36 text window table entries stores:

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text:
- The upper-left and lower-right corner definitions for the text window (coordinates are in text coordinates, not graphical screen coordinates).
- The MicroANSI screen font number for the given window.
- The current ANSI color attributes
- The current cursor X/Y location
- The status of the cursor (is it on or off)
- The current vertical scrolling margins (ANSI formatting)
- Whether the window is activated or deactivated.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: A text window can also be deactivated. If the current text window slot is deactivated then any raw text that is received from the host will be discarded (ie, not shown on screen at all). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: Having multiple defined text windows allows you to quickly switch from one text window configuration to another without losing any previously used information (color, location, cursor, etc). Note that the text contained inside the current text window is not stored as part of the text window definition - only the window's raw definition is preserved. See [1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) for the extended (resolution-independent) text window added in the 3.x era.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: The environment data table is a central table for the maintenance of critical values that define the characteristics of the RIPscrip environment. This data table holds up to 36 separate environments. The following pieces of information are stored in each entry:

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text:
- Current graphics style entry number
- Current button style entry number
- Current drawing port entry number
- Current text window entry number
- Current color palette entry number
- Current World coordinate dimensions (X and Y)
- Current [Base Math](../../glossary.md) settings (36 or 64)
- Current [coordinate size](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size) (2 through 5)
- Current color mode (color palette mode or direct RGB mode)
- Current mouse pointer number
- Current baud rate emulation value

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: When you switch from one environment to another, you are effectively performing an entire "context swapping" operation. This might best be taken with an example:

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: > Let's say you have set up all of your data tables to work with entry number 5 and entry 5 in each data table is the current one. This could have an entire drawing environment defined for a particular situation. Let's say that you have entry 6 in every data table defined with a completely different configuration of drawing environments. You could easily switch between one drawing environment to another simply by switching environments, in effect completely redefining your entire drawing world. Nothing is destroyed in this switching process, all you are doing is simply switching to another environment. You would still be free to return to the previous environment if you so desire (note that if you perform any reset operations though, you best make sure that you protect things or they will disappear when you reset).

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: Note that there isn't a "current mouse field data table entry". This is because there's no such thing as a current mouse field in the mouse field data table. So, switching from one environment to another has no effect on the current mouse fields (unlike it would with text windows, ports, graphical styles, palettes, etc).

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: The environment table is central to the 3.x backup/dialog system: HLP confirms the 36 slots, the unprotectable slot #0, the `$SENV$`/`$RENV$` backup variables, and environment header segments carrying coordinate-size and RGB-bit settings (below). _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: The mouse field data table is unlike the other data tables. It can hold up to 128 separate mouse field definitions and does not have a "current mouse field" entry number. Each mouse field that is defined gets added to the mouse field data table at the very end until 128 fields are defined, or the table is deleted and things start over. Mouse fields only pertain to drawing port #0, so they can only be on the screen, not on an offscreen drawing port. See [RIP_MOUSE](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse), [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) and [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) for more details on this special data table.

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver adds the `ID=n:` prefix convention for assigning numbered identities to mouse fields, readable back through `$FIELDID$` and used by the `.MSE` overlay scenes' entry/exit queries ([4.2](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md)). _Evidence: HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: Audio (New in 3.x)
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Audio (New in 3.x)
requirements.text: The scene header segment mechanism (below) includes an **audio** entry alongside the classic tables ("…mouse field / audio / graphics screen" in the header-segment error-string family), indicating the 3.0 engine tracks audio state as a headerable object class. No slot-count error strings for audio have been recovered, so its table dimensions are unconfirmed _(hypothesis: state entry rather than a 36-slot table)_. Audio behavior itself is covered in [4.4](4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md) and [4.5](4.5-audio-files.md).

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments and Table State
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments and Table State
requirements.text: The 3.0 engine's [scene header segments](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md) - the formalized successor to the 2.A1 RIP_HEADER idea - declare per-table state up front: RIPSCRIP.HLP's error-string family maps segments carrying flags and entry numbers for each object class - **button style, graphics style, drawing port, text window, color palette, environment, mouse field, audio, and graphics screen** - plus an environment segment with the coordinate size and direct-RGB bit count, general header flags, and a revision code. A scene can thus declare which table entries it expects before drawing begins. No wire-format example of a header segment has been recovered - the RIPtel demos use explicit prologue commands instead ([6.0](6.0-writing-rip-files.md)) - so the segment encoding remains undocumented _(hypothesis)_.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Data table entries by themselves have quite a bit of usefulness in short-term situations where a lot of different configurations need to be switched between fairly often. Their usefulness becomes even more powerful with the concept of protected data table entries. A protected entry is one that cannot be cleared by a normal reset operation or a clear table entry operation until the entry is unprotected, or until a "hard reset" operation is performed. In addition, they cannot be modified while they are protected (see below). _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: A "hard reset" is a complete reset of the RIPscrip environment. Typically, a hard reset should only be performed immediately after connection to a RIPscrip compatible host system to clear the slate so to speak. Other uses for a hard reset are when the RIPscrip environment is hopelessly corrupted due to line noise, or when a complete re-synchronization of the environment is about to commence. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Protected entries become quite powerful when you look at a larger host system. For example, let's say that throughout your system you use five different graphical style configurations all over the place, all of which require quite a bit of transmitted RIPscrip code. If you define each of these styles as separate entries and then protect them, you don't need to re-transmit those blocks of data again unless a hard reset operation is performed! This can mean quite a bit of saved data transmission, and consequently faster transmission times. The same concept applies to text windows, ports, button styles, graphics style, palette and environment tables. When taken from a system-wide perspective, where many sections of the system may be made by other manufacturers (eg, doors, BBS modules, etc), you may not be able to count on whether a section of the system uses one style or another, or does one kind of reset or another. Having protected entries gives you the ability to protect your data configurations so that these sub-sections do not destroy your data. When you return from the sub-section, simply re-activate your table configuration(s) and away you go. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: We just described that a protected data table entry cannot be deleted. We also mentioned that they cannot be modified. Let's clarify what we mean by not modifiable. A data table entry that is protected cannot be modified by any of the normal RIPscrip commands or [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md) that alter their basic configuration (eg, you cannot alter the foreground drawing color in a protected graphical style data table entry, etc). It should be noted however, that normal drawing operations like rectangles, circles, etc, can still be performed to a port that is protected. In this case, the port is protected from having its "configuration" modified (eg, the viewport cannot be modified nor can the actual port's orientation). The same applies to text windows (eg, you can output text to a text window, perform ANSI/VT-102 operations to it, erase it, etc, but you cannot redefine it or delete it). One tiny exception rests with text windows that support VT-102. VT-102 has an ANSI escape sequence that allows you to alter the wrap/chop setting of text windows. Since ANSI operations are allowed on protected text windows, this is permissible even though it seemingly violates the nature of modifying a text window's protected status. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Terminal emulation modes are also unaffected by a text window's protection status. If a text window is enabled, VT-102 mode can be turned on or off because this is a "global" setting, not a text window specific setting. Also, RIPscrip processing can be disabled via a special ANSI escape sequence ([1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md)). This does not affect protection of text windows or drawing ports either. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: With these things in mind, performing operations like "copying a port's data to another port" where one or both are protected is allowable because you are not altering the basic configuration of the ports in question, you are simply altering their data contents. This applies to "clipboard" related commands too which might dynamically pick and choose ports to define. Since a clipboard related command will auto-define a new port if one doesn't already exist, it will pick a currently undefined drawing port and define it (if it's not defined, then it cannot be protected). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver's PROTECT machinery is confirmed by its error strings, including the entry-0 exclusions listed above, and by the `$PROTECT$`/`$ISPROT$`/`$UNPROT$`-family text-variable processors present in its string table. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.text: _Switches to a new Drawing Style Context_

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: This command switches to a particular "drawing style". A drawing style is a combination of the following graphical settings: _(list as of v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text:
- Current drawing color
- Current background drawing color
- Current fill pattern number (or user-defined fill pattern)
- Current fill color
- Current line pattern number (or user-defined line pattern)
- Line pattern odd drawing rule (see [RIP_LINE_STYLE](2.1-lines.md#rip_line_style))
- Current mouse cursor style number
- Current font number (or font name for extended fonts)
- Current font size, orientation and horizontal/vertical alignment
- Current write mode (raster/transfer operation)
- Current color mode (palette or direct RGB)
- Current X/Y location (used with [RIP_TEXT](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_text) commands)
- Current image mode settings (see [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](4.1-jpeg-images.md#rip_image_style))

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: By default, all commands that alter the above modes will change the settings of Style #0. By switching Style Contexts, you are given the ability to alter which Style Context is being manipulated. After a given Style has been defined, you can quickly switch from one Style to another without having to re-transmit each and every mode command to recreate the environment.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: The first time you switch to a new Style Context, the contents of the current Style are copied into the newly selected Style. You are allowed up to 36 separate Styles (0-9, A-Z).

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: Whenever a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) function is executed, the contents of all Styles are reset to a default status which is the status of the drawing environment after resetting is complete.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_STYLE
requirements.text: The demos never switch style slots - they simply re-send the individual attribute commands before each drawing group instead. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A data backup area is a backup area that composes one base save area and ten data save regions for specific data table types. The data save regions are broken collectively up as a set of individually addressable data save slots (like an array in most programming languages), and a data save stack. Each data backup area can contain up to eleven separate, complete data tables of one particular type - one in the base save area, and up to ten other data tables in the data save slots or the data save stack, or in some combination of the two (save slots or stack).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver confirms all three mechanisms directly: the `$SAVE0$`-`$SAVE9$` / `$RESTORE0$`-`$RESTORE9$` slot variables and the slot-less `$SAVE$`/`$RESTORE$` pair in RIPTEL.HLP's variable tables, stack PUSH/POP via the RIPSCRIP.HLP error strings **"No slots available for PUSH"** and **"No stack to pop"**, and per-object save/restore of button styles, graphics styles, text windows, palettes, mouse fields, environments, ports, and screens. _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Each data backup area can store only one particular type of [data table](7.1-data-tables.md). For example, the color palette data backup area can only store color palette data tables (remember a color palette data table consists of 36 separate color palette definitions).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A data save slot is a backup area that is large enough to store an entire specific data table, or other object (graphics screen, mouse fields, etc). Each data backup area's save slots can hold one entire data table of the type designated for the data backup area. Each data save slot has a specific slot number associated with it (0-9). When the data in a data save slot is restored back to the actual RIPscrip drawing environment, that slot is deleted (cleared), providing that it isn't protected (see below).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A base save area is very similar to a data save slot, except that a base save area does not have a specific "slot number" associated with it. Unlike data save slots, when you restore a data table object from a base save area, the base save area is not cleared (ie, deleted) so it can be restored multiple times without losing the saved data (the base save area cannot be protected like data save slots can be - see below for more details).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Finally, we have stack save areas. Stack save areas are like a stack of plates - you put plates on top of the stack, and when you want one, you take one off the top of the stack. The plate at the bottom of the stack was the first plate placed on it, and to get to it, you need to take off each of the plates above it. When you place a data table onto a save stack, it is like placing a plate on top of our stack of plates. This is extremely useful (in fact, critical) to creating dialog boxes that overlap menus, and when you close the dialog box, you restore the menu's environment. The act of placing a data table onto a data save stack is called "pushing" a table onto the stack. The act of removing a table from the top of the stack is called "popping" a table from the stack. In order to remember where the "top" of the stack is (ie, how many layers are on the stack), a thing called a "stack pointer" is maintained internally which is simply a count of the number of items on the stack. Each time you add a new data table onto the stack, the pointer is increased by one (we have one more item on the stack).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: You can think of data tables and the data backup area conceptually in the following diagram:
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Notice how there are ten different data save slots, and ten different data save stack "locations". What this means is that individually, either one of these may hold ten complete data tables. But combined, they cannot both contain more than 10 complete data tables. What this means is that you can have 4 separate tables saved in the data save slots, and 6 data tables pushed onto the stack, but then you wouldn't be able to store one more data table into an "open" data save slot, or push it onto the save stack (the slot/stack system is effectively "full"). The diagram above shows a completely empty data backup area.
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.text: Let's take an example. Let's say we have tables saved to data save slots 1, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9 (six tables total), we could envision our data slot/stack areas like this (we have nothing on the stack yet in this example, so our stack pointer is 0, or pointing to the first stack entry which is open for filling):

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: We now have nine data tables stored in our data slot/stack system. We can only hold one more. If one more is pushed onto the stack, we would have the following:
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Our stack system is now full. We have four items on our stack and six in our data save slots. If we tried to push another data table onto our stack, the operation would be ignored (an error because our slot/stack system is full - the 3.0 driver's "No slots available for PUSH"). If we tried to store a data table to data save slot #2 (which is currently open), it would also be ignored because the slot/stack system is full. If however, we tried to save a data table onto data save slot #3 (which is occupied), the operation would be performed providing that data save slot #3 is not protected (see below).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A stack restore (also known as a "pop") is a method of restoring a data object from the data save stack into a data table. When you perform a stack pop, the data table at the top of the stack (the entry just below the stack pointer) is removed from the stack and placed in the appropriate data table (which one is based on the type of data that is stored in the data backup area). Once the restore operation is complete, the entry in that location of the stack is deleted (cleared), and the stack pointer is decremented by one, thus making room for one more entry in the data save slot/stack system to hold a new data table. (Popping an empty stack is an error - the 3.0 driver's "No stack to pop".)
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Each data backup area maintains its own stack pointer. Each backup area's stack pointer is unique and completely unrelated to the stack pointers of other backup areas. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: The base data save area is provided as a "temporary" storage location for data tables. The slot/stack system is designed for more permanent storage of tables.
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: All totalled, a data backup area can store eleven separate data tables, and each data table in a data backup area is of the same type of information (eg, text window, color palette, etc). If a data table has 36 separate data table entries in it, then a data backup area for that data table would hold 396 separate data table entries in it! This makes for a lot of backup storage. You cannot individually access sub-elements of a data table inside of a data backup area - you can only save/restore "entire" data tables at any one moment.
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Push and pop operations are vital to the concept of multiple overlapping windows and dialog boxes in RIPscrip. When you close a window, you need to restore the background graphics, mouse regions, text windows and any other data tables that were in use at the time the dialog/window was created. What if that restored background is itself a window that is on top of some background menu? That window would also have tables pushed (the background environment). When that window closes, it will pop the information and restore the background environment's configuration.

requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The Fourteen Copy Paths
requirements.text: There are fourteen distinctly separate ways of copying data tables/objects around. They are depicted in the following diagram and described in more detail immediately below:
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: The Fourteen Copy Paths
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: The Fourteen Copy Paths
requirements.text:
1. Copy a data table to the base save area
2. Copy the base save area to the data table
3. Copy a data table to a data save slot
4. Copy a data save slot to a data table
5. Push a data table onto the stack
6. Pop a data table from the stack into a data table
7. Copy one entry of a data table over another entry in the same table
8. Copy a data save slot to the base save area
9. Copy the base save area to a data save slot
10. Push the base save area onto the stack
11. Pop from the stack into the base save area
12. Push a data save slot onto the stack
13. Pop from the stack into a data save slot
14. Copy a data save slot to another data save slot
requirements.reason: Core base/slot/stack table save/restore exists for palette snapshots. Remaining backup-to-backup/multiple-destination copies, other object classes and variable orchestration are pending; no complete fourteen-copy-path claim.

requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._
requirements.reason: Layout, provenance, motivation or illustration of the separately tracked backup lifecycle/capacity operations.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: The way that a stack operates has been clearly outlined in the previous section. When you store a data table onto the stack, it grows by one table. When you pop a data table off of the stack, you reduce the contents of the stack by one data table (ie, that data table is deleted from the stack).
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: The base save area has already been described as a temporary storage location. A data table in the base save area remains in the base save area until it is either explicitly deleted, or until a hard reset of the RIPscrip environment is performed. In this manner, the base save area can be used as a source of data table copy operations many times and still read the same data table.
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: When you restore a data table from a data save slot back into the actual data table on the other hand, that data save slot is deleted (cleared) unless it is protected from deletion. In other words, just like individual data table entries, you can individually protect data save slots from deletion or overwriting. Only a data save slot that is actually "in use" can be protected - it is pointless to protect a data save slot that isn't holding a data table because what would you do with it? You couldn't store anything in it and you couldn't read anything from it, so this situation is not allowed.
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: There are only three ways of deleting or modifying a protected data save slot (two of which involve manually unprotecting the slot):
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text:
1. Explicitly unprotect the slot and then overwrite or delete it.
2. Explicitly unprotect the slot then copy the data table from it to the actual data table designed to work with that data. This deletes the contents of the slot once the copy operation is complete.
3. Perform a hard reset of the RIPscrip environment.
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: The base save area cannot be protected and neither can the data save stack. Protection goes against the very nature of these two backup areas.
requirements.reason: Owned backup-area lifecycle and capacity with clone/restore callbacks, independently tested ownership/failure paths and an actual complete palette-table adapter. Other object-class adapters and wire/text-variable orchestration remain separate pending requirements.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: It should be noted that when a data table is stored in the data backup area, any of the entries in that data table "retain" their protection status! This means that if you restore a data table from the backup area and put it back into action, the protection status of each entry in the table is restored as well.
requirements.reason: Core base/slot/stack table save/restore exists for palette snapshots. Remaining backup-to-backup/multiple-destination copies, other object classes and variable orchestration are pending; no complete fourteen-copy-path claim.

requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: You cannot protect an entire data table. This means that if you have entries in a data table that are protected and you perform a restore operation from a backup area, this will override any individual entries in the data table with those stored in the actual data table in the backup area. This is the only way that a data table entry's protection status can be bypassed.
requirements.reason: Core base/slot/stack table save/restore exists for palette snapshots. Remaining backup-to-backup/multiple-destination copies, other object classes and variable orchestration are pending; no complete fourteen-copy-path claim.

requirements.heading: Individual Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: There are data backup areas for the following types of information (not all of them are normal data tables per se): _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Individual Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Host commands drive these areas through the save/restore [text-variable](../../glossary.md) families in [5.1](5.1-text-variables.md#data-table-and-backup-area-text-variables) - `$SAVE$`/`$RESTORE$`, `$SAVE0$`-`$SAVE9$`/`$RESTORE0$`-`$RESTORE9$` and `$SAVEALL$`/`$RESTOREALL$` (graphics screen), `$SGS$`/`$RGS$` (graphics styles), `$SBS$`/`$RBS$` (button styles), `$STW$`/`$RTW$` (text windows), `$SCP$`/`$RCP$` (palettes), `$SMF$`/`$RMF$` (mouse fields), `$SCB$`/`$RCB$` (clipboard), `$SENV$`/`$RENV$` (environments) - plus the generic [`$COPY$`](5.1-text-variables.md#copy) and status queries [`$BACKSTAT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#backstat) and [`$INUSE$`](5.1-text-variables.md#inuse).

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table Save Area
requirements.text: A backup area that stores all currently defined simple mouse fields and mouse button fields currently active on the screen. The mouse field boundaries and any mouse button configuration data is stored. Mouse fields do not have a directly accessible data table. In other words, you cannot directly protect a specific entry in the mouse field data table. The mouse field data table is different than normal data tables in that they can have up to 128 separate table entries and are not directly accessible like other simpler data tables like graphical style data tables, etc. When a mouse button definition is restored, the graphics displayed for a button are not restored - only the internal mouse button field definitions are restored. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Screen Save Area
requirements.text: The screen save area is a special data backup area. The screen backup area has no real data table related to it, although you could think of it as a data table of video scan lines where each entry in the data table is one scan line of graphical data. The data save slots and the base save area of the screen backup area each contain a complete bitmap representation of a graphical screen, and its associated color palette. This backup area embodies some of the concepts of the drawing port backup area when it stores a Clipboard Port and also parts of the color palette backup area. This backup area allows you to have up to eleven separately saved graphical screens. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: Every command of the reconstructed RIPscrip 3.x inventory with its [command level](../../glossary.md), command type character, argument summary, lineage/evidence status, and one-line purpose, each symbol linked to its full entry.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: Argument notation follows [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#how-commands-are-documented): `name:width` fields are fixed-width numbers in the current [Base Math](../../glossary.md); `:XY` marks a variable-width coordinate (2 digits by default, adjustable via [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size)); `:CM` marks a color parameter that follows the current color mode; `text`/`filename` is a trailing text parameter; `...` marks variable-length commands; `<esc>` denotes the actual Escape character (ASCII 27).

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: TeleGrafix never published a 3.x language reference, so this inventory is an editorial reconstruction assembled from the 2.00 ALPHA 4 specification, the RIPSCRIP.HLP command-name inventory (~90 `RIP_*` names recovered from the RIPtel 3.1 help files and DLL string tables), the 116-script RIPtel demo corpus, and SyncTERM's open-source RIP 3.0 implementation - the **Added/Status** column carries both lineage and evidence status per the legend below.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: **Added/Status legend:**

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text:
- blank - carried from 1.54 or earlier into the 2.0 engine that 3.x inherits.
- `v1.54`, `v2.A0`-`v2.A4` - spec revision that introduced the command (2.00 ALPHA draft revisions; 3.x inherits the 2.0 engine).
- `3.0 (corpus)` - 3.x-era command recovered from the RIPtel demo-script census; documented in no published specification.
- `3.0 (HLP; corpus)` - 3.x-era command attested by the RIPSCRIP.HLP name inventory and the corpus, absent from the 2.00a4 draft.
- `HLP only` - named in the RIPSCRIP.HLP command-name inventory but with no observed wire syntax, no known opcode, and no implementation; listed unlinked (no full entry exists).
- `SyncTERM only` - known only from SyncTERM's descriptor table or source code; no spec, HLP, or corpus attestation; listed unlinked where no full entry exists.
- `deprecated v2.A2` - deprecated in that revision; still implemented by every shipping driver, so authors should avoid it and implementers still have to handle it. The linked page explains why.
- `obsolete v2.A1` - declared obsolete in that revision but still parsed by clients.
- (\*), (†), (‡), (§), (¶) - footnotes for special cases, listed [at the end of the page](#footnotes).

requirements.heading: Footnotes
requirements.text:
- (\*) The 2.00a4 draft assigns letter `b` to **both** RIP_SET_BASE_MATH and RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW - an unresolved collision in the draft. The shipping 3.0 driver moved base math to **`J`** (90 of 116 corpus files open with `!|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO`, and ONLINE.RIP annotates `J10` inline as "Set base math to MegaNums"), leaving `b` to the extended text window, exactly as SyncTERM's descriptor table also has it. _Evidence: corpus; SyncTERM._
- (†) The command name is an editorial hypothesis reconstructed from census evidence (demo comments, on-screen titles, or layout analysis); TeleGrafix's own name is unrecovered. The six skewed-oval names, by contrast, come verbatim from TeleGrafix's NEWCMDS.RIP comments and are not so marked; RIP_POLY_POLYGON's name is taken from its demo's own on-screen title _(hypothesis)_.
- (‡) The RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory lists this command under the 3.0 name `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`, and its error strings reference "encoded stream" file types - the mechanism survived into 3.x under the new name.
- (§) For `HLP only` names the level shown is inferred from the name's grouping in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory _(hypothesis)_; no opcode, wire syntax, or implementation is recovered, so these rows are unlinked (no full entry exists in this reference).
- (¶) The 3.x wire layout of RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE (26 fixed digits + font name, per TeleGrafix's crib `!|!sfFFFFZZOOSSCCBBCCWWRRRRRR` in FONTS.RIP) does **not** match the 2.00a4 draft's 13-character argument list, and field roles beyond the crib are _(hypothesis)_ - see the full entry. The rework predates 3.x: RIPterm Professional 2.0's SHADOW.RIP already drives `y` with the 26-character block.

requirements.heading: Announced but never specified
requirements.text: **RIP_FILE_DELETE** appears in the 2.00a4 v2.A3 revision history ("to remove unneeded JPEG or WAVE files off the user's hard disk") but received no command entry, opcode or argument list, and no such command name appears in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory. The capability is implemented as a text variable instead: `RIPSCRIP.HLP` carries the handler symbol `tvarProcFILEDEL` (the `tvarProc` prefix marking a text-variable processor), and `FILEDEL` is present in the shipping RIPterm 2.0/2.20.01/2.30 executables. Hosts use [`$FILEDEL(file,…)$`](9.1-text-variable-reference.md); see [5.5](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: Every pre-defined [text variable](../../glossary.md) known for RIPscrip 3.x, with its parameter form, type, effect, and evidence status, linked to its full entry. **Value** variables return text to the host; **Active** variables perform an action on the terminal (some also return data when used to query). Parameters shown in parentheses are optional unless the full entry says otherwise; the 2.0 parameterized forms supersede the 1.54 fixed names (`$SAVE(8)$` vs `$SAVE8$`). The 3.x inventory is triangulated from the RIPtel help files (roughly 60 data-returning and 60 command-performing variables), the demo corpus (269 distinct `$…$` forms in shipping scripts), and SyncTERM's 103-entry built-in table.

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: _User-defined variables - any `$IDENTIFIER$` with the `*`/`+`/`%`/`#`/`-`/`&` directives, positioning, questions, defaults and format options - are covered in [5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md#text-variable-creation-and-query); variables removed or renamed since 1.54 are listed in [5.1's rename note](5.1-text-variables.md)._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: The **Evidence** column uses the legend tags in compact form: `2.00a4` (documented in the published ALPHA 4 specification, which 3.x inherits), `WP` (3.0 white paper), `HLP` (RIPtel help / DLL string tables), `corpus` (RIPtel demo scripts), `ST` (SyncTERM implementation), _(hyp)_ (editorial inference). File names, `ripper.c` line numbers and divergence notes live on the full entries. A variable tagged only `2.00a4` is listed as inherited - documented for the engine 3.x inherits, with no independent 3.x-era attestation.
